media.caption: 正门。瓦斯涅佐夫设计的立面像一座古罗斯木头楼阁，正中嵌着莫斯科城徽上的圣乔治屠龙浮雕
进门先上一段铺红毯的楼梯，展厅从二楼的 18 世纪开始
列宾《伊凡雷帝杀子》，1885 年。暴怒的沙皇失手打死儿子，抱着他瞪大眼睛。这幅画先后两次被人袭击，1913 年被划了刀，2018 年又被人用金属杆砸坏玻璃，现在前面隔着护栏
克拉姆斯柯依《无名女郎》，1883 年。国内很多人认识这幅，但画上到底是谁，一百多年了也没人说得清
列维茨基《叶卡捷琳娜二世：正义女神神庙里的立法者》。女皇往祭坛上烧罂粟花，罂粟代表睡眠，意思是为了国家牺牲自己的安宁，很典型的宫廷宣传画
伊万·阿尔古诺夫《垂死的克娄巴特拉》，1750 年。阿尔古诺夫是舍列梅捷夫伯爵家的农奴画家，胸口那条小蛇就是故事的结局
费奥多尔·阿列克谢耶夫《莫斯科红场》，1801 年。他被叫作“俄国的卡纳莱托”，两百多年前的红场，瓦西里升天大教堂和斯帕斯塔都还认得出来
还是阿列克谢耶夫，《从彼得保罗要塞看宫廷沿岸街》，1794 年。对岸那一排里就有冬宫，和上一篇正好呼应
基普连斯基《戴罂粟花环的女孩》，1819 年在意大利画的。小姑娘的眼神有点警惕，不太像在乖乖当模特
基普连斯基《茹科夫斯基像》，1816 年。茹科夫斯基是诗人，也是普希金的前辈和朋友，背后阴沉的天和废墟是浪漫主义的标配
亚历山大·伊万诺夫《基督显现于民众》。画了二十年，宽七米多，画廊专门给它留了一个厅，站远了才看得全
普基廖夫《不相称的婚姻》，1862 年。年迈的官员娶年轻的新娘，新娘眼睛都哭红了。传说右边抱着胳膊瞪着他们的年轻人，就是画家本人
弗拉维茨基《塔拉卡诺娃公主》，1864 年。传说这个自称女皇之女的女人被关在彼得保罗要塞，大水灌进牢房，老鼠往床上爬。其实她在洪水前就病死了，但这个版本流传最广
费奥多尔·瓦西里耶夫《解冻》，1871 年。画这幅的时候他才二十一岁，两年后就死于肺结核。灰蒙蒙的一片，越看越冷
艾瓦佐夫斯基《彩虹》，1873 年。他一辈子画了六千多幅海，这幅一反常态，几乎全是浅色，彩虹淡到要找一下
弗鲁贝尔厅里的釉陶面具。弗鲁贝尔在阿布拉姆采沃的陶瓷作坊里做过不少这种东西，卷曲的头发像海浪
弗鲁贝尔《梦幻公主》，1896 年为下诺夫哥罗德博览会画的大幅装饰画，当年被评委会拒收，现在一整面墙都是它
弗鲁贝尔的《浮士德》三联画，1896 年给莫斯科一位富商宅邸里的哥特式书房画的
列宾《亚历山大三世在彼得罗夫宫庭院接见乡长》，1886 年。一院子的农民代表，表情各不相同，是列宾很擅长的群像
苏里科夫《近卫军临刑的早晨》，1881 年。1698 年近卫军叛乱后，彼得大帝在红场处决叛军，右边骑马的就是彼得。整幅画没有画行刑，只画了行刑前的那一刻
苏里科夫《缅希科夫在别廖佐沃》，1883 年。彼得大帝的头号宠臣失势后被流放西伯利亚，一家人挤在小木屋里。有人说要是缅希科夫站起来，头会撞到天花板
韦列夏金《帖木儿的门》，1872 年。雕花大门前站着两个守卫，背对着我们，门里是什么谁也看不到
韦列夏金《战败者·安魂祭》，1878–1879 年。俄土战争后，神父在一片铺满阵亡士兵的荒原上做祷告。韦列夏金自己上过战场，最后也死在战舰上
瓦斯涅佐夫《伊万王子骑灰狼》，1889 年。俄罗斯童话里的经典场景，画家就是设计画廊正门的那位
希施金《橡树林中的雨》，1891 年。希施金以画森林出名，这幅里的雨雾把远处的人和树都化开了
安托科尔斯基的大理石雕像《伊凡雷帝》。和列宾那幅放在一起看，是同一个沙皇的两种样子
雅罗申科《处处有生活》，1888 年。囚车的铁窗后面，一家人在给站台上的鸽子撒面包屑
克拉姆斯柯依《月夜》，1880 年。白衣女子坐在夜里的长椅上，整幅画都是凉凉的月光
克拉姆斯柯依《荒野中的基督》，1872 年。没有光环、没有神迹，就是一个人坐在石头上想事情
克拉姆斯柯依《五月之夜（美人鱼）》，1871 年，取材于果戈理的小说，月光下的水边坐着一群溺水姑娘变成的美人鱼
《非人手所造的救主》，12 世纪诺夫哥罗德的圣像，是馆里最古老的一批藏品之一，单独放在暗处的玻璃柜里
布拉兹《契诃夫像》，1898 年。契诃夫本人不太喜欢，说自己在画里的表情像刚闻了辣根
出门后旁边的新楼，外墙上印着馆藏画作的放大复制，看着像是彼得罗夫-沃德金的《浴红马》

stories.title: 圣彼得堡：一座用意志造出来的城
stories.titleEn: Saint Petersburg, a city built on will
stories.text:
在俄罗斯这一年多，去过不少城市，最喜欢的始终是圣彼得堡。一月和七月各去了一趟：一次大雪，白天短得只剩六个小时；一次白夜，太阳落下去没多久就又升起来。同一座城，两副面孔，底下是同一个灵魂。

[图]

## 一　沼泽上的意志

圣彼得堡不是自然长出来的城市，是一个人硬生生“想”出来的。1703 年 5 月，北方战争打到第三年，彼得一世刚从瑞典人手里夺下涅瓦河口，就在河口一座叫兔子岛的小岛上动工修建要塞，也就是今天的彼得保罗要塞，这一天被算作这座城的生日。那里原本是芬兰湾尽头的一片沼泽，地势低洼，常年潮湿，冬天封冻，秋天发洪水，任何一个正常的君主都不会把城建在这儿。但彼得要的就是这片水：俄罗斯没有一个像样的、通向欧洲的出海口，他要在这里造船、建海军，用后来普希金的话说，“打开一扇通向欧洲的窗”。

[图]

代价是惊人的。成千上万的农奴、士兵和瑞典战俘被征调过来，在泥水里打桩、挖渠、填地，死于寒冷、疾病和劳累的人不计其数，民间一直有“这座城建在白骨上”的说法。为了让城快点立起来，彼得下令全国其他地方一律不准盖石头房子，石匠只能来彼得堡干活；进城的大车和船只还得按规定捎上几块石头，算是“入城税”。1712 年前后，他干脆把首都从莫斯科迁了过来，逼着贵族们搬家、剃胡子、穿欧式衣服、学跳舞。圣彼得堡从诞生那天起，就是一座带着强烈意志的城市：它不顺应自然，而是和自然、和旧俄罗斯对着干。

[图]

1709 年波尔塔瓦一战，彼得大败瑞典国王卡尔十二世，北方战争的胜负从此定了下来。1735 年，为了纪念这场大胜，城西彼得霍夫夏宫的大瀑布中央立起了一尊镀金的参孙像，参孙双手撕开狮子的嘴：狮子是瑞典国徽上的动物，而波尔塔瓦会战那天正好是圣参孙节。彼得霍夫常被叫作“俄罗斯的凡尔赛”，宫殿正对着芬兰湾，彼得当年就在这里看他的舰队。二战时德军占领了这里，宫殿被烧成空壳，参孙像也不知所踪，今天看到的几乎都是战后一点点照原样复原的。冬天喷泉全部停了，园子里只剩下雪，金色的雕像在一片白里反倒更亮。

[图]

[图]

此后两百年，彼得堡一直是俄罗斯帝国的首都，也是一座革命的城市。1825 年十二月党人在枢密院广场起事；1881 年亚历山大二世在运河边被炸身亡；1905 年请愿的工人在冬宫前被枪杀，史称“流血星期日”；1917 年，二月革命推翻了沙皇，十月里阿芙乐尔号巡洋舰的一声空炮，成了攻打冬宫的信号。城市的名字也跟着时代换了好几次：一战时嫌“堡”字太像德语，改叫彼得格勒；1924 年列宁去世，改叫列宁格勒；1991 年市民投票，又改回圣彼得堡。不过本地人最常挂在嘴边的，还是那个亲昵的简称：“皮特”。

[图]

## 二　列宁格勒的 872 天

1941 年 9 月 8 日，德军攻占了拉多加湖边的什利谢利堡，列宁格勒和外界的陆路联系被彻底切断。围困从那天开始，一直到 1944 年 1 月 27 日才完全解除，整整 872 天。希特勒的打算不是攻进城，而是把它围死，让这座城连同城里的人一起从地图上消失。

第一个冬天最难熬。没有暖气，没有电，没有自来水，气温跌到零下三十度。1941 年 11 月下旬，面包配给降到最低点：工人每天 250 克，职员、家属和孩子只有 125 克，而那块“面包”里还掺着大量纤维素、麸皮和别的东西。人们煮皮带，刮墙纸上的浆糊，街上不时有人倒下就再也没起来，用雪橇拖着裹布的遗体去墓地，是那年冬天最常见的画面。十一岁的女孩塔尼娅·萨维切娃在一个小本子上，一页一页记下家人去世的日期，最后几页只写着：萨维切夫一家死了，全都死了，只剩下塔尼娅一个。她后来被疏散出城，但也没能活下来。围困期间死去的平民，各方估计从六十多万到一百多万不等，绝大多数死于饥饿。

维系这座城的，是冰上的“生命之路”：拉多加湖封冻以后，卡车冒着炮火和随时可能裂开的冰面，把粮食运进来，把老人和孩子运出去。而让这座城在精神上没有垮掉的，是一些今天听起来近乎不可思议的事。城里的广播几乎从没断过，没有节目的时候，喇叭里就放节拍器的声音，告诉大家城市还活着；诗人奥莉加·别尔戈利茨每天在电台里念诗。冬宫的工作人员把一百多万件藏品疏散到乌拉尔，自己留下来住在地下室，守着一屋子空画框，据说还给前线来的士兵对着空画框“讲解”上面原本挂着什么画。1942 年 8 月 9 日，肖斯塔科维奇的《第七交响曲》在被围困的城里演出，乐团是临时拼凑的，有乐手在排练期间饿死，演出通过扩音器对着德军阵地播放。据说多年以后，一位当年的德国士兵说，听到音乐的那一刻，他就知道这座城是拿不下了。

[图]

1945 年，列宁格勒成为第一批被称作“英雄城市”的城市。今天起义广场边那栋酒店的楼顶，每晚还亮着“英雄城市列宁格勒”几个大字；涅瓦大街 14 号的墙上，保留着当年的白底蓝字：“公民们！炮击时，街道这一侧最危险。”城北的皮斯卡廖夫公墓里，埋着约五十万围城死难者，纪念墙上刻着别尔戈利茨的诗句：“谁也没有被忘记，什么也没有被忘记。”每年 1 月 27 日，总有人去那里献花，有人还会放下一小块黑面包。

[图]

要理解圣彼得堡人，得先理解这 872 天。这座城挨过饿，失去了上百万人，却始终没有投降，也没有放弃那些“没用”的东西：诗、音乐、博物馆、体面。我觉得这就是这座城的精神内核，一种骄傲的、近乎固执的尊严。帝国的辉煌是它的外衣，这份在废墟里也要守住的东西，才是它的骨头。

## 三　圣彼得堡人

莫斯科人和彼得堡人互相看不顺眼是出了名的。俄罗斯有一大堆关于两座城的段子：同一样东西两边叫法都不一样，路缘石莫斯科叫 бордюр，彼得堡偏叫 поребрик；楼门洞莫斯科叫 подъезд，彼得堡叫 парадная；连街边的卷饼，一边叫 шаурма，一边叫 шаверма。有句老话说，莫斯科是俄罗斯的心脏，彼得堡是俄罗斯的头脑。莫斯科人嫌彼得堡人清高、慢吞吞、穷讲究；彼得堡人嫌莫斯科人眼里只有钱、太浮躁。彼得堡人很乐意把自己的城叫作“文化首都”，说话慢条斯理，用词考究，连排队都比莫斯科从容。

我的感受是，彼得堡人身上有一种很特别的自由。这种自由不张扬，是一种“我就这样”的松弛：穿什么都行，留什么头发都行，在河堤上坐一整晚也行，没人多看你一眼。街头艺人比莫斯科多得多，涅瓦大街上拉琴的、弹吉他的、敲木琴的、唱摇滚的，从下午一直演到后半夜。这里也是苏联摇滚的老家：1981 年列宁格勒摇滚俱乐部成立，“电影”乐队的维克多·崔、“水族馆”的格列本希科夫都是从这座城走出去的，崔还在一间叫“堪察加”的锅炉房里当过锅炉工，一边烧锅炉一边写歌。直到今天，这里的年轻人还是比别处更爱地下音乐、独立书店、老房子里的小酒吧和屋顶。

[图]

[图]

夏天的彼得堡是另一个世界。五月底到七月中是白夜，最亮的六月下旬，太阳晚上十点多才落，凌晨三点多又升起来，中间那几个小时天也不会真正黑下去，只是变成一种淡淡的蓝。整座城像是集体失眠：半夜十二点，河堤上坐满了人，喝酒的、弹琴的、接吻的，游船一艘接一艘从桥下穿过。凌晨一点多，涅瓦河上的桥一座接一座升起来给货船让路，岸边挤满了等着看开桥的人，桥面立起来的那一刻掌声和欢呼声一片；错过最后一班桥的人，就只能在对岸等到天亮。六月底还有“红帆节”，一艘挂着红帆的船在烟花里驶过涅瓦河，给中学毕业生庆祝。

[图]

[图]

七月那趟，正赶上午夜的宫廷桥白夜马拉松。几千人从涅瓦河边、从冬宫前跑过，路灯开着，天却没黑，路边的人喊着加油，跑者冲着镜头挥手、张开双臂，像过节一样。那几天我几乎没怎么睡，天一直亮着，总觉得睡觉是一种浪费。

[图]

[图]

白天去城西的芬兰湾边，又是另一种安静。有人赤脚走进凉凉的海水，有人在礁石上一坐就是一整个傍晚，沙滩上的石头被人一块块垒成小塔。波罗的海的水是灰蓝色的，不算好看，但很安静。

[图]

冬天则完全反过来。十二月最短的时候，白天不到六个小时，上午十点天才亮，下午四点就黑了，大多数日子天空是一整片灰。一月那趟正好赶上东正教圣诞节，大雪下了好几天，芬兰湾冻成了一望无际的冰原，有人支着小马扎在冰上凿洞钓鱼，有人就那么一个人慢慢走向白茫茫的中央。孩子们在雪地里打滚，大狗跟着一起疯；教堂里挤满来做圣诞礼拜的人，烛光一片。冬天的彼得堡是安静的、向内的，也是最“彼得堡”的。

[图]

[图]

[图]

彼得堡常被说成是俄罗斯最“欧洲”的城市，这话不假。街道的尺度、运河、咖啡馆、讲究的年轻人、对艺术和个人空间的尊重，都让人恍惚觉得是在阿姆斯特丹或者巴黎。但待久了会发现，它和西欧终究不一样。这里的天太低，冬天太长，历史太重。普希金写过在洪水里失去一切、最后发了疯的小职员，果戈里写过丢了外套就郁郁而终的小人物，陀思妥耶夫斯基让他的主人公在干草广场边的阁楼里发着高烧，还说这是全世界最抽象、最“蓄意”的城市。彼得堡人身上有一抹很淡的悲情：热闹的时候也带着一点清醒，狂欢的时候也知道狂欢会结束。白夜之所以疯得那么彻底，大概正是因为每个人都记得，冬天很快就会回来。

[图]

诗人布罗茨基被苏联驱逐出境，到死也没再回来，年轻时却写过：不选国家也不选墓地，要回瓦西里岛去死。很多彼得堡人对这座城的感情大概就是这样：抱怨它的天气、它的潮湿、它的不如意，但它是唯一的那一个。

[图]

## 四　石头写成的城

彼得堡是一座规划出来的城市。它没有莫斯科那种一圈套一圈、层层叠加的混乱，街道笔直，广场开阔，建筑沿着河岸整整齐齐地排开。彼得请来了意大利、法国、德国的建筑师，此后两百年里，特雷齐尼、拉斯特雷利、夸伦吉、罗西、蒙费朗……一代代人在这里把巴洛克、古典主义和帝国风格做到了极致。罗西设计的那条街，宽 22 米，两边楼高 22 米，长 220 米，比例严丝合缝。更关键的是，1844 年起城里有一条执行得很严的规矩：民用建筑不能高过冬宫。于是整座城的天际线几乎是平的，只有教堂的穹顶和海军部、彼得保罗大教堂的金色尖顶刺出来，站在高处看，像一片安静的石头海。

[图]

圣以撒大教堂是这片石头海里最大的那块。法国建筑师蒙费朗为它花了整整 40 年（1818—1858），一百多根整块花岗岩的柱子是从芬兰湾对岸的采石场运来的，金顶据说用掉了一百多公斤黄金。苏联时期它当过“无神论博物馆”，穹顶下还挂过傅科摆。爬上柱廊，整个市中心都在脚下：海军部的金针、冬宫、彼得保罗要塞，还有远处海边的拉赫塔中心。

[图]

和周围的欧式建筑格格不入的，是滴血救世主教堂。1881 年，亚历山大二世在格里博耶多夫运河边被民意党人的炸弹炸成重伤，当天就去世了，他的儿子在遇刺的地方盖起这座教堂，用的是莫斯科式的洋葱顶和彩砖。里面几乎每一寸墙面都是马赛克，加起来有七千多平方米。冬天傍晚亮灯以后，它在雪里像一则童话。

[图]

涅瓦大街是城市的主轴，一头是海军部，一头是亚历山大·涅夫斯基修道院。喀山大教堂仿照罗马圣彼得大教堂修了一道半圆形的柱廊，打败拿破仑的统帅库图佐夫就葬在里面；斜对面的胜家大楼，楼顶托着一只玻璃地球仪，原本是美国胜家缝纫机公司的办公楼，现在是城里最有名的书店“百年书屋”。新年前后，整条大街挂满了灯，从高处往下看，是一条发光的河。

[图]

[图]

再往城里走，有蓝色穹顶上撒满金星的伊兹梅洛夫斯基圣三一大教堂，有拉斯特雷利设计的蓝白色斯莫尔尼大教堂，还有运河上一座接一座的小桥，“北方威尼斯”的名字不是白叫的。格里博耶多夫运河一路弯到干草广场，那里就是《罪与罚》的地盘：拉斯柯尔尼科夫从他的阁楼走到放高利贷的老太婆家，书里写着，不多不少七百三十步。

[图]

艺术在这里不是装饰，是空气。冬宫里有三百万件藏品，俄罗斯博物馆里挂着列宾和艾瓦佐夫斯基，马林斯基剧院首演过《睡美人》和《胡桃夹子》。普希金、果戈里、陀思妥耶夫斯基、阿赫玛托娃、纳博科夫、布罗茨基，柴可夫斯基、里姆斯基-科萨科夫、肖斯塔科维奇……俄罗斯文化史上差不多一半的名字，都和这座城连在一起。

[图]

七月那趟我去了涅瓦大街尽头的亚历山大·涅夫斯基修道院，墓园里走一圈就是一部人物志，陀思妥耶夫斯基、柴可夫斯基、穆索尔斯基都葬在这里。我在一块花岗岩墓前停下，牌子上写着“Л. ЭЙЛЕР 1707—1783”，是数学家欧拉，他前后在彼得堡科学院工作了三十多年，最后也在这里去世。不远处还有一块刻着汉字的墓碑，是俄国汉学的奠基人比丘林，也就是雅金甫神父，他在北京住了十几年，把很多中国典籍第一次译成俄文。在俄罗斯的墓园里读到“無時勤勞 垂光史冊”八个字，感觉很奇妙。

[图]

唯一冲破这条天际线的，是 2019 年建成的拉赫塔中心，462 米，欧洲最高楼。它原本打算盖在市中心对岸，因为会破坏历史天际线，被市民和联合国教科文组织一路反对，最后只好挪到城市西北的海边。我挺喜欢这个结局：这座城愿意接纳新的东西，前提是别碰它的老规矩。

[图]

说到底，圣彼得堡是一座“本不该存在”的城市：建在沼泽上，冬天漫长又黑暗，被围困到几乎死绝，却一直站在那里，美得那么用力。它有欧洲的骨架，俄罗斯的灵魂，还有一种只属于它自己的、带着悲伤的骄傲。每次离开，我都觉得自己还会回来。

[图]
stories.textEn:
In more than a year in Russia I have been to a lot of cities, and Saint Petersburg is still my favourite. I went once in January and once in July: one trip buried in snow, with barely six hours of daylight; the other in the white nights, when the sun goes down and is back up again almost before you notice. Same city, two faces, one soul underneath. I want to write about it properly: first where it came from, then the people who live there, and finally its buildings and its art.

[图]

## I. Willpower on a swamp

Saint Petersburg did not grow on its own. One man willed it into existence. In May 1703, three years into the Great Northern War, Peter I had just taken the mouth of the Neva from the Swedes, and he began building a fortress on a small island there called Hare Island. That fortress is today's Peter and Paul Fortress, and that day counts as the city's birthday. The place was a swamp at the far end of the Gulf of Finland: low, wet all year, frozen in winter, flooded in autumn. No sensible ruler would have put a city there. But the water was exactly what Peter wanted. Russia had no proper sea gate to Europe, so he would build ships and a navy here, and, as Pushkin later put it, cut a window through to Europe.

[图]

The cost was staggering. Tens of thousands of serfs, soldiers and Swedish prisoners of war were brought in to drive piles, dig canals and fill land in the mud. Countless people died of cold, disease and exhaustion, and people still say the city was built on bones. To get it up faster, Peter banned stone construction everywhere else in the country, so stonemasons had nowhere to work but Petersburg, and every cart and ship entering the city had to bring a few stones as a kind of entry tax. Around 1712 he simply moved the capital here from Moscow and made the nobility relocate, shave their beards, dress like Europeans and learn to dance. From its first day, Petersburg was a city of sheer will: it did not adapt to nature, it fought against nature and against old Russia.

[图]

In 1709, at Poltava, Peter crushed Charles XII of Sweden, and the war was effectively decided. In 1735, to mark the victory, a gilded Samson tearing open a lion's jaws was set up in the middle of the Grand Cascade at Peterhof, west of the city. The lion was the beast on the Swedish coat of arms, and the battle of Poltava had fallen on St Samson's day. Peterhof is often called the Russian Versailles. The palace faces the Gulf of Finland, and Peter used to watch his fleet from here. In the Second World War the Germans occupied it, the palace was burnt to a shell and the Samson vanished; almost everything you see today was painstakingly rebuilt after the war. In winter the fountains are all switched off, the gardens are nothing but snow, and the gold statues shine even brighter against all that white.

[图]

[图]

For the next two hundred years Petersburg was the capital of the Russian Empire, and it was also a city of revolutions. In 1825 the Decembrists rose on Senate Square. In 1881 Alexander II was killed by a bomb beside a canal. In 1905 petitioning workers were shot in front of the Winter Palace, the day remembered as Bloody Sunday. In 1917 the February Revolution brought down the tsar, and in October a blank shot from the cruiser Aurora became the signal to storm the Winter Palace. The city's name changed with the times: during the First World War "-burg" sounded too German, so it became Petrograd; after Lenin died in 1924 it became Leningrad; in 1991 residents voted and it went back to Saint Petersburg. Locals, though, mostly just call it by its fond short name, "Piter".

[图]

## II. Leningrad's 872 days

On 8 September 1941 German troops took Shlisselburg on Lake Ladoga, and Leningrad's land links with the rest of the country were cut. The siege that began that day was not fully lifted until 27 January 1944: 872 days. Hitler's plan was not to storm the city but to starve it, to wipe it off the map together with everyone in it.

The first winter was the worst. No heating, no electricity, no running water, and temperatures down to minus thirty. In late November 1941 the bread ration hit its lowest point: 250 grams a day for workers, and just 125 grams for office staff, dependants and children, and that "bread" was padded out with cellulose, bran and whatever else could be found. People boiled leather belts and scraped the paste off wallpaper. People fell in the street and never got up, and sledges dragging bodies wrapped in cloth to the cemetery were the commonest sight that winter. An eleven-year-old girl, Tanya Savicheva, wrote down in a small notebook the date each member of her family died, page after page. The last pages say only: the Savichevs are dead, they are all dead, only Tanya is left. She was later evacuated, but she did not survive either. Estimates of civilian deaths in the siege range from over six hundred thousand to more than a million, most of them from hunger.

What kept the city alive was the Road of Life across the ice: once Lake Ladoga froze, trucks drove across it under shellfire, on ice that could crack at any moment, bringing food in and taking the old and the young out. What kept the city from breaking in spirit were things that sound almost unbelievable today. The city radio hardly ever went silent; when there was nothing to broadcast, the loudspeakers played a metronome, to let people know the city was still alive. The poet Olga Berggolts read poems on the radio every day. Hermitage staff sent more than a million objects away to the Urals and stayed behind themselves, living in the basements and guarding rooms of empty frames; it is said they even gave soldiers from the front "tours" of the empty frames, describing the paintings that used to hang in them. On 9 August 1942 Shostakovich's Seventh Symphony was performed in the besieged city by a scratch orchestra, some of whose musicians starved to death during rehearsals, and it was broadcast through loudspeakers towards the German lines. Years later, so the story goes, a former German soldier said that the moment he heard the music he knew the city could not be taken.

[图]

In 1945 Leningrad was among the first cities to be called a Hero City. Today the words "Hero City Leningrad" still light up every night on the roof of the hotel on Vosstaniya Square, and on the wall of 14 Nevsky Prospekt the old blue-on-white sign is still there: "Citizens! During shelling this side of the street is the most dangerous." At Piskaryovskoye Cemetery in the north of the city lie around half a million victims of the siege, and the memorial wall carries Berggolts's line: "No one is forgotten, nothing is forgotten." Every year on 27 January people come with flowers, and some leave a small piece of black bread.

[图]

To understand the people of Petersburg you have to understand those 872 days. The city starved and lost more than a million people, yet it never surrendered, and it never gave up the "useless" things: poetry, music, museums, dignity. That, to me, is the core of the city: a proud, almost stubborn dignity. The splendour of empire is its coat; this thing it held on to even in ruins is its bones.

## III. The people of Petersburg

Muscovites and Petersburgers famously get on each other's nerves. Russia is full of jokes about the two cities. The same thing has a different name in each: a kerb is бордюр in Moscow and поребрик in Petersburg; a building entrance is подъезд in Moscow and парадная in Petersburg; even the street wrap is шаурма in one and шаверма in the other. An old saying goes that Moscow is Russia's heart and Petersburg is its head. Muscovites find Petersburgers aloof, slow and fussy; Petersburgers find Muscovites money-obsessed and restless. Petersburgers like to call their city the "cultural capital". They speak slowly, choose their words with care, and even queue more calmly than Moscow does.

What I feel in Petersburgers is a very particular kind of freedom. It is not loud; it is a relaxed "this is just how I am". Wear whatever you like, grow your hair however you like, sit on the embankment all night, and nobody looks twice. There are far more street musicians than in Moscow: violins, guitars, a xylophone, rock bands, playing along Nevsky from the afternoon well into the night. This is also the home of Soviet rock. The Leningrad Rock Club opened in 1981; Viktor Tsoi of Kino and Boris Grebenshchikov of Aquarium both came out of this city, and Tsoi worked as a stoker in a boiler room called Kamchatka, writing songs between shovelling coal. Young people here still love underground music, independent bookshops, little bars in old buildings and rooftops more than anywhere else.

[图]

[图]

Summer Petersburg is another world. From late May to mid-July are the white nights. At their brightest, in late June, the sun sets after ten in the evening and rises again after three in the morning, and in between it never really gets dark, the sky just turns a pale blue. The whole city seems to have collective insomnia. At midnight the embankments are packed: people drinking, playing guitar, kissing, while tour boats pass under the bridges one after another. After one in the morning the bridges over the Neva rise one by one to let cargo ships through, the banks crowd with people waiting to watch, and when the spans lift there is applause and cheering. Miss the last bridge and you wait on the wrong side until morning. At the end of June there is also Scarlet Sails, when a ship with red sails glides down the Neva through fireworks to celebrate school graduates.

[图]

[图]

On the July trip I happened on the midnight White Nights marathon across Palace Bridge. Thousands of runners streamed past along the Neva and in front of the Winter Palace, under lit street lamps in a sky that refused to get dark, with people cheering at the roadside and runners waving at the camera and throwing their arms wide, like a festival. I barely slept those few days. It was light all the time, and sleep felt like a waste.

[图]

[图]

By day, the Gulf of Finland on the west side of the city has a different kind of quiet. People wade barefoot into the cool water, someone sits on the rocks for a whole evening, and the stones on the beach have been stacked into little towers. The Baltic is a grey-blue, not especially pretty, but very calm.

[图]

Winter is the exact opposite. At the shortest days in December there is less than six hours of daylight: it gets light at ten and dark at four, and most days the sky is one flat grey. My January trip fell on Orthodox Christmas. It snowed for days and the Gulf of Finland froze into an endless white plain. Some people set up little stools and fished through holes in the ice; someone just walked off alone towards the middle of all that white. Children rolled in the snow with big dogs going wild beside them, and the churches were full of people at Christmas services, a sea of candles. Winter Petersburg is quiet and inward-looking, and it is the most Petersburg it ever gets.

[图]

[图]

[图]

Petersburg is often called the most European city in Russia, and that is true. The scale of the streets, the canals, the cafés, the well-dressed young people, the respect for art and personal space can make you think for a moment you are in Amsterdam or Paris. But stay longer and you realise it is not Western Europe after all. The sky here is too low, the winter too long, the history too heavy. Pushkin wrote about a little clerk who loses everything in a flood and goes mad; Gogol wrote about a little man who loses his overcoat and dies of grief; Dostoevsky has his hero lie in fever in a garret near Haymarket Square, and calls this the most abstract and premeditated city on earth. There is a faint sadness in Petersburgers: a little sobriety even in the middle of the fun, an awareness, even while celebrating, that the celebration will end. Maybe the white nights are so wild precisely because everyone remembers that winter will soon be back.

[图]

The poet Joseph Brodsky was expelled from the Soviet Union and never came back, not even at the end, yet as a young man he wrote that he would choose neither country nor graveyard, but would come to Vasilyevsky Island to die. That is probably how many Petersburgers feel about their city: they complain about its weather, its damp, its disappointments, but it is the only one.

[图]

## IV. A city written in stone

Petersburg is a planned city. It has none of Moscow's ring-within-ring, layer-upon-layer chaos: the streets are straight, the squares are wide, and the buildings line up neatly along the water. Peter brought in architects from Italy, France and Germany, and over the next two centuries Trezzini, Rastrelli, Quarenghi, Rossi, Montferrand and others took the Baroque, Neoclassicism and the Empire style about as far as they could go. The street Rossi designed is 22 metres wide, its buildings are 22 metres high, and it is 220 metres long, the proportions locked together exactly. Even more important, from 1844 the city strictly enforced a rule that no civilian building could be taller than the Winter Palace. So the skyline is almost flat, broken only by church domes and the gold spires of the Admiralty and the Peter and Paul Cathedral. From up high it looks like a quiet sea of stone.

[图]

St Isaac's Cathedral is the biggest rock in that sea. The French architect Montferrand spent forty years on it, from 1818 to 1858. More than a hundred monolithic granite columns were shipped from quarries across the Gulf of Finland, and the gilded dome is said to have taken over a hundred kilograms of gold. In Soviet times it was a Museum of Atheism, with a Foucault pendulum hanging under the dome. Climb up to the colonnade and the whole centre lies at your feet: the Admiralty spire, the Winter Palace, the Peter and Paul Fortress, and far away by the sea, the Lakhta Center.

[图]

The one building that refuses to blend in with all this European architecture is the Church of the Savior on Spilled Blood. In 1881 Alexander II was mortally wounded by a bomb thrown by revolutionaries beside the Griboyedov Canal and died the same day. His son built this church on the spot where he was attacked, with Moscow-style onion domes and coloured brick. Almost every inch inside is mosaic, more than seven thousand square metres of it. On a winter evening, once the lights come on, it looks like a fairy tale in the snow.

[图]

Nevsky Prospekt is the city's spine, with the Admiralty at one end and the Alexander Nevsky Monastery at the other. Kazan Cathedral copied the curved colonnade of St Peter's in Rome, and Kutuzov, the commander who beat Napoleon, is buried inside. Across the street, the Singer Building carries a glass globe on its roof; it was built for the American Singer sewing machine company and is now the city's best-known bookshop, Dom Knigi. Around New Year the whole avenue is strung with lights, and from above it is a glowing river.

[图]

[图]

Go further in and there is the Trinity Cathedral of the Izmailovsky Regiment with its blue domes scattered with gold stars, Rastrelli's blue-and-white Smolny Cathedral, and bridge after little bridge over the canals; "Venice of the North" is not an empty nickname. The Griboyedov Canal winds down to Haymarket Square, which is Crime and Punishment territory: from his garret to the old moneylender's flat, Raskolnikov walks, the book says, exactly seven hundred and thirty steps.

[图]

Art here is not decoration, it is the air. The Hermitage holds three million objects (I wrote a separate story about it), the Russian Museum hangs Repin and Aivazovsky, and the Mariinsky premiered The Sleeping Beauty and The Nutcracker. Pushkin, Gogol, Dostoevsky, Akhmatova, Nabokov, Brodsky; Tchaikovsky, Rimsky-Korsakov, Shostakovich: nearly half the names in Russian cultural history are bound up with this city.

[图]

On the July trip I went to the Alexander Nevsky Monastery at the end of Nevsky. A walk round its cemeteries is a who's who: Dostoevsky, Tchaikovsky and Mussorgsky are all buried here. I stopped at a granite tomb whose sign read "Л. ЭЙЛЕР 1707–1783": the mathematician Leonhard Euler, who worked at the Petersburg Academy of Sciences for more than thirty years in total and died here. Not far away is a gravestone carved with Chinese characters, belonging to Nikita Bichurin, Father Iakinf, the founder of Russian sinology, who lived in Beijing for over a decade and was the first to translate many Chinese classics into Russian. Reading eight Chinese characters praising a lifetime of tireless work, in a Russian cemetery, was a strange and lovely feeling.

[图]

The only thing that breaks the skyline is the Lakhta Center, finished in 2019: 462 metres, the tallest building in Europe. It was originally meant to go up across the river from the centre, but residents and UNESCO fought it all the way because it would ruin the historic skyline, and in the end it was moved out to the seashore in the north-west. I rather like that ending: the city is willing to take in new things, as long as they leave its old rules alone.

[图]

In the end, Saint Petersburg is a city that should never have existed: built on a swamp, with long dark winters, besieged almost to death, and yet still standing, beautiful with all its might. It has a European skeleton, a Russian soul, and a sorrowful pride that belongs to it alone. Every time I leave, I feel sure I will be back.

[图]

stories.title: 北极圈七日求生纪实
stories.titleEn: Murmansk, where the sun never rises
stories.text:
摩尔曼斯克是北极圈里最大的城市，也是一座港口城市。北纬69度，墨西哥湾暖流一路北上，让这里的港口冬天也不封冻。我们去的时候是1月初，正好赶上极夜的尾巴。

[图]

去之前我对极夜的想象，是一天24小时都黑漆漆的。真到了才知道，极夜原来并不是一直天黑，而是太阳不会升起。中午前后有几个小时，天会亮起来，太阳就藏在地平线下面，整片天空被染成一种很深、很透的蓝，地平线那一圈泛着橙色和粉色，像日出，又像日落。就这样持续一两个小时，再慢慢暗回去，一整天都像是在黄昏里。

说实话，出发前我对零下二十度没有任何概念，穿了三件就去了。买的红眼航班，天还没亮就落地，走出机场的那一瞬间，脸像被人扇了一巴掌，鼻子里的水汽瞬间结冰扎得人生疼，我就知道事情不对劲了。

[图]

更要命的是，到了市区，我们找不到民宿在哪。对着导航转了一圈又一圈，楼都长得差不多，门全锁着，天是黑的，街上一个人也没有。没有地方可去，只能在大街上到处走，越走越冷，手指和脚趾慢慢没了知觉。那一刻我是真的以为自己要冻死在北极了。

最后救了我们的是一位天没亮就起来遛狗的居民。零下二十度，凌晨，遛狗，离谱。等那人牵着狗回来开楼门的时候，我们厚着脸皮跟了进去。上锁的居民楼过道里虽然也没有暖气，但我们在楼道里一直待到天亮，好歹保住了小命。

后来几天在街上观察，发现这里的居民仿佛都对寒冷免疫了。我裹得像个球，帽子、围巾、口罩一样不少，还是冻得直哆嗦；他们穿着单薄的外套，有的连帽子都不戴，慢悠悠地走在雪里，有说有笑。难道真的变异了吗……

[图]

城市边的山丘上，站着阿廖沙。

它的正式名字叫「苏联北极地区保卫者纪念碑」，1974年落成：一个披着军大衣、肩上挎着枪的士兵，雕像本身35米多，连底座有40多米高，落成时是全苏联第二高的雕塑。二战时德军从挪威打过来，前线就停在离摩尔曼斯克不远的地方，一僵持就是三年多。城里大部分房子都被炸毁了，这座城市却始终没有陷落。阿廖沙面朝西边，望着当年战线所在的方向。脚下有一团长明火，雪下了一层又一层，它却一直烧着。

[图]

我们去的那天雾很大，树上挂满了霜，站在山顶往下看，城市和海湾都淡在一片白里。

[图]

另一个有意思的故事是谢苗。

谢苗是一只猫，1987年，一户摩尔曼斯克人家开车经过莫斯科回家，带着家里的暹罗猫谢苗。谢苗在莫斯科跑丢了，怎么找都找不到。六年半以后的某一天，一只瘦得不成样子的猫出现在他们家门口，是谢苗。从莫斯科到摩尔曼斯克，将近两千公里，没人知道它是怎么走回来的。

2013年，城里给它立了一座铜像：一只小猫，扛着一根挑着小包袱的棍子，像刚刚走完那段漫长的路。我们是晚上去的，它身上落满了雪，每个来参观的人都在它头上浇水，结了一层厚厚的冰。

[图]

说回我们的民宿。那是一间温馨的小屋，经历过第一天早上的那场「生死劫」，它给了我满满的安全感。每天早晨醒来，窗外是一片蓝，楼顶、树枝、街道全都银装素裹，安安静静的。我站在窗边发呆，如果能一直在这里待下去就好了。

[图]

到了中午前后，天边会变成橙色和粉色。整个世界都是干净的：空气是干净的，雪是干净的，连路也是干净的。在外面走一整天回来，鞋子比我自己洗过还干净。

[图]

我们去的时候刚好是新年期间。在俄罗斯，新年比圣诞节隆重得多，假期从元旦一直放到1月上旬。市中心的广场上搭起了冰屋和巨大的灯饰，灯一亮，金色和蓝色铺满了整条街。穿着雪姑娘衣服的姑娘站在雪里和人合影，小孩在灯下的雪地里跑来跑去。北极的大都市过起年来，一点也不冷清。

[图]

[图]

吃的必须说说帝王蟹，真的好吃，是我吃过第二好吃的海鲜。第一名是在神户吃到的天妇罗。话说，天妇罗算海鲜吗？

[图]

港口边停着列宁号，世界上第一艘核动力破冰船，1959年开始服役，在北冰洋上破了三十年的冰，退役以后就停在这里，成了博物馆。

[图]

列宁号附近，立着一块写着这座城市经纬坐标的牌子。我们路过的时候，正好有人在那里求婚，单膝跪在雪地里，周围的人都停下来看。北极圈里，零下二十度，很浪漫。

[图]

旁边的栏杆上挂着一排爱情锁，每一把都裹着厚厚的冰渣。情侣们靠在栏杆边依偎、接吻，呼出来的气一下就变成了白雾。

[图]

当然，来摩尔曼斯克绕不开的还有追极光，和去巴伦支海边的捷里别尔卡，这又是和城市生活完全不同的另一段故事了。

[图]

太阳不升起的天空，冻到怀疑人生的清晨，楼道里的那几个小时，走了两千公里回家的猫，窗外的蓝，冰渣下的锁。这座城市给我的这些独特体验，真的很难忘。

[图]
stories.textEn:
Murmansk is the largest city inside the Arctic Circle, and a port city. It sits at 69 degrees north, yet the last of the Gulf Stream reaches this far and keeps the harbour from freezing even in winter. We went in early January, just catching the tail end of the polar night.

[图]

Before the trip, I imagined the polar night as twenty-four hours of darkness. It turns out the polar night is not endless dark; it is simply that the sun never rises. For a few hours around noon the sky does get light. The sun stays hidden below the horizon, the whole sky turns a deep, clear blue, and the horizon glows orange and pink, like sunrise, or sunset. It lasts an hour or two, then slowly fades back. The whole day feels like dusk.

Then there is the cold. Honestly, before I left I had no idea what minus twenty actually meant, and I went in three layers. We took a red-eye, landed before dawn, and the moment I stepped out of the airport it felt like a slap across the face. I knew something had gone wrong.

[图]

Worse, once we got into the city we couldn't find our apartment. We circled again and again with the map, every building looked the same, every door was locked, it was dark, and there was no one on the street. With nowhere to go we just kept walking, colder and colder, until I could no longer feel my fingers or toes. At that point I genuinely thought I was going to freeze to death in the Arctic.

In the end we were saved by a dog. More precisely, by a local who had got up before dawn to walk it. Minus twenty, the middle of the night, walking the dog. Absurd. When they came back and unlocked the building door, we shamelessly followed them in. The locked building had heating, and we stayed in the stairwell until it got light. At least we survived.

Over the next few days I watched people on the street, and the locals seemed completely immune to the cold. I was wrapped up like a ball, hat, scarf and mask, and still shivering; they strolled through the snow in thin jackets, some without even a hat, chatting and laughing. Have they actually mutated?

[图]

On a hill at the edge of the city stands Alyosha.

Its official name is the Monument to the Defenders of the Soviet Arctic, unveiled in 1974: a soldier in a greatcoat with a rifle over his shoulder. The figure alone is over 35 metres tall, more than 40 with the pedestal, and when it opened it was the second-tallest statue in the Soviet Union. In the Second World War the German army came in from Norway, and the front stopped not far from Murmansk and stayed there for more than three years. Most of the city's houses were bombed out, yet the city never fell. Alyosha faces west, towards where the front line used to be. At his feet burns an eternal flame; snow falls layer after layer, and it keeps burning.

[图]

The day we went it was very foggy, the trees were covered in frost, and from the top of the hill the city and the bay faded into white.

[图]

The other thing I remember is Semyon.

Semyon is a cat. In 1987 a family from Murmansk was driving home through Moscow with their Siamese cat, Semyon. He ran off in Moscow and they never found him. Six and a half years later, a cat so thin he was barely recognisable turned up at their door. It was Semyon. Moscow to Murmansk is nearly two thousand kilometres, and nobody knows how he walked home.

In 2013 the city gave him a bronze statue: a little cat carrying a stick with a bundle tied to the end, as if he had just finished that long road. We went at night, and he was covered in snow.

[图]

Back to our apartment. It was a cosy little place, and after that first morning's brush with death it made me feel completely safe. Every morning I woke up to blue outside the window, the rooftops, branches and streets all dressed in white and perfectly quiet. I would often just stand at the window, thinking how nice it would be to stay here forever.

[图]

Around noon the horizon turns orange and pink. The whole world is clean: the air is clean, the snow is clean, even the roads are clean. After a whole day of walking outside, my shoes were cleaner than if I had washed them myself.

[图]

We happened to be there over New Year. In Russia, New Year is a much bigger deal than Christmas, and the holiday runs from the first of January well into the second week. The central square was filled with ice houses and huge light displays; when the lights came on, gold and blue covered the whole street. A girl dressed as the Snow Maiden stood in the snow taking photos with people, and kids ran around in the snow under the lights. An Arctic city celebrating New Year is anything but quiet.

[图]

[图]

As for food, I have to mention the king crab. It was genuinely delicious, the second-best seafood I have ever had. First place goes to the tempura I had in Kobe. Then again, does tempura even count as seafood?

[图]

At the harbour lies the Lenin, the world's first nuclear-powered surface ship. It went into service in 1959, broke ice in the Arctic Ocean for thirty years, and since retiring has been moored here as a museum.

[图]

Near the Lenin stands a sign with the city's coordinates. As we walked past, someone was proposing right there, down on one knee in the snow, with people stopping to watch. Inside the Arctic Circle, at minus twenty. Very romantic.

[图]

On the railing nearby hangs a row of love locks, each one coated in a thick crust of ice. Couples leaned against the railing, holding each other and kissing, their breath turning instantly to white mist. It had a real feeling to it.

[图]

Of course, no trip to Murmansk is complete without chasing the northern lights, or going out to Teriberka on the Barents Sea. Both deserve a story of their own, so I'll leave them for later.

[图]

A sky where the sun never rises, a morning so cold it made me question my life choices, a few hours in a stairwell, a cat who walked two thousand kilometres home, the blue outside the window, the locks under the ice. The things this city gave me are hard to forget.

[图]

stories.title: 开往世界尽头的路
stories.titleEn: Teriberka, the road to the end of the world
stories.text:
从摩尔曼斯克去捷里别尔卡，一百多公里，地图上看着不远，路上要开好几个小时。这是通往村子的唯一一条路，路况十分恶劣，周围都是无人区，冬天一场暴风雪就能把它封住。

我们天没亮就出发。出了城，楼房和路灯很快就没了，只剩下车灯照着的一小段路。路面被压成了一层硬冰，坑坑洼洼，车一直在颠，偶尔对面来一辆车，远远地就能看见两团光在雪雾里晃。路两边是一排排电线杆，跟着路一直伸到看不见的地方。

[图]

再往前开，路就变成了苔原中间的一道缝。没有树，没有房子，没有人，只有起伏的雪地，一直铺到天边。车里很安静，大家都不怎么说话，就看着窗外。那种感觉很难形容，像是在往世界的尽头开。

天边一点点亮起来，地平线那一圈先是橙色，再往上是粉色，然后是很深的蓝。极夜里太阳不会升起来，这就已经是一天里最亮的时候了。

[图]

然后，风车出现了。

一开始只是地平线上几根细细的白线，越开越近，越来越多，一台接一台，站满了整片雪原。这是科拉风电场，北极圈里最大的风电场，五十多台风机，每一台都有几十层楼那么高。

我们下车站在路边。零下二十度，风很大，吹得人站不稳，耳朵里只有风声和叶片转动的嗡嗡声。身后是橙红色的天，风车的影子一台一台黑下来，又高又安静，慢慢地转。人站在下面，小得像一个点。那一刻真的被震撼到了，说不出话，只想一直看下去。

[图]

到捷里别尔卡的时候，天已经是那种深深的蓝了。前一天刚好是满月，月亮一整天都挂在山头上，没有落下去。

捷里别尔卡是巴伦支海边的一个小渔村，只有几百个人，因为电影《利维坦》在这里拍摄才被更多人知道。往北再没有陆地，就是北冰洋了。

[图]

[图]

最先看到的是海在冒烟。

一大片白雾从海面上升起来，贴着水面慢慢飘，把对面的山都遮住了一半。墨西哥湾暖流的尾巴一路流到这里，海水比空气暖得多，零下二十度的冷空气一碰到海面，水汽就变成了雾。我们沿着海滩走，人走进雾里，一下就只剩下一个影子。

[图]

海边有一个用木头搭的王座，坐上去，背后就是整片巴伦支海。还有人穿着橙色的衣服直接走进海里，零下二十度，冬泳，北极人果然都是变异的。

[图]

村子的海湾里停着几条渔船，被海烟裹着，像是飘在半空中。岸上躺着搁浅多年的旧船，锈迹斑斑，和雪地上那副巨大的鲸鱼骨架一起，安安静静地待在世界的边上。

[图]

[图]

中午十二点半，天边最亮。太阳就在地平线下面，把一整排山都照成了粉色。

[图]

[图]

我们往海边的岩石上走。雪下面是红褐色的石头，风把雪吹得一块一块的，脚下全是冰。爬到高处往下看，海浪一层一层拍上来，撞在礁石上碎成白沫，再远一点，就是雾，和看不到头的海。

[图]

[图]

月亮就在身边，好像伸手就能摘下来。大家在石头上轮流摆姿势，捧月亮、抱月亮，冻得手指都伸不直了，还是玩得停不下来。

[图]

再往里走，有一片冰封的海湾和一道冻住的瀑布。水流在半路上停住了，变成一层一层发蓝的冰，挂在红色的岩壁上。整个世界只剩下三种颜色：白的雪，红的石头，蓝的天。

[图]

[图]

下午两点不到，天又开始暗下来。最后那一点光沉到山后面，山的轮廓变成黑色，天边还留着一道橙色。这一整天，太阳一次都没有出来过。

[图]

天黑以后，在村子里遇到了一头驯鹿，在雪地上慢悠悠地走，一点也不怕人。

[图]

回去的路还是那条路，一样的黑，一样的颠。但我一直记得那天早上路边的风车，还有那片冒着烟的海。北极的风景好像不是用来看的，是用来站在里面，感受自己有多小的。
stories.textEn:
From Murmansk to Teriberka is a little over a hundred kilometres. It doesn't look far on the map, but the drive takes hours. It is the only road to the village, and in winter a single snowstorm can close it.

We set off before dawn. Once out of the city the buildings and street lights disappeared fast, leaving only the short stretch of road in our headlights. The surface was packed into a hard, rutted sheet of ice, and the car bounced the whole way. Now and then an oncoming car appeared, two blobs of light swaying in the snow haze long before you could see the car. Power lines ran alongside, following the road off into nowhere.

[图]

Further on, the road became a thin seam through the tundra. No trees, no houses, no people, just rolling snow all the way to the horizon. It went quiet in the car; nobody talked much, we just watched out of the window. It is hard to describe. It felt like driving towards the end of the world.

Slowly the sky began to brighten: orange along the horizon, pink above it, then a deep blue. In the polar night the sun never rises, so this was already as bright as the day would get.

[图]

Then the wind turbines appeared.

At first they were just a few thin white lines on the horizon. As we got closer there were more and more, one after another, filling the whole snowfield. This is the Kola Wind Farm, the largest wind farm inside the Arctic Circle, more than fifty turbines, each as tall as a skyscraper.

We got out and stood by the road. Minus twenty, the wind strong enough to push you off balance, nothing in your ears but the wind and the hum of the blades. Behind us the sky was orange-red, and the turbines stood against it one by one in black, tall and silent, turning slowly. Standing underneath, a person is just a dot. I was genuinely stunned. I couldn't say anything; I just wanted to keep looking.

[图]

By the time we reached Teriberka, the sky had turned that deep blue. The moon had been full the day before, and it hung over the hills all day without ever setting.

Teriberka is a small fishing village on the Barents Sea, home to a few hundred people, better known since the film Leviathan was shot here. North of it there is no more land, only the Arctic Ocean.

[图]

[图]

The first thing we saw was the sea smoking.

A wide white mist rose off the water and drifted slowly along the surface, hiding half the hills on the other side. The tail of the Gulf Stream reaches this far, so the sea is much warmer than the air; when minus-twenty air touches it, the vapour turns straight into fog. We walked along the beach, and anyone who stepped into the mist became just a silhouette.

[图]

On the shore stands a throne made of logs. Sit on it and the whole Barents Sea is at your back. Some people in orange suits walked straight into the sea. Minus twenty, winter swimming. Arctic people really have mutated.

[图]

A few fishing boats lay in the bay, wrapped in sea smoke as if floating in mid-air. On the shore lay old wrecks, stranded for years and covered in rust, keeping quiet company with a huge whale skeleton in the snow at the edge of the world.

[图]

[图]

At half past twelve the sky was at its brightest. The sun was just below the horizon, turning a whole line of hills pink.

[图]

[图]

We climbed onto the rocks by the sea. Under the snow the stone was reddish brown, the wind had blown the snow into patches, and everything underfoot was ice. From up high we watched the waves roll in layer after layer, shatter into white foam on the rocks, and beyond them only mist and endless sea.

[图]

[图]

The moon was right beside us, close enough to pick. We took turns posing on the rocks, holding the moon, hugging the moon, fingers too frozen to straighten, and still couldn't stop.

[图]

Further in there is a frozen bay and a frozen waterfall. The water stopped halfway down and turned into layers of bluish ice hanging on the red rock. The whole world came down to three colours: white snow, red stone, blue sky.

[图]

[图]

Before two in the afternoon it was getting dark again. The last of the light sank behind the hills, their outlines turned black, and a band of orange stayed on the horizon. All day, the sun never came out once.

[图]

After dark we met a reindeer in the village, strolling across the snow, not the least bit afraid of people.

[图]

The way back was the same road, just as dark and just as bumpy. But I keep thinking about the turbines by the road that morning, and that smoking sea. Arctic landscapes aren't really for looking at. They are for standing inside, and feeling how small you are.

来摩尔曼斯克，我最憧憬的就是极光。出发前那几天，我一天要打开好几次极光预报 App，盯着上面的强度曲线和云图看。预报说 1 月 2 号晚上的强度最高，为了赶上这一晚，我们把行程整个往前挪：1 月 1 号晚上，新年的第一天，就背着相机上了飞机。

[图]

红眼航班天没亮就落地，接着又在零下二十度的街头折腾了一早上，几乎没合过眼。从机场进城的大巴上，所有人都缩在座位里，脸上写着困。到了市区，天还黑着，一轮月亮挂在楼群上空，又大又圆，亮得出奇。当时只觉得好看，没想到它会是当晚的主角。

白天随便补了一会儿觉，入夜之后，我们就跟着当地的极光猎人出发了。车一开出城，问题就摆在眼前：云很厚，一层压着一层，偶尔裂开一道缝，月光就从那里漏下来。那几天正好是满月，月亮把整片云照得发白，四周还套着一圈大大的月晕。追极光最怕的两样东西，云和月亮，那晚一个不落全到齐了。

[图]

接下来就是漫长的寻找。车在荒无人烟的雪原里奔驰，窗外一片漆黑，只有车灯照亮前面一小段路，和路边一堆一堆的雪。车偶尔停下来，大家裹紧衣服下车，仰着头在雪地里站一会儿，看看天，冻得直跺脚，再默默回到车上，换个方向继续开。就这样，前前后后开了三四个小时。

凌晨十二点半多，车又一次停下。终于有人发现，北边的云缝里好像有一点绿。我盯着看了很久，才勉强看出一条很淡很淡的影子，灰白里透着一点点绿，像有人往玻璃上哈了一口气。举起相机一拍，屏幕上亮起来的，却是一条清清楚楚的绿色丝带，正在慢慢地扭动、流淌。

[图]

肉眼里，它始终是淡淡的，要不是有相机，我都不敢确定自己真的看见了。它在云缝里飘了一会儿，越来越淡，十来分钟后就再也找不到了。我们又在雪地里站了很久，等它回来，它没有回来。

回去的路上，车里很安静。回到民宿已是后半夜，我脱下冻得发硬的外套，倒头就睡。从 1 月 1 号晚上出发算起，差不多两天没有好好睡过，换来的是一条淡淡的绿。累是真的累，失落也是真的失落。
stories.textEn:
[图]

Of everything on the Murmansk trip, the northern lights were what I looked forward to most. In the days before we left I checked an aurora forecast app several times a day, watching the activity curve and the cloud maps. The forecast said the night of January 2 would be the strongest, so we moved the whole trip forward to catch it. On the evening of January 1, the first day of the new year, I was on a plane with my camera.

[图]

The red-eye landed before dawn, and then we spent the morning stumbling around the streets at minus twenty, with almost no sleep. On the bus from the airport everyone was slumped in their seats, exhaustion written all over their faces. When we reached the city it was still dark, and a huge, round moon hung over the apartment blocks, strangely bright. At the time I just thought it was pretty. I had no idea it would be the star of the night.

[图]

We grabbed a little sleep during the day, and after dark we set off with an aurora-chasing tour. As soon as we were out of the city, the problem was obvious: the clouds were thick, layer upon layer, and every so often a gap opened and moonlight leaked through. It was right around the full moon, and it lit the whole cloud deck white, ringed by a wide halo. The two things an aurora chaser fears most, clouds and the moon, both turned up that night.

[图]

Then came the long search. The car raced across empty snowfields in total darkness, the headlights picking out only a short stretch of road and the snowbanks along it. Now and then we stopped, everyone bundled up and climbed out, stood in the snow staring at the sky and stamping our feet against the cold, then quietly got back in and drove off in another direction. We kept this up for three or four hours.

A little after half past midnight we stopped again. Finally someone noticed a hint of green in a gap in the clouds to the north. I stared for a long time before I could make out a very faint shape, greyish with the slightest touch of green, like breath fogging a window. I raised the camera, and on the screen was a clear green ribbon, slowly twisting and flowing.

[图]

To the naked eye it stayed faint the whole time. Without the camera I wouldn't have been sure I had seen anything at all. It drifted in the gap for a while, growing paler, and after ten minutes or so it was gone. We stood in the snow a long time waiting for it to come back. It didn't.

The ride back was quiet. By the time we reached the apartment it was the middle of the night; I peeled off a jacket gone stiff with cold and fell straight into bed. Counting from the evening of January 1, I had gone nearly two days without proper sleep, and what I got for it was ten minutes and one faint streak of green. I was tired, truly tired, and disappointed too.

stories.title: 伏努科沃机场的三脚架
stories.text:
[图]

去土耳其之前，我心里最惦记的一件事，是这趟终于能带上三脚架爽拍。伊斯坦布尔的夜景、卡帕多奇亚的热气球，在脑子里预演过好几遍。出发那天凌晨四点就出了门，天还黑着，三脚架就绑在包上。

[图]

我们坐的是胜利航空，俄罗斯的廉航。到了伏努科沃机场，外面一片大雾。值机的工作人员一看三脚架，说超尺寸了，要加钱托运。三脚架才两千卢，托运却要四千。可舍不得扔，咬咬牙还是交了。

接下来的事情开始变得离谱。工作人员办到一半，人跑了，很久都不回来。我们在柜台前干等，又到处找人，最后换了另一个人来接手。他办完之后却告诉我：这个应该自己拎上飞机，不用托运。我觉得奇怪，但既然是他们自己这么说，也就没多想。

到了登机口，检票员又把我拦下，说三脚架必须托运，要带上飞机，得再交六千卢。我把前面的经过从头解释了一遍：是你们的人让我自己拎上来，托运的钱我也已经交过了。对方一句也不听，只是一直摇头，no, no, no，要么交钱，要么别上飞机。

六千卢实在过于离谱了。最后，三脚架只好扔在了登机口。两千的三脚架，加上四千的托运费，前前后后白白亏了六千卢。

[图]

飞机起飞，钻出云层，窗外是一整片云海。我坐在座位上，心里还堵着一口气。

[图]

后来飞过雪山，又飞过大海，窗外的风景一段比一段好看。

[图]

快落地的时候，土耳其的海岸线出现在窗外，海水是一种很透的绿。

[图]

到了伊斯坦布尔，阳光很好，红色的国旗在风里飘。这一趟没了三脚架，没法爽拍了，可旅行才刚刚开始。
stories.textEn:
[图]

Before the Turkey trip, the thing I was most excited about was finally bringing my tripod and shooting to my heart's content. Istanbul at night, the balloons over Cappadocia: I had rehearsed them in my head again and again. On the day we left I was out the door at four in the morning, still dark, with the tripod strapped to my bag.

[图]

We were flying Pobeda, a Russian budget airline. At Vnukovo the fog was thick. The check-in agent took one look at the tripod and said it was oversized and had to be checked for a fee. The tripod had only cost two thousand rubles, and checking it was four thousand. But I couldn't bring myself to throw it away, so I paid.

Then things got absurd. Halfway through, the agent simply walked off and didn't come back for a long time. We waited at the counter, then went looking for someone, and eventually another agent took over. When he finished, he told me the tripod should go in the cabin with me, no need to check it. That seemed odd, since I had already paid, but it was their own staff saying so, so I didn't think much of it.

At the gate, the boarding agent stopped me again: the tripod had to be checked, and taking it on board meant paying another six thousand rubles. I explained the whole story from the start: your own colleague told me to carry it on, and I had already paid to check it. She wouldn't hear a word of it, just kept shaking her head, no, no, no. Pay, or don't fly.

Six thousand rubles was more than I could pay. In the end the tripod stayed behind at the gate. A two-thousand-ruble tripod plus a four-thousand-ruble fee: six thousand rubles gone for nothing.

[图]

The plane took off and broke through the clouds into a sea of white. I sat there, still fuming.

[图]

Later we flew over snowy mountains, then over the sea, each view better than the last. I kept shooting, and kept thinking: if only I still had the tripod.

[图]

Just before landing, the Turkish coastline appeared below the window, the water a clear, glassy green.

[图]

Istanbul was all sunshine, red flags snapping in the wind. No tripod this time, no shooting to my heart's content, but the trip had only just begun.

stories.title: 猫才是伊斯坦布尔的主人
stories.text:
到伊斯坦布尔的第一顿饭，刚坐下就发现桌布底下的藤椅上睡着一只小猫。服务员看了一眼，没赶它，绕过去给我们上菜。后来才明白，这在土耳其再正常不过：海边、公园、清真寺门口、商店的柜台上，到处都是猫，而且没有一只怕人。它们不属于哪一家，而是属于整条街。

[图]

土耳其人为什么这么爱猫？最常听到的答案是宗教。伊斯兰传统里，猫被看作干净的动物。圣训里记载，猫喝过的水仍然可以用来做礼拜前的净身，因为它“常在你们身边走动”。先知有位门徒，因为总在袖子里揣着一只小猫，被大家叫作“阿布·胡莱拉”，意思就是“小猫的父亲”，这个外号后来比他的本名还出名。流传最广的是另一个故事：先知的猫穆艾扎睡在他的袍袖上，他宁可把袖子剪掉也不愿吵醒它。不过这个故事在早期典籍里找不到出处，更像是后人加上去的，但足够说明猫在人们心里的地位。相比之下，狗在传统观念里被认为不洁，所以清真寺里常见猫进进出出，很少见到狗。

[图]

[图]

第二个原因是这座城本身。伊斯坦布尔两千多年来都是港口，船从地中海、黑海各处开过来，带来货物，也带来老鼠。猫跟着船上岸，替人看粮仓、守码头，人也乐意养着它们。奥斯曼时期，有钱人会在遗嘱里设立“瓦合甫”，也就是慈善基金，除了修清真寺、喷泉和施粥所，也有专门拿钱喂街上猫狗和鸟的。喂流浪动物在这里不是谁的私人爱好，而是一种积德的善事，几百年下来成了习惯。

[图]

到了现代，这份习惯写进了法律。2004 年土耳其通过《动物保护法》，禁止捕杀和虐待流浪动物，要求市政府给它们绝育、打疫苗，再放回原来的街区。2021 年修法以后，动物在法律上不再被当作“物品”，而是“有生命的个体”，虐待动物可以坐牢。所以在伊斯坦布尔，经常能在路边看到市政府摆的猫屋、水碗和自动喂食器，绝育过的猫耳朵上会有一个小缺口。

[图]

[图]

这里的猫还有自己的名人。圣索菲亚大教堂里住过一只叫格莉的虎斑猫，2009 年奥巴马来参观时摸过它的头，它就此成了网红，2020 年去世时全城都在悼念。卡德柯伊有一只叫通比利的胖猫，总是用一个很像人的姿势靠在路边台阶上，2016 年它死后，街坊们在它常待的那个位置给它立了一座铜像。同一年还有一部纪录片《爱猫之城》（Kedi），跟拍了七只伊斯坦布尔的街猫，片子里一位老人说，猫知道人对它们好，只是不说出来。

[图]

这趟拍得最多的地方，是吉汉吉尔一条窄窄的台阶。傍晚路过时，台阶上下密密麻麻全是猫，橘的、白的、三花的，几十只安安静静地等着。没过多久，一位穿黄衣服的女士提着袋子出来，一路往下撒猫粮，猫们这才一下子活了过来。

[图]

[图]

所以与其说土耳其人养猫，不如说猫和人一起住在这座城里。人给它们吃的、给它们地方睡，它们就在海边晒太阳、在长椅上打盹、在镜头前打哈欠。来之前以为伊斯坦布尔的主角是清真寺和博斯普鲁斯海峡，走了一圈才发现，这座城真正的主人是猫。

[图]

[图]
stories.textEn:
Our first meal in Istanbul: we sat down and noticed a kitten asleep on the wicker chair under the tablecloth. The waiter glanced at it, didn't shoo it away, and simply stepped around it with our plates. Over the next few days I learned this is completely normal in Turkey. By the sea, in parks, at mosque doors, on shop counters, there are cats everywhere, and not one of them is afraid of people. They belong to no household, and somehow to the whole street.

[图]

Why do Turks love cats so much? The answer you hear most is religion. In Islamic tradition the cat is a clean animal. A hadith says water a cat has drunk from can still be used for ablution before prayer, because cats are always moving among you. One of the Prophet's companions carried a kitten in his sleeve so often that people called him Abu Hurairah, "father of the kitten", and the nickname outlived his real name. The most famous story is another one: the Prophet's cat Muezza fell asleep on his robe, and he cut off the sleeve rather than wake it. That tale doesn't appear in the early sources and was probably added later, but it shows how people feel. Dogs, by contrast, are traditionally considered unclean, which is why cats wander in and out of mosques while dogs rarely do.

[图]

[图]

The second reason is the city itself. For over two thousand years Istanbul has been a port. Ships from across the Mediterranean and the Black Sea brought goods, and rats. Cats came ashore with the ships to guard granaries and docks, and people were happy to keep them. In Ottoman times the wealthy set up charitable endowments, vakıf, in their wills: besides mosques, fountains and soup kitchens, some paid specifically to feed the city's cats, dogs and birds. Feeding street animals here was never a private hobby but a good deed, and centuries later it is simply habit.

[图]

In modern times the habit became law. Turkey's 2004 Animal Protection Law bans killing or abusing strays and requires municipalities to neuter, vaccinate and return them to their neighborhoods. A 2021 amendment stopped treating animals as "property" and made cruelty punishable by prison. So in Istanbul you constantly see cat houses, water bowls and feeding machines put out by the city, and neutered cats carry a small notch in one ear.

[图]

[图]

The cats even have celebrities. Gli, a tabby who lived in Hagia Sophia, was petted by Barack Obama in 2009 and became internet-famous; when she died in 2020 the whole city mourned. In Kadıköy a chubby cat named Tombili was known for leaning against a step in an oddly human pose; after he died in 2016 the neighbors put up a bronze statue of him in his usual spot. The same year the documentary Kedi followed seven Istanbul street cats.

[图]

The place I photographed most on this trip was a narrow stairway in Cihangir. Passing by at dusk, the steps were covered in cats, ginger, white and calico, dozens of them waiting quietly. Soon a woman in yellow came down with a bag and scattered food all the way down the stairs, and the cats came alive at once. Someone nearby told me she comes at this hour every day, and has for years.

[图]

[图]

So it's less that Turks keep cats than that cats and people share the city. People feed them and give them somewhere to sleep; the cats sunbathe by the sea, nap on benches and yawn for the camera. I came thinking Istanbul's stars were the mosques and the Bosphorus. After walking around, I realized the city's real owners are the cats.

[图]

[图]

stories.title: 开往格雷梅的夜巴
stories.text:
从伊斯坦布尔去卡帕多奇亚，我们又一次选了夜巴：省下一程交通费，顺便再省一晚房费。坐过大阪到东京那一趟之后，我越来越确信，夜巴就是穷游的神。

出发前照例跟着谷歌地图去车站，然后照例，谷歌地图又抽风了。不知道为什么，它在土耳其的表现格外差：公交线路和到站时间经常是错的，寻路的逻辑也很迷，有些路干脆不在地图上，它宁可领着你绕一大圈。这次就是这样，跟着它走了一段，越走越不对劲，眼看就要赶不上发车。最后还是靠这些年在路上攒下的经验，自己判断方向，找到了正确的路，一路小跑，总算掐着点赶到了车站。

结果发现其实根本不用跑。我们在始发站，车照样晚点了半个多小时。那半个小时里，我们一遍遍核对车票，盯着车站的信息屏，逮着人就问，生怕是自己搞错了站台、错过了车。可站台上没有广播，也没有任何通知，车就是还没来。就这么简单，就这么离谱。

这段小插曲，也给整趟夜巴定下了基调：和日本夜巴那种准时、克制、甚至有点压抑的氛围，完全是两回事。

[图]

车开出来时已经很晚了，城里还在堵车。车上的人很少，后面几站又陆陆续续上来一些，到最后也只坐满了三分之一左右。人少，反倒让我把每个人都记得很清楚。

印象最深的是一位独自带着婴儿的妈妈。车上有三位司机，同时也兼任服务员，一路上轮流帮忙照看这对母子，抱一会儿孩子，哄一会儿，好让妈妈吃点东西、歇口气。还有一个跟男朋友告别的女生，车来了，两个人还抱在一起满脸的依依不舍，最后才一步三回头地上了车。

夜里的高速上，服务员时不时过来送零食、泡茶，还会停下来找大家聊天。知道我们是中国人，就跟我们学几句中文；路过那位妈妈的座位，又逗一逗孩子。整个车厢松松散散、热热闹闹的，像一间会移动的客厅。和日本夜巴里大家屏着呼吸、生怕弄出一点声响的样子比起来，简直是两个世界。

[图]

一晚上在服务区停了好几次。每次迷迷糊糊醒过来，窗外都是差不多的样子：黑漆漆的高速，亮着灯的加油站，服务区里的小超市。

直到第二天清晨，我被刺眼的阳光晒醒。往窗外一看，人一下子清醒了。地形完全变了，两边是一望无际的平原，偶尔冒出几座奇形怪状的山，说是山，其实更像一个个凸起的土包。平原上散着一群群说不上品种的羊，一条公路从中间穿过去，把两边隔开，我们的大巴就这样孤零零地在这条路上奔驰。

[图]

又开了一阵，路边出现了一个同样孤零零的服务区，这才重新见到了人和车。服务区商店里的两兄弟热情得很，非要跟我们聊几句，我就给他们拍了张合影。

[图]

转过头，加油站正逆着清晨的太阳：明明还是早上，光已经烈得晃眼，又拍下一张。

[图]

越接近格雷梅，原本荒凉的景色里，终于点缀上了一些小镇的房屋，各种奇形怪状的岩石也多了起来。先是远处一座布满洞穴的石头山，是乌奇希萨尔城堡；然后是成片发白的岩谷和土丘；再往前，天上飘起了一只热气球。

[图]

[图]

[图]

最后终于到了小镇。算下来，整趟车晚点了好几个小时。要是在日本，司机这份工作怕是已经保不住了吧。可在土耳其，好像谁也不着急，到后来，连我们自己也不着急了。
stories.textEn:
From Istanbul to Cappadocia we took a night bus again: it saves the fare, and a night's accommodation while you're at it. After the Osaka to Tokyo run, I'm more convinced than ever that the night bus is the budget traveller's best friend.

As usual we followed Google Maps to the bus station, and as usual Google Maps lost the plot. For some reason it is especially bad in Turkey: bus routes and arrival times are often wrong, the routing logic is baffling, and some streets simply aren't on the map, so it would rather send you on a long detour. That's exactly what happened. The further we followed it, the more wrong it felt, until we were about to miss the departure. In the end it was years of experience on the road that saved us: we worked out the direction ourselves, found the right way, and half-ran the rest, arriving just in time.

Then it turned out there had been no need to run. We were at the starting station, and the bus was still more than half an hour late. For that half hour we checked our tickets again and again, stared at the departure board and asked anyone we could find, terrified we had the wrong platform and had missed it. There was no announcement, no notice of any kind. The bus just hadn't come. As simple as that, and as absurd as that.

That little episode set the tone for the whole trip: nothing like the punctual, restrained, almost oppressive atmosphere of a Japanese night bus.

[图]

It was late by the time we pulled out, and the city was still jammed. There were very few people on board; a few more got on at later stops, but in the end the bus was only about a third full. With so few passengers, I remember every one of them.

The one I remember most was a mother travelling alone with a baby. There were three drivers on the bus, who doubled as attendants, and all night they took turns looking after the two of them: holding the baby for a while, rocking it, so she could eat something and catch her breath. There was also a girl saying goodbye to her boyfriend. The bus had arrived and the two of them were still wrapped around each other, kissing and hugging, faces full of reluctance, until she finally climbed aboard, looking back at every step.

Out on the dark highway the attendants kept coming round with snacks and tea, and stopping to chat. When they found out we were Chinese, they had us teach them a few words; passing the mother's seat, they'd play with the baby. The whole bus was loose and noisy, like a living room on wheels. Compared with a Japanese night bus, where everyone holds their breath for fear of making a sound, it was another world.

[图]

We stopped at service areas several times through the night. Every time I half-woke, the view was much the same: a pitch-black highway, a lit-up petrol station, a little shop.

Then, the next morning, I was woken by glaring sunlight. One look out of the window and I was wide awake: the land had completely changed. On both sides lay endless plains, broken now and then by oddly shaped hills, or really more like mounds of earth. Flocks of sheep of some breed I couldn't name were scattered across them, and a single road cut straight through the middle, with our bus racing along it all alone.

[图]

A while later an equally lonely service area appeared by the road, and we finally saw people and cars again. The two brothers running the shop were incredibly friendly and insisted on chatting with us, so I took their picture.

[图]

Turning round, I saw the petrol station backlit by the morning sun. It was still early, yet the light was already blinding, so I took another.

[图]

As we got closer to Göreme, the bare landscape finally gained a scattering of small-town houses, and the strange rock formations multiplied. First a stone hill riddled with holes in the distance, Uçhisar Castle; then whole valleys of pale rock and mounds; and further on, a hot-air balloon drifting in the sky.

[图]

[图]

[图]

At last we reached the town. All told, the bus was several hours late. In Japan, the driver would probably have lost his job. In Turkey, nobody seemed in a hurry, and in the end, neither were we.

stories.title: 两个胜利日
stories.text:
1945 年 5 月 8 日深夜，德国在柏林郊外的卡尔斯霍斯特签下无条件投降书。签字时柏林是 22 点 43 分，莫斯科已经过了午夜，是 5 月 9 日。所以西欧把欧战胜利纪念日定在 5 月 8 日，苏联和后来的俄罗斯过的是 5 月 9 日。

这场被俄罗斯人称为「伟大卫国战争」的仗，苏联死了大约两千七百万人，几乎每个家庭都有人没能回来。也正因为这样，胜利日在俄罗斯不只是一个节日，更像是全国性的家祭。它也不是一开始就这么隆重：战后头几年放假，1948 年起又改回了工作日，直到 1965 年胜利二十周年才重新放假、恢复红场阅兵，1995 年以后阅兵才年年都办。今天的胜利日有一套固定的流程：上午红场阅兵，白天胸前别着黑橙相间的圣乔治丝带，举着先辈照片参加「不朽军团」游行，各个公园都有露天演出，晚上十点全城几个地方同时放礼炮烟花。

我在莫斯科过了两个胜利日，2025 年一次，2026 年一次。

2025 年是胜利八十周年，整个办得很夸张。二十多个国家的领导人来到红场，中国人民解放军仪仗队也走进了阅兵方阵，在红场上大放光彩。

可惜那天上午我没出门，下午才去了莫大，在主楼前后转了一圈，然后上麻雀山等烟花。

[图]

[图]

节日的气氛前几天就有了。莫斯科航空学院里办了军事装备展，装甲车、吉普车就停在教学楼前，学生们可以随便摸真枪真炮，扛着枪和穿迷彩服的军人合影。台上一个穿着华丽的女生唱起了《喀秋莎》，歌声婉转悠扬，落落大方，直击灵魂。

[图]

[图]

傍晚时分，复古老车齐刷刷开上街头，车上插着旗子，放着老歌，一辆接一辆地游街。麻雀山小小的观景台开始聚人，没一会儿就堵得水泄不通，前胸贴后背。天黑下来，莫大主楼上演起了灯光秀，媒体的长枪短炮也早早架好了。

[图]

[图]

十点整，烟花在河对岸炸开，一轮接着一轮，把整片夜空染得通红。人们随着烟花一起大喊「乌拉！」「俄罗斯！」，好不热闹。那一晚的莫斯科，是真的在过节。

[图]

[图]

2026 年这一次，我花了一整天，想好好深度体验一回，可惜完全没有了前一年的规模。

[图]

战争局势越来越紧张，当天莫斯科市区的移动网络直接断了。上午我挤到红场边上看阅兵，看到的只有几架飞机拖着三色烟掠过斯大林式高楼，以及方阵走过，好不寒酸。但人群依然热情，有人披着国旗，有人披着苏联红旗，地铁里还能遇到穿着军装、胸前挂满勋章的老兵。

[图]

[图]

[图]

[图]

站了一上午，下午又一路赶着跑了中央武装力量博物馆、阿尔巴特街、胜利公园和俯首山的胜利博物馆。到处都在演出：军乐队在博物馆的大楼梯上奏乐，展厅里有人唱老歌，礼堂里坐得满满当当。

[图]

[图]

[图]

阿尔巴特街上，一位白发老人站在路边，手里拿着稿子，对着来往的行人演讲；整条街上都是街头艺人，唱歌的、拉琴的、表演的，一个挨着一个。

[图]

[图]

[图]

[图]

天黑以后，红场边上，老兵们的家人纷纷举着牌子走上街头游行。警车在周围鸣着警笛，绕了一圈又一圈。

[图]

晚上回到扎里亚季耶公园，在克里姆林宫对面等烟花。可是到了十点，夜空一片安静，烟花没有来。持续了这么多年的惯例，就这样被打破了。

[图]

聚在观景台上的人们很是失望。有人拉起了手风琴，大家围成一圈，一首接一首地唱起了老歌。可就连这点事，也很快引来了警察，人群被驱散了。

[图]

这和 2025 年简直不像是同一个节日。也许这场战争对俄罗斯来说，确实是一个错误。原本纪念胜利与和平的日子，放在 2026 年这个节点上看，也颇有几分讽刺的意味了。
stories.textEn:
Late on 8 May 1945, Germany signed its unconditional surrender at Karlshorst, on the edge of Berlin. It was 22:43 in Berlin, but already past midnight in Moscow, so it was 9 May. That is why Western Europe marks Victory in Europe on 8 May, while the Soviet Union, and Russia after it, celebrates on 9 May.

The Soviet Union lost around 27 million people in what Russians call the Great Patriotic War; almost every family has someone who never came home. So Victory Day in Russia is less a holiday than a nationwide day of remembrance. It was not always this grand: it was a day off for the first few years after the war, became a working day again in 1948, and only got its day off and its Red Square parade back for the 20th anniversary in 1965. The parade has been held every year only since 1995. Today the day follows a set routine: a parade on Red Square in the morning; during the day, people wear the black-and-orange St George ribbon and carry portraits of their relatives in the Immortal Regiment march; concerts in every park; and at ten in the evening, salutes and fireworks go up across the city at once.

I spent two Victory Days in Moscow, one in 2025 and one in 2026.

2025 was the 80th anniversary, and it was huge. Leaders from more than twenty countries came to Red Square, and the honour guard of the Chinese People's Liberation Army marched in the parade and stole the show.

Sadly I stayed in that morning. I only went out in the afternoon, walked around the main building of Moscow State University, and then went up to Sparrow Hills to wait for the fireworks.

[图]

[图]

The holiday mood had started days earlier. The Moscow Aviation Institute held a military equipment show, with armoured vehicles and jeeps parked right in front of the lecture halls; students could handle real guns and pose with soldiers in camouflage. On stage, a girl in a beautiful dress sang Katyusha, her voice clear and graceful, completely at ease. It went straight to the soul.

[图]

[图]

Towards evening, vintage cars rolled out onto the streets one after another, flags flying and old songs playing. The small viewing platform on Sparrow Hills started to fill up, and before long it was packed shoulder to shoulder. When it got dark, the university's main building lit up with a light show, and the press had their cameras set up well in advance.

[图]

[图]

At ten sharp the fireworks burst over the far bank of the river, wave after wave, turning the whole sky red. People shouted "Ura!" and "Rossiya!" with every burst. That night, Moscow was truly celebrating.

[图]

[图]

In 2026 I gave it a whole day, hoping to really take it all in. But nothing was on the scale of the year before.

[图]

With the war situation getting tenser, the mobile network in central Moscow was simply cut off that day. In the morning I squeezed in near Red Square to watch the parade. All I saw were a few planes trailing tricolour smoke past a Stalinist high-rise, and the columns marching by. It felt rather shabby. Yet the crowd was as warm as ever: some wrapped in the Russian flag, some in the Soviet red banner, and on the metro you could still meet veterans in uniform with medals covering their chests.

[图]

[图]

[图]

[图]

After standing there all morning, I spent the afternoon rushing between the Central Museum of the Armed Forces, the Arbat, Victory Park and the Victory Museum on Poklonnaya Hill. There were performances everywhere: a military band playing on a museum's grand staircase, people singing old songs in the exhibition halls, an auditorium packed to the last seat.

[图]

[图]

[图]

On the Arbat, a white-haired old man stood by the road with his notes in hand, giving a speech to the passers-by, while the whole street was lined with buskers, singing, playing, performing, one after another.

[图]

[图]

[图]

[图]

After dark, by Red Square, the families of veterans came out onto the streets carrying placards. Police cars circled around them, sirens wailing, round and round again.

[图]

In the evening I went back to Zaryadye Park, across from the Kremlin, to wait for the fireworks. But ten o'clock came and the sky stayed silent. The fireworks never came. A tradition kept for so many years was simply broken.

[图]

The people gathered on the viewing platform were bitterly disappointed. Someone started playing an accordion, everyone formed a circle, and they sang old songs one after another. Even that soon drew the police, and the crowd was dispersed.

[图]

It hardly felt like the same holiday as in 2025. Perhaps this war really was a mistake for Russia. A day meant to remember victory and peace looks more than a little ironic from where 2026 stands.

stories.title: 格雷梅的雨
stories.text:
来土耳其之前，我最期待的就是卡帕多奇亚的热气球。清晨几百只气球一起升起来，从那些奇形怪状的岩石上空飘过去，这样的画面在网上看过太多次，总想亲眼看一回。

热气球受天气影响很大，只在特定月份的晴朗无风的清晨起飞。等到我们真把行程排下来，留给卡帕的清晨只剩一个。剩下的日子，一半在伊斯坦布尔，一半在路上。那时候看看天气预报，连续的晴天，觉得也够了，赶上一次就行。

到格雷梅的那天是个大晴天，天蓝得发亮，头顶慢悠悠地飘过一只热气球。我隔着电线拍下一张，心想这只是预告，明天早上才是正片。可曾想，这竟是我们这次旅程见到的唯一的热气球。

[图]

那几天卡帕一直是这样的天，每天都晴。偏偏我们留下的那个早上，下雨了。

天刚亮就出了门，地上是湿的，天是灰的，空中一只气球也没有。热气球怕风怕雨，这种天气是不会飞的，心里其实早就明白，可还是撑着伞在乌奇希萨尔站了很久，总觉得云说不定一会儿就散了。

[图]

没有热气球的卡帕多奇亚也不难看。城堡还在，岩柱还在，被雨打湿以后颜色深了一些，远处的山压得很低。只是看什么都像隔了一层，心思总往天上跑。

[图]

在镇子里随便走了走，巷子很安静，石墙湿漉漉的，没什么人。

[图]

后来雨停了，太阳出来，路边的水洼里映着一片蓝天，和前一天拍热气球时一模一样。

[图]

只是我们该走了。
stories.textEn:
Before Turkey, the thing I was looking forward to most was the hot-air balloons of Cappadocia. Hundreds of them rising together at dawn, drifting over all those strangely shaped rocks: I had seen the picture online so many times that I just wanted to see it once for real.

But when we actually planned the trip, Cappadocia got a single morning. The rest of the days went half to Istanbul and half to the road. At the time that seemed enough: the balloons only fly at dawn anyway, and one go would do.

The day we reached Göreme was perfectly clear, the sky a bright, glossy blue, and a single balloon drifted slowly overhead. I shot it through the power lines and thought: this is just the trailer, tomorrow morning is the real thing.

[图]

Cappadocia had been like that for days, sunny every single day. Only on the one morning we had, it rained.

We went out as soon as it was light. The ground was wet, the sky was grey, and there was not a single balloon in the air. Balloons don't fly in wind or rain, and deep down I knew it already, yet I stood under an umbrella in Uçhisar for a long time anyway, half believing the clouds might clear at any minute.

[图]

Cappadocia without balloons is still not bad to look at. The castle was still there, the rock spires were still there, a shade darker from the rain, with the far hills sitting low under the clouds. It's just that everything felt a step removed, and my mind kept drifting up to the sky.

[图]

We wandered around town for a bit. The lanes were quiet, the stone walls damp, hardly anyone about.

[图]

Later the rain stopped and the sun came out. A puddle by the road held a patch of blue sky, exactly the sky I had photographed the balloon in the day before.

[图]

Only by then, it was time for us to leave.

stories.title: 伊斯坦布尔：一座城，三个名字
stories.text:
伊斯坦布尔是世界上少有的横跨两个大洲的大城市。博斯普鲁斯海峡从中间穿过，北通黑海，南接马尔马拉海，西岸是欧洲，东岸是亚洲。欧洲这一侧又被一道叫金角湾的海湾分成两半：南边是老城，北边是加拉塔和贝伊奥卢。来之前只知道它有名，走了三天，才慢慢把这几块拼到一起。

[图]

这座城先后用过三个名字。公元前七世纪，希腊人在这里建了殖民城邦拜占庭。公元 330 年，罗马皇帝君士坦丁把首都迁到这里，城市改叫君士坦丁堡。西罗马灭亡以后，东罗马（后人叫它拜占庭帝国）又在这里撑了一千年。1453 年，奥斯曼苏丹穆罕默德二世攻破城墙，这里成了奥斯曼帝国的首都，一直到 1922 年帝国解体。前后算下来，它做了将近一千六百年的首都。1923 年土耳其共和国成立，首都定在安卡拉，但伊斯坦布尔至今仍是土耳其人口最多、经济最重要的城市。

“伊斯坦布尔”这个名字，一般认为来自希腊语里的“进城去”。奥斯曼人口头上早就这么叫，正式改名却要等到 1930 年。

海峡是这座城的主干道。渡轮就是公交的一部分，刷交通卡就能上，二十来分钟就从欧洲到了亚洲。傍晚坐船过海，会经过海中小岛上的少女塔。这座塔的历史能追溯到古代，现在的样子大多是十八、十九世纪重建的，当过灯塔，也当过瘟疫流行时的隔离站。

[图]

金角湾是一个天然深水港。拜占庭人守城时，在湾口拉过一条大铁链挡住敌船。1453 年围城，穆罕默德二世干脆让人把战船从加拉塔背后的山坡上拖过去，绕开铁链放进湾里。对岸山坡上那座圆锥顶的石塔叫加拉塔塔，1348 年由热那亚人修建。当时加拉塔是热那亚商人的居留地，有自己的城墙，塔就是城墙的一部分。

[图]

如今塔下全是上坡的小街和咖啡馆，白天排队上塔，天黑以后塔身亮灯，露台上坐满了人。

[图]

伊斯坦布尔的建筑，可以从圣索菲亚讲起。它在公元 537 年由查士丁尼皇帝建成，中央穹顶直径三十多米、离地五十多米，此后将近一千年里，一直是世界上最大的教堂。1453 年它被改成清真寺，外面陆续加了宣礼塔；1934 年共和国把它改成博物馆；2020 年又改回清真寺，游客现在仍然可以进去。

奥斯曼人接手这座城以后，没有拆掉圣索菲亚，而是学它。之后几百年的大清真寺，基本沿用了同一套结构：中间一个大穹顶，四周用半穹顶和小穹顶一层层托住，外面立起细高的宣礼塔。圣索菲亚对面的苏丹艾哈迈德清真寺就是这样，1616 年建成，有六座宣礼塔，里面贴了两万多块伊兹尼克瓷砖，以蓝色为主，所以又叫蓝色清真寺。我们去的时候，有一座宣礼塔还裹着脚手架。

[图]

把这套做法推到成熟的是建筑师锡南，他一生主持修建了三百多座建筑。他为苏莱曼大帝修的苏莱曼尼耶清真寺，1557 年完工，建在老城的一座山头上。从金角湾北岸往回看，老城山脊上是一个接一个的穹顶和宣礼塔，日落时只剩剪影，这是伊斯坦布尔最容易认出来的一道天际线。

[图]

离圣索菲亚不远是大巴扎，1455 年前后开始修建，是世界上最古老、规模最大的室内市场之一，六十多条街巷，四千来家店铺，头顶是彩绘的拱顶。卖得最多的是地毯、首饰、香料，还有用彩色玻璃拼起来的马赛克灯。从大巴扎往金角湾走是一路下坡，两边全是批发小摊，人比大巴扎里还多。

[图]

过了金角湾到贝伊奥卢，街景一下子换成了欧洲的样子。十九世纪这一带叫佩拉，外国使馆、商行和银行都聚在这里，沿街是新古典主义和新艺术风格的石头楼，还有带玻璃顶的拱廊。主街独立大街一公里多长，全程步行，只有一辆红色的怀旧电车在中间慢慢开，从塔克西姆开到隧道站。“隧道”指的是 1875 年通车的一段地下缆索铁路，是世界上第二古老的地铁，仅次于伦敦。

[图]

独立大街的另一头是塔克西姆广场，广场中间是 1928 年落成的共和国纪念碑。周围的山坡上，公寓楼一栋挨一栋，一直排到海边。

[图]

共和国成立后的十几年里，土耳其做了一连串改革：政教分离，1928 年废除阿拉伯字母、改用拉丁字母，1934 年女性获得选举权。这些改革到今天仍有争论，但留下的结果在伊斯坦布尔街头很容易看到：戴头巾的和不戴头巾的走在同一条街上，清真寺的宣礼声和酒吧的音乐隔得不远，大家都习以为常。

在埃米诺努的广场上，有一个声援巴勒斯坦的摊位，几位戴头巾的女士举着旗子和标语，旁边有人停下来拍照，也有人径直走过。在这里，把自己的立场摆到广场上是很平常的事。

[图]

比建筑更让我记得住的是人。伊斯坦布尔人对陌生人很少设防，在街上举起相机，换来的多半不是躲开，而是一个笑脸或者一个姿势。巴拉特从前是犹太人、希腊人和亚美尼亚人聚居的街区，彩色的房子顺着山坡排上去。在那里，一扇窗户里的孩子看见镜头，一下全挤到栏杆前面比手势。傍晚在街上碰到两位大哥，相机一举，他们就并排站好了。这座城几百年来一直住着不同的人，大概也是它对外人这么自然的原因。

[图]

到了晚上，城市也没有要睡的意思。九点多的地铁照样挤满了人。2013 年开通的马尔马拉线从海峡底下穿过去，欧亚两岸之间坐地铁只要几分钟。海峡上的游船还在开派对，舞者转着圈跳到了客人的桌子中间。

[图]

三天下来，最深的印象是这座城很“满”：两千多年的历史压在几座山头上，教堂、清真寺和欧式公寓挤在一起，海峡里船来船往，街上人多、猫多，声音也多。但它并不让人紧张。这里的人愿意跟你打招呼，愿意让你拍，也愿意把自己的想法说出来。做了一千六百年首都的城市，见过的外人太多了，早就不把你当外人。
stories.textEn:
Istanbul is one of the few great cities that sit on two continents. The Bosphorus runs through the middle of it, linking the Black Sea to the north with the Sea of Marmara to the south: Europe on the west bank, Asia on the east. The European side is split again by an inlet called the Golden Horn, with the old city to the south and Galata and Beyoğlu to the north. I knew the name long before I came; it took three days of walking to fit these pieces together.

[图]

The city has gone by three names. In the 7th century BC, Greek colonists founded Byzantium here. In AD 330 the Roman emperor Constantine moved his capital here and the city became Constantinople. After the Western Empire fell, the Eastern Roman Empire (what we now call the Byzantine Empire) held on here for another thousand years. In 1453 the Ottoman sultan Mehmed II broke through the walls, and the city became the Ottoman capital until the empire was dissolved in 1922. All told, it was a capital for almost 1,600 years. When the Republic of Turkey was founded in 1923 the capital moved to Ankara, but Istanbul is still the country's largest city and its economic centre.

The name "Istanbul" is usually traced to a Greek phrase meaning "into the city". The Ottomans had used it in speech for centuries, but it only became the official name in 1930.

The strait is the city's main road. Ferries are part of public transport: tap your transit card and you are in Asia in twenty minutes or so. Crossing at dusk, you pass the Maiden's Tower on its islet in the water. Its history goes back to antiquity, though what you see today was mostly rebuilt in the 18th and 19th centuries. It has served as a lighthouse, and as a quarantine station during epidemics.

[图]

The Golden Horn is a natural deep-water harbour. The Byzantines defended it by stretching a great chain across its mouth. During the siege of 1453, Mehmed II simply had his warships hauled over the hill behind Galata and slid into the inlet past the chain. The stone tower with the conical roof on the far slope is the Galata Tower, built by the Genoese in 1348. Galata was then a Genoese trading colony with its own walls, and the tower was part of them.

[图]

Today the streets around it are steep lanes lined with cafés. By day people queue to climb the tower; after dark it is lit up and the terraces below fill with people.

[图]

Istanbul's architecture starts with Hagia Sophia. Completed under Emperor Justinian in 537, its central dome is over thirty metres across and more than fifty metres above the floor, and for nearly a thousand years it was the largest church in the world. In 1453 it became a mosque and minarets were added over time; in 1934 the Republic turned it into a museum; in 2020 it became a mosque again. Visitors can still go in.

When the Ottomans took the city, they did not tear Hagia Sophia down; they learned from it. For centuries afterwards the great mosques followed the same scheme: one large central dome, held up by tiers of half-domes and smaller domes, with slender minarets outside. The Sultan Ahmed Mosque across the square is a textbook case. Finished in 1616, it has six minarets and more than twenty thousand İznik tiles inside, mostly blue, hence the name Blue Mosque. When we visited, one of the minarets was still wrapped in scaffolding.

[图]

The architect who brought this formula to maturity was Sinan, who oversaw more than three hundred buildings in his lifetime. His Süleymaniye Mosque, built for Suleiman the Magnificent and finished in 1557, stands on one of the old city's hills. Looking back from the north shore of the Golden Horn, the ridge is lined with dome after dome and minaret after minaret, and at sunset only the silhouettes remain. It is the skyline everyone recognises.

[图]

Not far from Hagia Sophia is the Grand Bazaar, begun around 1455 and one of the oldest and largest covered markets in the world: some sixty streets, around four thousand shops, under painted vaults. Carpets, jewellery and spices sell best, along with mosaic lamps pieced together from coloured glass. Walking from the bazaar down to the Golden Horn is downhill all the way, past wholesale stalls on both sides, and the crowds are even thicker than inside.

[图]

Cross the Golden Horn into Beyoğlu and the streets suddenly look European. In the 19th century this area was called Pera, home to foreign embassies, trading houses and banks, and the streets were lined with neoclassical and Art Nouveau stone buildings and glass-roofed arcades. The main street, İstiklal Avenue, runs for more than a kilometre and is pedestrian only, except for a red heritage tram that trundles down the middle from Taksim to Tünel. "Tünel" refers to an underground funicular opened in 1875, the second-oldest underground railway in the world after London's.

[图]

At the other end of İstiklal is Taksim Square, with the Republic Monument, unveiled in 1928, at its centre. On the hillsides around it, apartment blocks stand shoulder to shoulder all the way down to the water.

[图]

In its first fifteen years or so, the Republic pushed through a series of reforms: separating religion from the state, replacing the Arabic script with the Latin alphabet in 1928, and giving women the vote in 1934. The reforms are still argued over today, but their results are easy to see on Istanbul's streets: women with and without headscarves walk the same pavements, the call to prayer and the music from the bars are never far apart, and nobody finds any of it strange.

On a square in Eminönü there was a stall in solidarity with Palestine. A few women in headscarves held flags and placards; some passers-by stopped to take photos, others walked straight past. Here, putting your views out on a public square is an ordinary thing to do.

[图]

What stayed with me more than the buildings was the people. Istanbulites are rarely guarded with strangers. Raise a camera in the street and you are more likely to get a smile or a pose than someone turning away. Balat was once home to Jewish, Greek and Armenian communities, and its painted houses climb the hillside. There, a group of children spotted the camera and crowded up to the bars of their window, making hand signs. One evening we ran into two men on the street; the moment I lifted the camera, they stood side by side for a portrait. A city that has housed so many different peoples for so many centuries probably finds outsiders nothing unusual.

[图]

At night the city shows no sign of going to sleep. The metro is still packed after nine. The Marmaray line, opened in 2013, runs under the strait, so crossing between Europe and Asia by train takes only a few minutes. Out on the Bosphorus the party boats are still going, a dancer spinning her way between the guests' tables.

[图]

After three days, what struck me most was how full this city is: more than two thousand years of history piled onto a few hills, churches, mosques and European apartment blocks crammed together, ships coming and going in the strait, the streets busy with people, cats and noise. Yet none of it feels tense. People here are happy to say hello, happy to be photographed, and happy to say what they think. A city that was a capital for sixteen centuries has seen so many outsiders that it no longer treats you as one.
