stories.title: 俄罗斯乡村，菲涅耶沃的夏至
stories.text:
六月，同学邀请我去他家在菲涅耶沃的小屋住几天，顺便参加村里的夏至祭典。菲涅耶沃在莫斯科东北一百来公里，已经出了莫斯科州，属于弗拉基米尔州的基尔扎奇区，一片森林和草地中间零零散散的木头房子。

[图]

其实这不是我第一次来。一月份我就跟他来过一趟，那时候整片林子被大雪压着，路两边的树全弯了腰，车在雪道里慢慢往里挪。

[图]

到了先得铲雪，才能把院子的门推开。

[图]

屋里靠一个铁炉子取暖，进门第一件事就是把火生起来。连摩托车都停在屋里过冬。桌上摆着自家腌的黄瓜，配上热乎乎的饭菜，外面零下二十度，屋里暖得让人不想动。

[图]

夏天再来，完全是另一个地方。草长到膝盖，森林绿得发黑，晚上十点天还亮着。

在莫斯科，所有人都在赶：地铁里小跑着换乘，扶梯上左边要留给赶时间的人，咖啡拿在手上边走边喝。到了这里，时间像是被拉长了。早上没人定闹钟，饭什么时候做好什么时候吃，一下午坐在院子里聊天也没人觉得浪费。

祭典一早就开始了。我本来以为就是村里人凑在一起吃吃喝喝，结果一到场就被镇住了：大家换上了民族服装，女生穿着长长的萨拉凡裙，头上包着印花头巾，男生是红色的立领衬衫系着腰带；有人敲大鼓，有人抱着传统弦乐器边走边弹边唱。

[图]

更让我惊讶的是，这些人几乎个个多才多艺。白天看着就是普普通通的村民，换上衣服就能弹能唱，能在马背上拉弓射箭，能给孩子们排一整台节目。他们也特别热情开放，看我一个外国面孔，主动过来拉我说话、教我规矩、叫我一起玩，一点不见外。

女生们围坐在长桌边，用野花和枝叶编花环，编好了戴在头上，一整天都不摘。

[图]

然后是牵手转圈。所有人手拉着手围成一个大圈，跟着歌声一圈一圈地转，越转越快，大人小孩笑成一片。俄语叫它 хоровод（圆圈舞），是斯拉夫乡村最古老的集体舞之一。

[图]

草地边上还有马。会骑的人在马背上射箭表演，不会骑的也能被牵着走上一圈。

[图]

还有各种小游戏。一个披着山羊头的扮演者在人群里乱窜，追着小孩子跑，孩子们又怕又想凑上去。

[图]

最有意思的是许愿丝带。大家把写了心愿的彩色丝带挂在一棵小白桦树上，然后女生们围着树守护丝带，男生们想办法冲进去抢。一边拼命护，一边拼命抢，场面一度非常混乱。

[图]

傍晚，几个人扛着一个用稻草扎成的大草人，带着整支队伍穿过田野走到河边，把草人扔进河里，送走旧的，迎接新的。

[图]

接下来是河边的重头戏：男生和女生分开，女生在上游，男生在下游，各自下河洗浴。上游的女生把头上的花环抛进水里，花环顺着水漂下来，下游的男生去接。按老传统，谁接到了哪个姑娘的花环，就跟她有了缘分。

[图]

天黑以后，篝火点起来了。大家围着火堆跳舞唱歌，一直跳到火慢慢小下去。等篝火快烧完的时候，开始有人一个助跑跳过火堆，一个接一个，男生跳，女生跳，手拉手一对一对地跳。据说跳过去，就把身上的晦气和病痛都留在了火里。

[图]

这天最重要的事，是我遇上了传奇摄影师梅利尼科夫。

瓦列里·梅利尼科夫（Валерий Мельников），1973 年出生在俄罗斯南部的斯塔夫罗波尔边疆区，学新闻出身，在《生意人报》做了十来年图片记者，2009 年起在「今日俄罗斯」国际通讯社。二十多年来他一直在拍冲突地区：车臣、南奥塞梯、黎巴嫩、马里、叙利亚，2014 年起拍顿巴斯，凭这组照片拿过 2017 年荷赛（World Press Photo）长期项目类一等奖，此外还拿过 POY、索尼世界摄影奖、LensCulture 等一长串奖。平时只在获奖作品里见过的名字，就这样拿着相机站在我旁边。

[图]

于是我跟着他，还有另外几个摄影师，在祭典上一通爽拍。从下午的阳光拍到日落，再拍到篝火边。

[图]

天黑以后光越来越难，篝火是唯一的光源。人站在火边，脸被照得通红，身后是一片黑，这样的光一年也遇不上几次。

[图]

几个人趴在草地上找角度，谁也不在乎衣服上沾了多少泥。

[图]

一直玩到深夜，临走前跟新认识的朋友们在篝火前合了张影。

[图]

祭典结束后，我们又在小屋住了几天。桌上永远堆满吃的，草莓和樱桃都是院子里刚摘的。

我们还一起去了附近的加加林坠机地点。1968 年 3 月 27 日，人类第一位进入太空的宇航员尤里·加加林和飞行教官谢廖金驾驶米格-15UTI 教练机做训练飞行，坠毁在基尔扎奇区诺沃肖洛沃村附近的树林里，两人都没能生还。离小屋并不远，如今那里立着一座纪念碑，四周还是安安静静的森林。

[图]

回到院子里，就是烧烤。肉提前腌好，串上铁签架在炭火上，烤得滋滋冒油。

[图]

等肉的工夫，钻进菜园里摘草莓，伸手就能从树上摘樱桃。

[图]

这几天过得飞快，每天都很快乐。这大概是离开这个国家前夕我所收到的最好的礼物。

[图]
stories.textEn:
In June, a classmate invited me to spend a few days at his family's dacha in Fineevo and join the village's midsummer festival. Fineevo is about a hundred kilometres northeast of Moscow, just past the border of Moscow Oblast in the Kirzhach district of Vladimir Oblast: wooden houses scattered between forest and meadow.

[图]

It wasn't actually my first time there. I had come with him once in January, when the whole forest was buried in snow, the trees on both sides of the road bent under the weight, and the car crept along the snowy track.

[图]

Before we could even open the gate we had to dig our way in.

[图]

The house is heated by an iron stove, and the first thing you do when you walk in is get the fire going. Even the motorbike spends the winter indoors. On the table: home-pickled cucumbers and hot food. Minus twenty outside, and so warm inside you never want to move.

[图]

In summer it is a different place altogether. The grass is knee-high, the forest so green it is almost black, and it is still light at ten at night.

In Moscow everyone is in a hurry: jogging between metro lines, keeping the left side of the escalator free for people who are late, drinking coffee on the move. Here time seems to stretch. Nobody sets an alarm, you eat whenever the food is ready, and spending a whole afternoon chatting in the garden is not considered a waste.

The festival started in the morning. I had expected a few villagers eating and drinking together, and was stunned the moment we arrived: everyone was in folk costume, women in long sarafans with printed headscarves, men in red high-collared shirts with sashes. Someone was beating a big drum, others were playing traditional string instruments and singing as they walked.

[图]

What surprised me even more was how talented everyone was. People who look like ordinary villagers during the day change clothes and suddenly they can play, sing, shoot a bow from horseback, and put on a whole show with the kids. They were also incredibly warm and open. Seeing a foreign face, they came over to talk, explained the customs and pulled me into the games without a second thought.

The women sat around a long table weaving wreaths out of wildflowers and leaves, and wore them all day.

[图]

Then came the round dance. Everyone held hands in a big circle and turned with the song, faster and faster, adults and children laughing together. In Russian it is called a khorovod, one of the oldest communal dances of the Slavic countryside.

[图]

There were horses at the edge of the meadow. Those who could ride shot arrows from the saddle; those who couldn't were led around for a lap.

[图]

And all kinds of games. Someone in a goat's head ran through the crowd chasing the kids, who were both scared of it and desperate to get close.

[图]

My favourite was the wish ribbons. Everyone tied coloured ribbons with their wishes onto a young birch, then the girls formed a ring around the tree to guard them while the boys tried to break through and snatch them. One side defending with everything they had, the other attacking with everything they had: total chaos.

[图]

In the evening a few men shouldered a big straw effigy and led the whole procession across the fields to the river, where it was thrown into the water: sending off the old, welcoming the new.

[图]

Then came the main event by the river. Men and women split up, women upstream and men downstream, and went into the water to bathe. The women threw their wreaths into the river, the wreaths floated down, and the men tried to catch them. By old tradition, whoever catches a girl's wreath is bound to her by fate.

[图]

After dark the bonfire was lit. Everyone danced and sang around it until it slowly burned down. When it was nearly out, people started taking a run-up and leaping over it, one after another: men, women, couples hand in hand. Jump over, they say, and you leave your bad luck and illnesses in the fire.

[图]

The most important thing that happened that day was meeting the legendary photographer Melnikov.

Valery Melnikov was born in 1973 in Stavropol Krai in southern Russia and studied journalism. He spent about ten years as a staff photographer at Kommersant and joined the Rossiya Segodnya news agency in 2009. For more than twenty years he has photographed conflict zones: Chechnya, South Ossetia, Lebanon, Mali, Syria, and from 2014 the Donbas, work that won him first prize in the Long-Term Projects category at World Press Photo 2017, alongside a long list of other awards including POY, the Sony World Photography Awards and LensCulture. A name I had only ever seen next to award-winning pictures was standing right next to me with a camera.

[图]

So I tagged along with him and a few other photographers and we shot the festival to our hearts' content, from the afternoon sun through sunset to the bonfire.

[图]

After dark the light got harder and harder, and the fire was the only source. People standing next to it, faces lit red, nothing but black behind them: you don't get light like that many times a year.

[图]

We lay down in the grass looking for angles, nobody caring how much mud ended up on their clothes. Shooting alongside someone like him, watching how he looks and how he waits, taught me more than any tutorial.

[图]

We stayed until late at night, and before leaving took a photo with our new friends in front of the fire.

[图]

After the festival we stayed at the dacha for a few more days. The table was always piled with food, the strawberries and cherries freshly picked from the garden.

We also went together to the nearby site where Gagarin's plane went down. On 27 March 1968, Yuri Gagarin, the first human in space, and his flight instructor Vladimir Seryogin crashed in a MiG-15UTI trainer during a training flight, in the woods near the village of Novoselovo in the Kirzhach district. Neither survived. It isn't far from the dacha; today a memorial stands there, surrounded by the same quiet forest.

[图]

Back in the garden: barbecue. The meat marinated in advance, threaded onto steel skewers and laid over the coals until it sizzled.

[图]

While we waited for the meat, we went into the vegetable patch to pick strawberries, and picked cherries straight off the tree.

[图]

Those days flew by, and every one of them was happy. Back in Moscow I was swept straight back into the metro, the escalators and the coffee, but I keep thinking of that little house, the round dance in the meadow, and the wreaths floating down the river.

[图]

stories.title: 混进复活节
stories.text:
在俄罗斯，复活节是东正教一年里最大的节日，比圣诞节还要隆重。东正教按旧历（儒略历）推算日子，所以复活节常常和西方的不在同一天：2026 年天主教和新教的复活节是 4 月 5 日，俄罗斯的是 4 月 12 日。节前有七个星期的大斋，不吃肉蛋奶；节前那个周六，大家提着篮子去教堂，里面装着高高的复活节面包、奶渣做的甜点和染好的彩蛋，排队等神父洒圣水。

重头戏在复活节前一夜。礼拜从深夜开始，快到零点时，神父举着十字架和圣像，领着所有人捧着蜡烛绕教堂走一圈，这叫十字游行。回到门口，神父高喊“基督复活了！”，所有人齐声回“真的复活了！”，一晚上要来回喊好多遍，礼拜一直持续到凌晨。莫斯科最隆重的一场在基督救世主大教堂，由牧首亲自主持，电视上全程直播。

[图]

那天晚上下着雨。我以为救世主大教堂九点开始仪式，到时候会开门让普通人进去，就冒着雨赶了过去。到了才发现，那天晚上它根本不对外开放，能进去的都是受了邀请的人。我只能和一群同样进不去的人站在外面，淋着雨看里面的直播。

不甘心就这么回去，我在附近找了一座小教堂。到的时候，教堂的小院已经被围得水泄不通，人从教堂里面一直挤到院子，又从院子漫到外面的马路上。零点前后，里面传出一声“基督复活了！”，院子里、马路上的人一起喊回去：“真的复活了！”一遍接一遍，一浪高过一浪。我站在人堆里，被震得有点发愣。

[图]

接下来是很长的唱诗和一个接一个的仪式。神父隔一阵就再喊一遍“基督复活了”，大家就再回一遍。教会斯拉夫语我一句也听不懂，只能跟着人群站着，看手里的蜡烛一点点烧短。

[图]

后来不知道从哪一刻起，大家突然开始排队。我不明白在排什么，前后左右全是人，想挤出去也挤不出去，干脆就跟着往前挪。挪到前排才看明白：神父端着圣杯，正用一把小勺挨个给人喂圣餐。圣餐是一小块发酵的面包，泡在兑了温水的红葡萄酒里，两样一起盛在勺里送进嘴里。按东正教的说法，它们在礼拜中已经真正变成了基督的身体和血，领了圣餐，就是和基督合为一体。

[图]

按规矩，能领圣餐的是受过洗的东正教徒，事先还要斋戒、告解。可我已经排到这儿了，这时候掉头走好像更奇怪。轮到我的时候，神父看着我问了一句，我脑子一抽，说：我是基督徒。

接下来就是破绽百出。别人双手交叉抱在胸前，我的手不知道往哪放；该做什么、做完往哪走，全靠偷看前面的人，慢半拍地照着学。整个过程尬到想原地钻进地里。神父和旁边帮忙的人大概早就看出了端倪，但谁也没说什么，只是笑了笑，让我过去了。谢天谢地。

[图]

第二天出门，街上还是一片过节的样子，莫斯科河边摆满了彩绘的大彩蛋。被雨浇，被关在门外，又被人群裹着领了一回圣餐，总之是一段很奇特的经历。

[图]
stories.textEn:
In Russia, Easter is the biggest feast of the Orthodox year, bigger even than Christmas. The Orthodox Church still reckons it by the old Julian calendar, so it often falls on a different day from the Western one: in 2026, Catholic and Protestant Easter was on April 5, the Russian one on April 12. Before it come seven weeks of Great Lent with no meat, eggs or dairy. On the Saturday before, people carry baskets to church, packed with tall Easter bread, a sweet curd dessert and dyed eggs, and queue for the priest to sprinkle them with holy water.

The main event is the night before Easter. The service starts late; shortly before midnight the priests lead everyone, candles in hand, behind the cross and icons around the church in a procession. Back at the doors the priest calls out "Christ is risen!" and the whole crowd answers "Truly He is risen!", back and forth again and again, and the service goes on until early morning. Moscow's grandest one is at the Cathedral of Christ the Saviour, led by the Patriarch himself and broadcast live on TV.

[图]

It was raining that night. I thought the service at Christ the Saviour started at nine and that they would open the doors to ordinary people, so I hurried over in the rain. Only when I got there did I find out that it was not open to the public at all that night; only invited guests could go in. All I could do was stand outside with a crowd of other people who couldn't get in either, getting rained on and watching the live stream of what was happening inside.

Not ready to give up and go home, I found a small church nearby. By the time I got there its little yard was packed solid: people filled the church, spilled into the yard, and from the yard out onto the street. Around midnight a voice from inside called "Christ is risen!", and everyone in the yard and on the street shouted back "Truly He is risen!", again and again, each wave louder than the last. Standing in the middle of it all, I was a little stunned.

[图]

Then came a long stretch of singing and one ritual after another. Every so often the priest called out "Christ is risen" once more, and everyone answered once more. I couldn't understand a word of Church Slavonic, so I just stood with the crowd and watched my candle burn down.

[图]

At some point, I don't know when, everyone suddenly started lining up. I had no idea what for, there were people on every side, I couldn't squeeze my way out, so I just shuffled forward with them. Only near the front did I see what it was: a priest holding the chalice, giving communion to each person in turn from a little spoon. Communion is a small piece of leavened bread soaked in red wine mixed with warm water, both given together on the spoon. In Orthodox teaching they have truly become the body and blood of Christ during the service, and receiving them means being united with Christ.

[图]

By the rules, communion is for baptised Orthodox Christians, who are also supposed to fast and go to confession beforehand. But I had already made it this far, and turning back now seemed even stranger. When my turn came the priest looked at me and asked something, and in a moment of madness I said: I'm a Christian.

What followed gave me away at every step. Everyone else stood with their arms crossed over their chest; I didn't know what to do with my hands. What to do, and where to go afterwards, I worked out by peeking at the person in front of me and copying them half a beat late. The whole thing was so awkward I wanted the floor to swallow me. The priest and his helpers must have seen right through me, but nobody said a thing. They just smiled and let me through. Thank God.

[图]

The next day the streets still felt like a holiday, and along the Moskva River stood rows of big painted Easter eggs. Rained on, shut out, then swept along by a crowd into taking communion: all in all, a very strange experience.

[图]

stories.title: 五月的金环小镇
stories.titleEn: Suzdal and Vladimir: small towns in May
stories.text:
五月初，我们一行人从莫斯科坐上火车，一路颠簸，来到了弗拉基米尔火车站。车站看起来很有年代感，站房、站台、指示牌，处处透着一股苏联味，像是几十年都没怎么变过。

因为战争的原因，火车站附近没有网络，手机地图打不开，消息也发不出去。一群人站在站前东张西望，差点走丢。

[图]

好在汽车站就在火车站边上。我们挤上一辆满载的巴士，坐着的、站着的、抱着包的，一车人摇摇晃晃，开到了苏兹达尔小镇的中心。

[图]

苏兹达尔是一个风景很优美的地方。镇子不大，人口不到一万，却是莫斯科东北“金环”古城里很有名的一座。镇中心人很多，游客来来往往，到处是教堂，白墙、金顶、蓝顶，随便一抬头就是一座。

[图]

广场上有拉手风琴的大爷，有打扮得花花绿绿、等着驮游客的小马，有穿着传统长裙的姑娘，还有马车在街上慢慢走。

[图]

[图]

街边有卖鱼干的摊子，老人坐在白墙下歇脚。

[图]

往河边走，草地高高低低，远处又是一排教堂的尖顶。

[图]

[图]

到了镇子边缘的居民区，气氛一下子变了。游客少了，换成一栋栋木头房子，墙刷成蓝的、黄的、绿的，门廊和窗框上都是雕花，透着一股惬意舒适的味道，很有民俗风味。有人在院子里翻地，准备种菜。

[图]

[图]

孩子们在广场上玩耍，跑来跑去，骑车的男孩翘着前轮从面前经过。

[图]

[图]

居民区静谧慵懒，猫猫到处走，有的趴在窗帘后面，有的蹲在路中间晒太阳，一点也不怕人。

[图]

五月的天气渐渐回暖，太阳晒在身上暖洋洋的。晚上我们在镇上住下。

[图]

[图]

傍晚出门，走到河边。太阳慢慢落下去，教堂的圆顶被染成金色，河边坐着看日落的人，游船慢悠悠地从水面上开过。

[图]

[图]

[图]

路上还碰到些意想不到的：停在路边的中国房车，开到这不知得多久；还有被主人牵着散步的小家伙。

[图]

第二天上午，我们又在镇上转了一圈。修道院的城墙，白色的教堂，窗台上的花，院门上坐着的小熊。

[图]

[图]

[图]

走累了，就往草地上一躺，旁边还有山羊在吃草。配上五月回暖的天气，让人想在户外就这么坐一整天，什么也不干。

[图]

下午我们回到弗拉基米尔。弗拉基米尔也差不多是这个氛围，城比苏兹达尔大一些，同样到处是教堂，同样不紧不慢。八百多年前，这里是弗拉基米尔-苏兹达尔公国的都城，山坡上的圣母升天大教堂建于 12 世纪，金顶远远就能看见。

[图]

街上跑着红色的无轨电车，老人坐在纪念碑前晒太阳。

[图]

站在山上往下看，克利亚济马河从城边流过，河上架着长桥，再远就是一望无际的树林和平原。

[图]
stories.textEn:
In early May, a few of us took the train out of Moscow and rattled our way to Vladimir station. The station looked its age: the building, the platforms, the signs all had that Soviet feel, as if nothing had changed in decades.

Because of the war, there was no mobile internet around the station. Maps wouldn't load and messages wouldn't send, and we stood outside looking around and very nearly got lost.

[图]

Luckily the bus station is right next door. We squeezed onto a packed bus, people sitting, standing, hugging their bags, and swayed all the way to the centre of Suzdal.

[图]

Suzdal is a beautiful place. It's a small town of fewer than ten thousand people, but one of the best-known old towns on the Golden Ring north-east of Moscow. The centre was busy with visitors, and there were churches everywhere: white walls, gold domes, blue domes. Look up anywhere and there's one.

[图]

On the square there was an old man playing the accordion, ponies decked out in bright colours waiting for riders, a girl in a traditional dress, and carriages rolling slowly down the street.

[图]

[图]

There was a dried-fish stall by the road, and an old man resting by a white wall.

[图]

Towards the river the meadows rose and fell, with another row of church spires in the distance.

[图]

[图]

Out at the edge of town, in the residential streets, the mood changed. Fewer tourists, more wooden houses painted blue, yellow and green, with carved porches and window frames. It felt easy and comfortable, full of folk charm. Someone was turning the soil in a backyard, getting ready to plant.

[图]

[图]

Kids were playing on the square, running around, and a boy rode past us on his back wheel.

[图]

[图]

The streets were quiet and lazy, and cats wandered everywhere: one behind a curtain, one sitting in the middle of the road in the sun, not bothered by anyone.

[图]

May was warming up, and the sun felt good. That night we stayed in town.

[图]

[图]

At dusk we walked down to the river. The sun sank, the domes turned gold, people sat on the bank watching, and a boat slid slowly across the water.

[图]

[图]

[图]

We came across a few surprises too: a Chinese camper van parked by the road, and a little animal out for a walk on a leash.

[图]

The next morning we wandered around town again: the monastery walls, a white church, flowers on a windowsill, a teddy bear sitting on a gate.

[图]

[图]

[图]

When we got tired we just lay down in the grass, with a goat grazing nearby. With May warming up like that, you could sit outside all day and do nothing at all.

[图]

In the afternoon we went back to Vladimir, and it had much the same feel: a bit bigger than Suzdal, just as full of churches, just as unhurried. More than eight hundred years ago this was the capital of the Vladimir-Suzdal principality, and the Dormition Cathedral on the hill, built in the 12th century, shows its gold domes from far away.

[图]

Red trolleybuses ran down the street, and an old couple sat in the sun by a monument.

[图]

We squeezed in for a selfie too. From the hill you could see the Klyazma river running past the city, a long bridge across it, and beyond that, forest and plain as far as the eye could see.

[图]

stories.title: 厄尔布鲁士，和山下的小城
stories.titleEn: Elbrus, and the towns below it
stories.text:
十一月底，我们飞去俄罗斯南部，为的是爬厄尔布鲁士——高加索山脉的最高峰，也是欧洲最高峰。飞机落在矿水城，我们没在那儿多停，直接去了离得不远的五山城住下，作为上山前的落脚点。

[图]

矿水城和五山城给人的第一印象很像：都透着一股衰败的气息。路边停着锈透了的老伏尔加，楼房外墙斑驳，街上没什么人，天一暗下来就更显冷清。只有站到高处往下看，才发现城市其实铺得很开，傍晚灯火一点点亮起来，倒也有几分温柔。

[图]

爬山那天一早跟团出发，车往山脚下开。越往里走山越深，沿途是一个接一个的小镇，散落在不同的山谷里，彼此之间隔着大片荒山，像一座座被隔离开的孤岛。我很惊讶，这么深的大山里居然有这样的定居点，有房子、有小商店、有人家，人们就这样一代代住在这里。

[图]

[图]

到了山脚，我们坐缆车上山。缆车一段接一段往上爬，窗外从枯黄的山坡变成雪坡，最后只剩一片白。到了终点加拉巴什站，海拔三千八百多米，我已经明显胸闷气短，走几步就喘，脑袋也有点发胀。可就在这样的地方，居然还有很多滑雪的人，扛着雪板在雪坡上来来去去，好像稀薄的空气对他们一点影响都没有。

[图]

[图]

[图]

[图]

山上还有狐狸，一点也不怕人，大大方方地在游客中间转悠，被围了一圈人拍照也不躲。

[图]

下山之后，我们体验了一些俄式农家乐。印象最深的是一种水，喝起来有一股很重的铁锈味，泉眼边上结满了白色的结晶。听当地人说，这水喝了对身体好。我们也跟着喝了几口，那股锈味实在让人难忘。

[图]

[图]

同行的团里还有一对年轻夫妻，两个人感情特别好，一路上说说笑笑，看着就让人觉得幸福洋溢。他们也很热心，一路找我们聊天，导游用俄语讲解的时候就在旁边帮我们翻译。分别时还送了我们贴纸。我只是随口提过一句自己的生日，没想到他们真的记住了，到了那一天准时发来祝福。萍水相逢，能被这样认真地对待，真是很友好的人。

再说回五山城。待得越久，越觉得它颓势尽显：老房子年久失修，墙皮一块块剥落，看得出曾经的体面，如今只剩个架子。这大概也是大部分俄罗斯小城的现状。

[图]

[图]

这里的有轨电车还是那种究极老式的，车厢又小又旧，轨道很窄，也修得很烂，坐在车上一路颠来颠去。车上还保留着传统的随车售票员，上车后售票员挨个走过来收钱、给票。

一天晚上，我们坐着小电车在城里乱逛，一直坐到了一个荒凉的车站。四周黑灯瞎火，车站简陋得像农村的茅厕。很难想象，离城中心不过几公里，就是这样的地方。

在那里我们还碰到了几个中国留学生。如果是我，在这样一个偏远的小地方留学，怕是真要抑郁了。

小城也让我们几个中国人成了稀客，路过的人都得多看一眼，孩子们看到了也尤其兴奋，纷纷跟同伴指着说“快看有中国人”，感觉十分有趣。

[图]

[图]

最后一天我们去爬城边的另一座小山，马舒克山。那天起了大雾，我们依然坐缆车上山。这缆车也是究极老古董了，前苏联留下来的遗产：一根缆绳上只挂着两辆大车厢，一上一下来回跑，晃晃悠悠的，看着十分不安全。

[图]

到了半山腰，窗外已经全是一片白，什么也看不见。到了山顶更是安静得吓人，雾把一切都吞掉了，偶尔从雾里走出一个人影，活像寂静岭，好不瘆人。

[图]

[图]

下山的时候，我们决定不走寻常路，结果走了一连串六十度陡坡，连滚带爬地往下挪，沿途手机还没信号。好在山不大，最后还是走了出来，雾也慢慢散了，山下的城市重新露了出来。

[图]
stories.textEn:
At the end of November we flew to southern Russia to climb Elbrus, the highest peak of the Caucasus and of Europe. We landed in Mineralnye Vody, didn't linger, and went straight on to nearby Pyatigorsk, our base before the mountain.

[图]

Mineralnye Vody and Pyatigorsk left the same first impression: both felt like they were slowly fading. Rusted-through old Volgas parked by the road, peeling façades, hardly anyone on the streets, and even emptier once it got dark. Only from higher ground did you see how far the city actually spreads, its lights coming on one by one at dusk, which had a certain gentleness to it.

[图]

On climbing day we set off early and drove toward the foot of the mountain. The deeper we went, the bigger the mountains got. Along the way came one small town after another, each in its own valley, cut off from the next by long stretches of bare mountain, like islands. I was amazed that people had settled this deep in the mountains at all: houses, little shops, families, generation after generation.

[图]

[图]

At the foot we joined a tour group and took the cable cars up. One stage after another, the view outside changed from yellowed slopes to snowfields and finally to nothing but white. By the top station, Garabashi, at over 3,800 metres, my chest felt tight and I was short of breath after a few steps, my head slightly swollen. And yet there were plenty of skiers up there, boards on their shoulders, going up and down the slopes as if the thin air meant nothing to them.

[图]

[图]

[图]

[图]

There were foxes too, completely unafraid of people, strolling among the tourists and not bothered at all by the circle of cameras around them.

[图]

Back down, we tried a bit of Russian farmstay life. What stuck with me most was a kind of water that tasted strongly of rust, the spring rimmed with white crystals. The locals said it's good for you. We drank a few mouthfuls too; that rusty taste is hard to forget.

[图]

[图]

In our group was a young couple who clearly got on wonderfully, laughing and chatting the whole way; just looking at them made you feel happy. They were warm-hearted too, kept talking with us, and translated the guide's Russian commentary for us. When we parted they gave us stickers. I had only mentioned my birthday in passing, but they actually remembered it, and on the day a message arrived wishing me happy birthday. To be treated with that much care by people we had only just met: truly kind people.

Back to Pyatigorsk. The longer we stayed, the more obvious its decline: old houses left to decay, plaster falling off in patches, traces of former dignity with only the frame left standing. That is probably how most small Russian towns are now. The cats, at least, seemed to be doing fine.

[图]

[图]

The trams here are the most old-fashioned kind imaginable: small, worn-out cars on a narrow, battered track that bounces you around the whole way. There's still a conductor on board who comes round to each passenger to take the fare and hand out tickets.

One evening we rode the little tram around aimlessly until we ended up at a desolate stop. Pitch dark all around, and the shelter so crude it looked like a village outhouse. Hard to imagine that just a few kilometres from the centre, this is what you find.

There we ran into a few Chinese students studying in town. If I had to study somewhere this remote, I think I'd genuinely get depressed.

[图]

[图]

The last day was a fun one. We went up another, smaller mountain on the edge of town, Mashuk. A thick fog had rolled in, but we took the cable car up anyway. It's a true antique, a Soviet relic: just two big cabins on one cable, one going up while the other comes down, swaying all the way and looking anything but safe.

[图]

Halfway up there was nothing but white outside the window. At the top it was eerily silent, everything swallowed by the fog, now and then a figure emerging out of it. It felt just like Silent Hill, and properly creepy.

[图]

[图]

On the way down we decided to go off the beaten path, which meant a series of sixty-degree slopes, half sliding and half crawling down, with no phone signal along the way. Luckily the mountain isn't big, and we found our way out in the end, just as the fog lifted and the city below came back into view.

[图]

stories.title: 俄罗斯小趣事合集
stories.text:
### 走路送外卖的外卖员

在国内，外卖小哥约等于电动车。到了俄罗斯，我第一次见到走路送外卖的：背着一个方方正正的大箱子，在人行道上快步走，有的甚至一路小跑。Yandex 的、Samokat 的，什么颜色的背包都有。莫斯科很多外卖和生鲜是从附近的小仓库发出来的，离得近，走过去也来得及。下雪天也一样，箱子上积着一层雪，照样走。

偶尔也能看到更花哨的玩法，坐地铁，坐公交，开私家车，轮滑，滑板，骑自行车，甚至中途停下来一场酣畅淋漓的乒乓对决...俄罗斯的外卖员，是真的和国内截然不同的风格。还在观光巴士门口见过一个俄罗斯小男孩，书包上印着大大的中文“外卖”，不知道他知不知道是什么意思。

[图]

### 经典 Ozon 手提袋

Ozon 是俄罗斯最大的电商平台之一，在这里网购，东西通常寄到楼下的自提点，自己下楼去取。自提点附赠经典蓝色手提袋，莫斯科人似乎尤其偏爱这个袋子，于是街上、地铁里，总能看到拎着 Ozon 蓝色大袋子的人，男女老少，几乎成了一种街景。

### 办事效率

在俄罗斯办事，效率低得夸张：一件事要跑好几趟，窗口的人说走就走，换一个人来又是另一套说法。依稀记得办理入学手续和入住宿舍手续，以及各种生活基础设施，连续被踢皮球，搞了十几天才安定下来，期间踩坑交冤枉钱无数次；作为对比，来交大留学的同学一天就搞定了所有事项。学校国际化办每天必定大排长龙，要办点事还得从上班时间之前开始排队，不知道的还以为是学校发金条了。服务业大部分享受周末双休，着实让人羡慕，但作为市民来说体验可能不是很好。待久了也就学会了，办事之前先把心理预期降到最低，能一次办完算惊喜。

### 二次元不能上桌吃饭

东亚流行文化在俄罗斯年轻人里其实很受欢迎，但它好像始终上不了台面。最直观的就是二次元店：它们很少堂堂正正地开在街面上，常见的样子是门口立一块角色立牌（最常见的是原神角色或者五条悟），店一层是正常商品，额外内容开在地下室里，要顺着店里一个很隐蔽的楼梯往下走才能找到。阿尔巴特街的纪念品店门口站着一个甘雨，旁边是经典套娃和“我爱阿尔巴特”，画风十分混搭。红场边上扎里亚季耶公园观景台的长椅上，也有人悄悄贴过一张可莉贴纸，某一次再去的时候，已经不见了。

[图]

[图]

相比之下圣彼得堡就开放得多，年轻人穿着打扮也亚文化得多，最明目张胆的是一家火影主题的拉面店，直接开在涅瓦大街附近，并不会有人对此感到奇怪。店里的菜单做成了忍者世界地图，墙上贴满客人画的角色，晚上十点还坐得挺满。街边停着的痛车，在这里也不稀奇。

[图]

[图]

### 主动合影，然后收钱

红场周边是这类人的大本营。穿着沙皇袍子的大胡子、扮成历史人物的演员，会主动走过来，热情地握手、搭肩、摆姿势。拍完以后，才说这是要付钱的。克里姆林宫墙外还有放鸽子的：一不留神，鸽子已经站到你胳膊上了，接下来的流程同上。这一套在很多旅游城市都有，莫斯科也没有例外，第一次来的游客基本都会被招呼一遍。近年来甚至发展成了中国游客特攻，学几句中文，一边念叨着习近平万岁中国万岁，一边伸手要钱，人民币也行，属实给他们学到了...

相比之下，随处可见的街头艺人就实在多了。涅瓦大街上一位老爷爷，他牌子上写的是“Лаю счастья”，把俄语里的“祝你幸福”改了一个字，变成了“汪你幸福”；捐款的转账方式也直接写在牌子上，明码标价，童叟无欺。

[图]

### 零零碎碎

最后是一些能让人多看两眼的东西。

先是在俄罗斯冒出来的中国元素。2026 年除夕，红场边上立起一块红色大屏，写着“莫斯科的中国新年”，直播央视春晚，旁边就停着转播车。莫斯科傍晚七点，北京已经快到零点，雪下得正大，屏幕前还是站了不少人。

[图]

红旗在莫斯科和圣彼得堡的商场里都摆了展台，俄文广告写着“我在莫斯科，想你了”，旁边配一句直译过来的中文“我在莫斯科很想你”；到了圣彼得堡，城市名一换，又是同一套。因为西方的制裁，众多品牌退出俄罗斯市场，红旗逐渐取代了原本迈巴赫的地位，成为了豪华商务轿车的首选。

[图]

北极圈里的超市货架上摆着农夫山泉，179 卢（约十多块）一瓶。圣彼得堡的书店里能找到俄文版的《黑猫警长》。

[图]

还有摩尔曼斯克超市里做成抱枕的表情包猫咪，圣彼得堡街头贴满贴纸的 Cybertruck，厕所里画得一丝不苟的如厕告示，以及某天深夜路过时，人行道上的一摊血。

[图]

[图]
stories.textEn:
After a while in Russia I had collected a pile of small things: not big enough for a story of their own, too good to throw away. So here they are, all together.

### Couriers on foot

Back in China, a food delivery courier basically means an electric scooter. In Russia I saw couriers delivering on foot for the first time: a big square box on their back, walking fast down the pavement, some of them almost jogging. Yandex, Samokat, backpacks in every colour. A lot of Moscow's food and grocery delivery goes out from small warehouses close by, so walking is fast enough. Snow doesn't stop them either; they just keep walking with a layer of snow on the box.

Now and then you see fancier ways of getting around: metro, bus, private car, inline skates, skateboard, bicycle, even a stop halfway for a hard-fought game of ping-pong. Russian couriers really are a different breed. I also once saw a Russian boy at a sightseeing bus with "外卖", Chinese for food delivery, printed in big letters on his backpack. I doubt he knew what it meant.

[图]

### The classic Ozon bag

Ozon is one of Russia's biggest online shops. Your orders usually go to a pickup point downstairs and you go fetch them yourself, and the pickup point hands out its classic blue bag. Muscovites seem especially fond of it, so on the street and in the metro you keep seeing people carrying big blue Ozon bags, young and old. It has become part of the scenery.

### Getting things done

Getting anything done in Russia is absurdly slow: one errand takes several trips, the person at the window can just walk off, and the next person tells you something completely different. I remember enrolling, moving into the dorm and setting up all the basics of daily life: I got passed from desk to desk for more than ten days before things settled, and paid for plenty of mistakes along the way. A classmate who went on exchange to Jiao Tong University sorted everything in a single day. The university's international office always has a long queue; to get anything done you have to start queuing before it even opens, as if they were handing out gold bars. Most services take the whole weekend off, which is enviable for the staff but not so great for everyone else. Eventually you learn: lower your expectations as far as they go before you start, and if it gets done in one go, that's a bonus.

### Anime doesn't get a seat at the table

East Asian pop culture is genuinely popular with young Russians, yet it never quite gets a seat at the table. The anime shops show it best: they rarely sit proudly on the street. The usual setup is a character standee by the door (most often a Genshin character or Gojo Satoru), normal goods on the ground floor, and the real stuff in a basement, down a well-hidden staircase. On the Arbat, a Ganyu standee stands guard outside a souvenir shop, next to matryoshkas and an "I love Arbat" sign. Quite the mix. On a bench at the Zaryadye Park viewpoint, someone once quietly stuck a Klee sticker. The next time I went, it was gone.

[图]

[图]

St Petersburg is far more relaxed, and its young people dress far more alternatively. The boldest example is a Naruto-themed ramen shop right off Nevsky Prospekt, and nobody finds it strange. The menu is a map of the ninja world, the wall is covered in customers' fan art, and it was still busy at ten at night. An anime-wrapped car parked on the street is nothing unusual here either.

[图]

[图]

### Photos first, payment later

The streets around Red Square are their home turf. Bearded men in tsar robes and actors dressed as historical figures walk up to you, shake your hand, throw an arm around your shoulder, strike a pose. Only after the photo do they mention that it costs money. Outside the Kremlin wall there are the pigeon men: before you know it a pigeon is standing on your arm, and then the same routine follows. Plenty of tourist cities have this, and Moscow is no exception; almost every first-time visitor gets the treatment. Lately it has even evolved into a special service for Chinese tourists: they learn a few phrases of Chinese, chant "long live China" and hold out a hand. Yuan accepted. They've really done their homework.

By comparison, the street performers everywhere are refreshingly honest. An old man on Nevsky Prospekt has a sign that says "Лаю счастья": he changed one letter of the Russian "wishing you happiness" so it reads "barking you happiness". How to donate is written right there on the sign too. No surprises.

[图]

### Odds and ends

Finally, a few things that made me look twice.

First, the bits of China that pop up in Russia. On Chinese New Year's Eve 2026, a big red screen went up by Red Square under the words "Chinese New Year in Moscow", showing the CCTV Spring Festival Gala live, with the broadcast truck parked right next to it. It was seven in the evening in Moscow and nearly midnight in Beijing, snowing hard, and there was still a crowd in front of the screen.

[图]

Hongqi has stands in malls in both Moscow and St Petersburg. The Russian ad says "I'm in Moscow, I miss you", with a literal Chinese translation next to it; in St Petersburg they just swap the city name.

[图]

There is Nongfu Spring water on supermarket shelves inside the Arctic Circle, and Inspector Black Cat in Russian at a St Petersburg bookshop.

[图]

And then meme cats turned into pillows in a Murmansk supermarket, a sticker-covered Cybertruck in St Petersburg, a meticulously illustrated toilet notice, and, walking home late one night, a pool of blood on the pavement.

[图]

[图]

stories.title: 战争离日常有多远
stories.titleEn: How Far the War Is from Everyday Life
stories.text:
常有人问我，住在莫斯科，能不能感觉到战争和危险。老实说，大部分时候感觉不到。新闻里隔三岔五会刷到哪里又挨炸了，看一眼，划过去，第二天照常上课、吃饭、坐地铁。真正能感受得到的，是一些零零碎碎的小事。

最显眼的是征兵广告。墙上贴的、高架桥边的大屏上放的，都是穿迷彩的士兵，旁边配一串很大的数字，告诉你签合同能拿多少钱，地铁里各个要道都偶尔坐着征兵办的人。刚来的时候我会停下来看两眼，后来就和楼盘广告、外卖广告一样，成了城市背景的一部分。

[图]

征兵这件事，对身边的俄罗斯同学来说并不遥远。俄罗斯实行义务兵役制，男生到了年龄都要服一年兵役，上大学可以延缓。所以同学们平时不太为自己担心，可聊着聊着，常常会有人提起自己的哪个好友、哪个同学签了合同上了前线，最后没能回来。说的人语气很平静，听的人也不知道该接什么。

这几年，征兵的范围也在一点点扩大：服兵役的年龄上限从 27 岁提到了 30 岁，听说连上大学也不一定能延缓了，拿了永居的外国人也被要求去服兵役。对我们这些外国留学生来说，这条线好像也在慢慢往这边挪。

然后是物价。东西在涨，不是一下子涨很多，而是隔一阵再去超市，发现熟悉的那几样又贵了一点。货架上的促销牌越贴越多，加油站牌子上的数字也一直在往上走，直到 26 年 7 月这会，全国已经因为炼油厂频繁被炸出现了用油短缺，加油站大排长龙。没法说出具体涨了多少，但钱包的感觉是诚实的。

[图]

最让人头疼的是网络。手机流量动不动就没了，有时候是一大片地方的移动网络一起断掉，地图打不开，打车软件转圈，只能到处找 wifi。时间长了，大家都练出了一种本能：一进咖啡店先问 wifi 密码。

还有定位。导航几乎不可用，定位永远在谢列梅捷沃，打车的时候司机也找不到你在哪。一开始以为是手机坏了，后来才知道这是常态，大家都一样。

除此之外，战争的痕迹就藏在一些不太起眼的角落：晚上路口站着巡逻的警察，公交站对面的广告牌上是军人的照片，胜利公园的博物馆里多了一个展区，迷彩服、头盔和无人机被摆进了玻璃柜。

[图]

离危险最近的一次，是 2026 年三月在伊斯特拉。那天去新耶路撒冷修道院，天特别蓝，我正在院子里拍照，天上突然“砰”的一声巨响，把所有人都吓了一大跳。抬头一看，蓝天上只剩一坨黑烟在慢慢散开：一架无人机刚刚就在我眼前被击落了。

[图]

可吓完那一下，大家很快就像什么都没发生过一样。拍照的接着拍照，做礼拜的接着进教堂做礼拜，抬头多看两眼天空的人都没几个。我站在那儿愣了好一会儿，才明白过来，这大概就是这里的人和战争相处的方式。

所以大多数时候，日子该怎么过还是怎么过。最能说明这一点的，是周末的高尔基公园。

[图]

那个周末天特别好，公园门口摆满了热气球和花坛，人多得走不动。河边的木台子上放着一副半人高的国际象棋，背后喷泉一直在喷。突然看见一群人戴着耳机手舞足蹈，两步一停，领队穿得花里胡哨，跟着看了一会发现原来是俄式 city walk...

[图]

大草坪上躺着晒太阳的人，广场上有人拍照、有人散步、有人带着孩子跑来跑去，谁也看不出这个国家正在打仗。

我在公园里找了家餐厅吃了顿午饭，然后沿着河边一路往前走。克里米亚桥边有个卖画的小市场，河边的台阶上坐满了人。

[图]

第二年春天我又去了那一带，还是一样：小孩爬上墙头坐成一排，河边的躺椅上有人在看书，旁边的秋千一直有人在荡。

[图]

太阳落山的时候，河边的木栈道被照成金色，有人骑车经过，有人站在栏杆边发呆。

[图]

天黑以后，公园里的路灯一盏盏亮起来，人还没走完。新闻里的那些事，好像离这里很远，又好像就在旁边。不过在莫斯科待久了，我大概也学会了这里的人的那种方式：该担心的担心一下，然后周末照样去公园。
stories.textEn:
People often ask me whether you can feel the war living in Moscow. Honestly, most of the time you can't. Every so often the news says somewhere got hit again; you read it, scroll past, and the next day you still go to class, eat lunch and ride the metro. What you actually notice are small, scattered things.

The most visible are the recruitment ads. Posters on walls, giant screens by the overpasses: a soldier in camouflage next to a very large number telling you how much you get for signing a contract. When I first arrived I'd stop and look. Later they just became part of the city's background, like ads for new apartments and food delivery.

[图]

For my Russian classmates, conscription isn't distant at all. Russia has compulsory military service: men of the right age serve a year, and going to university lets you defer it. So most of my classmates don't worry much for themselves, but every so often in conversation someone mentions a good friend, or a classmate, who signed a contract, went to the front and never came back. They say it calmly, and the rest of us don't really know what to say.

Over the past few years the net has been widening bit by bit: the upper age limit for service went from 27 to 30, I've heard that being at university no longer guarantees a deferral, and foreigners with permanent residency are being called up too. For foreign students like us, that line seems to be creeping a little closer.

Then there are prices. Things go up, not all at once, but every time you go back to the supermarket, the few things you always buy cost a little more. The promo stickers on the shelves keep multiplying, and the numbers on the petrol station signs keep climbing. I can't tell you exactly how much, but your wallet knows.

[图]

The real headache is the internet. Mobile data drops out all the time; sometimes the mobile network goes down across a whole area at once. Maps won't load, the taxi app just spins, and you go hunting for wifi. After a while everyone develops the same reflex: walk into a café, ask for the wifi password first.

And then there's GPS. You're following the map and suddenly your little arrow jumps a few kilometres away, sometimes somewhere else entirely, and the taxi driver can't find you. At first I thought my phone was broken. Later I learned it's just normal, and it happens to everyone.

Beyond that, the war shows up in corners you don't really notice: police patrolling a crossing at night, a billboard with a soldier on it across from the bus stop, a new section in the museum at Victory Park where camouflage, helmets and drones sit behind glass.

[图]

The closest I came to danger was in Istra, in March 2026. I was at New Jerusalem Monastery on a day with a perfectly blue sky, taking photos in the grounds, when there was a huge bang overhead and everyone jumped. I looked up and all that was left was a lump of black smoke slowly drifting apart: a drone had just been shot down right in front of me.

[图]

But once the shock passed, everyone carried on as if nothing had happened. The people taking photos went on taking photos, the people at the service went on into the church, and hardly anyone looked up at the sky a second time. I stood there for a while before it sank in that this is probably how people here live with the war.

So most of the time, life goes on as it always has. Nothing shows it better than Gorky Park on a weekend.

[图]

That weekend the weather was perfect. The park entrance was packed with hot-air balloons and flower beds, and so many people you could barely move. On a wooden deck by the water stood a half-human-sized chess set, with the fountain going behind it. I held up my phone and drifted along with the crowd for a while: a Russian-style city walk.

[图]

People lay on the big lawn soaking up the sun; on the square they took photos, strolled, chased their kids around. Nothing about it told you the country was at war.

I had lunch at a restaurant in the park, then walked along the river. Near the Crimean Bridge there's a little market of painters selling their work, and the steps by the water were full of people.

[图]

I went back the next spring, and it was the same: kids climbing up and sitting in a row on top of a wall, someone reading on a deckchair by the river, the swings next to it never empty.

[图]

When the sun goes down, the boardwalk by the river turns gold; someone cycles past, someone leans on the railing and stares at the water.

[图]

After dark the park lights come on one by one and people are still there. The things in the news feel very far away from here, and at the same time right next door. But after living in Moscow for a while, I think I've picked up the local way of dealing with it: worry about what you need to worry about, and then go to the park on the weekend anyway.

stories.title: 从航空航天看俄罗斯和苏联
stories.titleEn: Russia and the Soviet Union, seen through its planes and rockets
stories.text:
[图]

我在莫斯科航空学院留学。主楼门口停着一架蓝白涂装的战斗机，下雪天、大晴天，它都昂着头对着校门。每天从它鼻子底下走过，久了就像看门的大爷，谁也不会多看一眼。

在俄罗斯待久了会发现，俄罗斯人一说起航空航天，语气就很特别：骄傲里带着一点怀旧。这份骄傲是有来由的。1957 年 10 月 4 日，苏联把人类第一颗人造卫星「斯普特尼克」送上了轨道；1961 年 4 月 12 日，加加林坐着「东方一号」绕地球飞了一圈，成了第一个进入太空的人。这一天后来成了俄罗斯的航天节。

[图]

VDNKh 的宇宙馆门口立着一枚「东方号」火箭，是莫斯科最热门的合影点之一。周末来这里散步的一家老小，在火箭底下排队拍照，小孩子仰着头看，大概和几十年前他们的爷爷奶奶一样。

不过要说跟这些东西朝夕相处，还得是在学校里。

[图]

航空学院有一座玻璃大厅，里面塞满了真家伙：飞船舱段、返回舱、探测器、火箭发动机，挤得像个仓库。更离谱的是，大厅中间就摆着课桌，学生们在火箭和飞船中间上课。我第一次从楼上往下看，愣了好一会儿。

[图]

联盟号的轨道舱、对接口、绿色的保温层，一节一节摆在那里。外壳磨得发亮，线缆露在外面，看得出来不是做给游客看的模型。

[图]

有的教室干脆把一个剖开的返回舱搬了进来，就杵在讲台边上。老师讲到哪儿，大家就凑过去看到哪儿。

[图]

还有一些长着大锅盖天线、底下带着支架的探测器。苏联当年往金星和火星发过一长串探测器，其中金星系列真的在金星表面着陆，还传回了照片。那是一个人类连月球都还没摸透的年代。

[图]

发动机是另一大宗。四个喷口挤在一起的那种，看着就很有苏联味儿。到今天，俄罗斯送航天员去空间站用的联盟号火箭，往上数，和送加加林上天的那一枚是同一个家族。

[图]

一块铁皮铭牌上写着「СССР」，底下一行「MADE IN USSR」，那是一台来自十八世纪的老古董机器。我们上实践课要穿蓝色的大褂，站在这些东西旁边，总有一种自己也成了展品的错觉。

课上，老师讲起这些总是如数家珍：第一颗卫星，第一个上太空的人，第一次太空行走，第一个空间站……这些「第一」一届一届地讲下去，讲了几十年。听多了，你会注意到一件事：故事几乎都停在了上个世纪。

[图]

航天大厅的顶层还有一间屋子，平时没人进去，地上、墙边堆满了落灰的画像、图纸和老教具：金星号的飞行示意图，宇航员的合影，正中间那幅大画像是科罗廖夫。它们大概曾经挂在教室里，后来一张张摘下来，摞在这里，就再也没人动过。

[图]

联盟号返回舱里窄得惊人，三个人要蜷着腿，躺在按身形定做的座椅里。旁边站着一套航天服，还有一面满是按钮和仪表的控制台。这些东西摸上去都是凉的，有些按钮已经泛黄了。

今年一月，大雪后放晴的一个周日，我和朋友坐电气火车去了莫斯科郊外的莫尼诺。

[图]

火车往东北出城，会先经过科罗廖夫，那才是真正意义上的「航天城」。苏联载人航天的设计局和飞行控制中心都在那里，城市的名字就来自苏联航天的总设计师科罗廖夫。再往东一些，就是莫尼诺，一座和空军绑在一起的小城：这里有过机场，有过空军学院，热闹过很多年。后来学院搬走了，机场也不再飞了，留下最有名的，是俄罗斯空军中央博物馆。

博物馆就建在老机场上。雪很厚，路上没几个人，四周安静得只能听见自己踩雪的声音。整个地方给人的感觉，就像是被时间轻轻放下了。

[图]

室内展厅讲的是苏联空军的历史。在一个角落，我看到一面红色的锦旗，上面用中文写着「苏中两国人民及其军队的团结友谊万岁」，落款是「中国军事留学生敬赠」，纪念苏联陆海空军建军四十周年。算一下，那是 1958 年。将近七十年前，也有一批中国留学生在苏联学航空，和现在的我差不多大。

[图]

露天展区才是重头戏。最先撞进眼里的是米-12，人类造过的最大的直升机，只造了两架原型机，没有量产。站在它底下，像站在一栋楼的屋檐下。

[图]

再往里走，是尾翼上写着 СССР-77106 的图-144。这是苏联的超音速客机，1968 年的最后一天首飞，比协和式还早了两个月。可它真正载客的日子很短，没多久就退出了航线，最后停在了这片雪地里。

[图]

一排排轰炸机、直升机，翅膀上压着厚厚的雪。一块石头上的牌子写着「英雄飞行员之路」，前面放着花圈。很多飞机就这样常年露天停着，有的蒙皮已经斑驳。在大太阳底下，它们很好看；可说实话，也有点像一片飞机的墓地。

[图]

老机库里放着更早的家伙：二战时的战斗机，木头和帆布做的双翼机。机库本身也老了，铁架子，大玻璃窗，下午的太阳从窗格里斜着照进来。

[图]

走着走着，头顶突然飞过一架大飞机，四个发动机，轰隆隆地拖着白线，来自附近的军事基地。在一院子再也不会起飞的飞机中间，抬头看见一架还在飞的，那一瞬间有点恍惚。

加加林的故事，结局不在太空。1968 年 3 月 27 日，他和飞行员谢廖金驾驶一架米格-15 教练机训练时坠毁，那年他才 34 岁。坠机的地方在弗拉基米尔州基尔扎奇附近的林子里。今年夏至我们去乡下过节，那天也去了那里。

[图]

林子边上放着一架米格-15，还有一个银色的铁球，模样像东方号的返回舱，背后是一座小教堂。

[图]

纪念碑是一根细长的红色石柱，上面刻着两个人的侧脸。旁边有一棵白桦被栏杆围了起来，牌子上写着：这是飞机坠落时撞断的十四棵树之一。花一直有人在换。

今天的俄罗斯也还在飞。

[图]

2026 年的胜利日，我在红场边上看到几架飞机拖着三色烟掠过斯大林式高楼。只是那一年的阅兵已经冷清了很多，这段我在《两个胜利日》里写过。

[图]

毕业那天，我又进了一次学校的机库。新飞机和旧飞机挤在一起，学生们穿着学位服在机翼底下拍照，好像这里的一切都还在照常运转。

在莫斯科的这些日子，我对这些老古董的感情越来越复杂。它们确实了不起：一个国家从战争的废墟里爬出来，十几年后就把卫星和人送上了天。可是在莫尼诺的雪地里，在航空学院的课堂上，我也一次次感觉到，人们讲起这些辉煌，越来越像在讲一位已经过世的长辈：语气里有骄傲，也有一点不愿意说出口的落寞。

辉煌是真的，衰落也是真的。站在加加林坠机的那片林子里，我想的倒不是苏联有多伟大，而是那些人本身：一群人，在一个并不容易的年代，拼了命地想飞得更高一点。这份心情不属于哪一个国家，也不该只留在课本和博物馆里。
stories.textEn:
[图]

I studied at the Moscow Aviation Institute (MAI). In front of the main building stands a blue-and-white fighter jet. Snow or sun, it keeps its nose up toward the gate. I walked under that nose every day, and after a while it was like the old doorman: nobody looked twice.

Spend enough time in Russia and you notice that when people talk about aviation and space, their voice changes: pride, with a little nostalgia mixed in. The pride has its reasons. On 4 October 1957 the Soviet Union put Sputnik, the first artificial satellite, into orbit. On 12 April 1961 Yuri Gagarin flew once around the Earth in Vostok 1 and became the first human in space. That day later became Russia's Cosmonautics Day.

[图]

Outside the Cosmos pavilion at VDNKh stands a Vostok rocket, one of the most popular photo spots in Moscow. Families out for a weekend walk queue up beneath it, and the kids crane their necks the same way their grandparents probably did decades ago.

But if you want to live alongside these things every day, you need to be at the school.

[图]

MAI has a glass hall crammed with the real thing: spacecraft modules, descent capsules, probes, rocket engines, packed in like a warehouse. The wild part is that there are desks right in the middle, and students have class between the rockets and spaceships. The first time I looked down from the upper floor, I just stood there for a while.

[图]

Soyuz sections sit there one after another: the orbital module, the docking port, the green insulation. The metal is worn shiny and the cables hang out. These are clearly not models made for tourists.

[图]

Some classrooms simply have a cut-open descent capsule standing next to the lectern. Wherever the teacher points, everyone leans in to look.

[图]

Then there are probes with big dish antennas and landing legs. The Soviet Union sent a long line of probes to Venus and Mars, and the Venera landers actually touched down on the surface of Venus and sent back pictures. This was a time when people had barely figured out the Moon.

[图]

Engines are another big category. The ones with four nozzles bunched together look about as Soviet as anything can. Even today, the Soyuz rocket that carries cosmonauts to the space station belongs, if you trace it back, to the same family as the rocket that launched Gagarin.

[图]

A metal nameplate reads "СССР", and below it "MADE IN USSR". For lab classes we wore blue coats, and standing next to all this I sometimes felt like I had become an exhibit too.

In class, teachers tell these stories like family treasures: the first satellite, the first man in space, the first spacewalk, the first space station. These "firsts" have been passed down class after class for decades. Hear them often enough and you notice something: almost every story stops in the last century.

[图]

At the top of the space hall there is a room nobody really goes into. Portraits, drawings and old teaching models are piled on the floor and against the walls under a layer of dust: a flight diagram of a Venera probe, group photos of cosmonauts, and in the middle a large portrait of Korolev. They probably once hung in classrooms, then came down one by one and were stacked up here, and nobody has touched them since.

[图]

The Soyuz descent capsule is astonishingly cramped: three people lie with their knees drawn up in seats moulded to their bodies. Next to it stands a spacesuit, and a control panel covered in buttons and dials. Everything is cold to the touch, and some of the buttons have turned yellow.

This January, on a Sunday when the sky cleared after a heavy snowfall, my friends and I took the suburban train to Monino, outside Moscow.

[图]

Heading northeast out of the city, the train first passes Korolyov, the real "space city". The Soviet crewed spaceflight design bureau and mission control are there, and the town is named after Sergei Korolev, the chief designer of the Soviet space program. A little further east is Monino, a small town tied to the air force: it had an airfield and an air force academy, and it was busy for many years. Later the academy moved away and the airfield stopped flying. What remains best known is the Central Air Force Museum.

The museum sits on the old airfield. The snow was deep, there were few people around, and it was so quiet that all I could hear was my own footsteps. The whole place felt as if time had gently set it down and walked away.

[图]

The indoor halls tell the history of the Soviet air force. In one corner I found a red silk banner with Chinese writing: "Long live the unity and friendship of the peoples and armies of the Soviet Union and China", signed "Presented by Chinese military students", for the fortieth anniversary of the Soviet armed forces. Do the math and that is 1958. Almost seventy years ago, Chinese students about my age were also in the Soviet Union learning to build and fly planes.

[图]

The outdoor display is the main event. The first thing that hits you is the Mi-12, the largest helicopter ever built. Only two prototypes were made and it never went into production. Standing underneath it feels like standing under the eaves of a building.

[图]

Further in is a Tu-144 with СССР-77106 on its tail. It was the Soviet supersonic airliner, first flown on the last day of 1968, two months before Concorde. But its life carrying passengers was very short. It soon left service, and ended up parked here in the snow.

[图]

Rows of bombers and helicopters, wings loaded with thick snow. A plaque on a stone reads "Alley of Hero Aviators", with a wreath in front of it. Many of these planes stand outdoors all year, and some of their skins have gone patchy. In the bright sun they look beautiful; to be honest, they also look a bit like an aircraft graveyard.

[图]

The old hangars hold even earlier machines: Second World War fighters, biplanes made of wood and canvas. The hangars themselves are old too, iron frames and big glass windows, the afternoon sun slanting in through the panes.

[图]

As we walked, a big four-engined plane suddenly passed overhead, rumbling and trailing white lines. Among a whole yard of planes that will never take off again, looking up at one that still flies was a strange moment.

Gagarin's story does not end in space. On 27 March 1968, he and the pilot Vladimir Seryogin crashed in a MiG-15 trainer during a training flight. Gagarin was only 34. The crash site is in the woods near Kirzhach, in the Vladimir region. On the summer solstice this year, when we went to the countryside for the festival, we went there too.

[图]

At the edge of the woods stands a MiG-15, and a silver metal sphere shaped like a Vostok descent capsule, with a small church behind it.

[图]

The memorial is a slender red stone column carved with two faces in profile. Nearby, a birch tree is fenced off, and the sign says it is one of fourteen trees cut down by the plane as it fell. Someone keeps changing the flowers.

Russia is still flying today.

[图]

On Victory Day 2026, from the edge of Red Square, I watched a few planes trail tricolour smoke past a Stalinist high-rise. That year's parade was a much quieter affair, which I wrote about in "Two Victory Days".

[图]

On graduation day I went into the school's hangar one more time. New planes and old planes crowded together, students in gowns posed under the wings, as if everything here were still running as usual.

Over my time in Moscow, my feelings about these old machines kept getting more complicated. They really are remarkable: a country crawled out of the ruins of war, and a dozen years later it had put a satellite and a man into space. But in the snow at Monino and in the classrooms at MAI, I kept feeling that people talk about this glory more and more the way you talk about a relative who has passed away: with pride, and a sadness nobody quite says out loud.

The glory was real, and so is the decline. Standing in the woods where Gagarin fell, I wasn't thinking about how great the Soviet Union was. I was thinking about the people themselves: a group of people in a hard time, trying with everything they had to fly a little higher. That feeling doesn't belong to any one country, and it shouldn't only live in textbooks and museums.

stories.title: 世界第四公交城市之阿布扎比？
stories.titleEn: Abu Dhabi: Grandeur and Taxi Fares
stories.text:
[图]

在迪拜待了几天，我们抽出一整天去了趟阿布扎比。阿布扎比是阿联酋的首都，从迪拜开车过去要一个多小时。一天排了三个地方：上午卢浮宫，下午总统府，傍晚到晚上是谢赫扎耶德大清真寺。走完这一天，我对阿布扎比的印象就俩：一个字，豪；另一个是，没车寸步难行。

[图]

出门的时候还在迪拜，车窗外一块巨大的广告牌写着“别跟堵车较劲，去打反派”，是阿布扎比华纳兄弟乐园的广告。当时只觉得好玩，没想到这一天最大的反派，就是交通。

第一站是阿布扎比卢浮宫，在萨迪亚特岛上，2017 年开的馆。它和巴黎卢浮宫是合作关系，名字是“借”来的，很多展品也是从法国的博物馆借过来的。建筑是让·努维尔设计的，最出名的是头顶那个巨大的穹顶：好几层镂空的金属格子叠在一起，像一张编出来的网。阳光从格子缝里漏下来，在地上、墙上、水面上打出一片碎碎的光斑，而且随着太阳移动一直在变，这就是所谓的“光之雨”。

[图]

穹顶下面是一片白色的方盒子展厅，像一座小城，海水直接引到建筑之间。站在穹顶底下吹着海风，很难相信外面是三十几度的大太阳。

[图]

展厅里的光也是设计过的，阳光穿过一格一格的窗棂落在墙上，人走过去就成了剪影。

展品是按时间顺序排的，不按国家分，从史前一直走到当代，同一个房间里可能挨着放着不同文明差不多同一时期的东西。走到欧洲那几间，满墙都是镶着金框的油画。

[图]

[图]

这幅画几个男人围着桌子打牌，旁边还有个人靠在沙发上，像是在看热闹，我在前面站了挺久。

[图]

再往后走一下子就跳到了现代：大片泼洒出来的红，还有用人体蘸着蓝颜料印在纸上的人形。

[图]

最后有一间几乎全黑的屋子，只有正中间一个黑色的圆，周围的线条全往它那里收。站在里面有点晕，说不上看懂了，但印象很深。

[图]

从展厅出来，穹顶的边上就是海，对面能看到阿布扎比的楼群。

[图]

[图]

逛完卢浮宫已经下午了，接下来去总统府。问题就在这里：阿布扎比的几个景点分散在不同的岛和区，彼此隔着几公里到十几公里，中间是宽阔的大马路和高架，根本没法走。公交几乎等于没有，有也不知道多久一班。能选的只有打车，而这里的出租车价格一点都不客气。一天下来，打车钱是这趟最心疼的一笔支出，钱包大出血。

离谱的是，2025 年 Time Out 杂志按本地人的打分排了一份全球公共交通满意度榜，阿布扎比排世界第四。我盯着计价器一路往上跳，实在想不通这个第四是怎么来的，大概投票的本地人都是开着自家的车去投的吧。

总统府叫 Qasr Al Watan，意思是“国家之宫”，是阿联酋总统和政府平时接待外国元首、开会的地方，这几年开放给游客参观。一进去就明白什么叫豪：白色的石头外墙，金色的穹顶，大厅的顶有几十米高，满是花纹，正中间垂下一盏巨大的吊灯。

[图]

[图]

外面的院子同样是一水儿的白，拱廊下挂着一排排灯，门洞外是修得整整齐齐的棕榈树和草坪。

[图]

在总统府外面歇了一会儿，对面就是阿布扎比的天际线。

[图]

快走的时候太阳已经低下来了，门口有穿白袍的人骑着马经过，整个画面金灿灿的。

最后一站是谢赫扎耶德大清真寺，又是一趟打车。远远看到它的时候天还亮着，白色的穹顶和宣礼塔立在一片车流后面，看上去比想象中还要大。

[图]

这座清真寺 2007 年建成，用阿联酋的开国总统扎耶德的名字命名，他本人就葬在这里。它有八十多个穹顶、上千根柱子，外墙和地面铺的都是白色大理石，柱子上镶着彩色的石头拼成的花藤。参观是免费的，但对着装有要求，女生要穿长袍、包头巾。

[图]

我们到的时间刚好，赶上了日落。太阳下去以后，天一点点变成蓝紫色，廊柱底下的灯亮起来，倒映在旁边的水池里。

[图]

[图]

进到礼拜大厅里，就是另一个层次的豪了。地上铺着据说是世界上最大的手工编织地毯之一，头顶挂着好几盏缀满水晶的大吊灯，金色、绿色、红色，一层一层，亮得晃眼。

[图]

[图]

天完全黑下来以后，清真寺外墙打上了蓝色的灯光，整座建筑和它在水里的倒影连在一起，比白天还要好看。听说这套灯光会随着月亮的圆缺变化。

出来以后又要面对老问题：怎么走。晚上的路边空荡荡的，只有路灯和呼啸而过的车，我们沿着大路走了好一段，才找到能拍清真寺倒影的地方。

[图]

最后我干脆坐在水边，把相机里的照片导进电脑，对着眼前的清真寺修起了图。阿布扎比给我的感觉就是这样：每一个地方都豪得让人说不出话，但从一个地方到另一个地方，全靠钱包硬扛。
stories.textEn:
[图]

After a few days in Dubai, we set aside a whole day for Abu Dhabi. It's the capital of the UAE, a bit over an hour's drive from Dubai. We planned three stops: the Louvre in the morning, the presidential palace in the afternoon, and the Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque from dusk into the night. By the end of the day my impression of Abu Dhabi came down to two things: everything is lavish, and without a car you can't get anywhere.

[图]

We were still in Dubai when we set out, and a giant billboard outside the window said "Don't fight traffic, fight villains", an ad for Warner Bros. World Abu Dhabi. I just found it funny at the time. I didn't know yet that the biggest villain of the day would be getting around.

First stop: the Louvre Abu Dhabi, on Saadiyat Island, opened in 2017. It works in partnership with the Louvre in Paris: the name is "borrowed", and so are many of the works, on loan from French museums. The building is by Jean Nouvel, and its famous part is the enormous dome overhead: several layers of perforated metal lattice stacked on top of each other, like a woven net. Sunlight leaks through the gaps and scatters spots of light across the floor, the walls and the water, shifting all the time as the sun moves. That's what they call the "rain of light".

[图]

Under the dome sits a cluster of white box-like galleries, like a little town, with seawater channelled right between the buildings. Standing in the shade with the sea breeze, it was hard to believe it was over thirty degrees in the sun outside.

[图]

Even the light inside the galleries is designed: sunlight falls through the lattice windows onto the walls, and anyone walking past turns into a silhouette.

The collection is arranged by time rather than by country, from prehistory all the way to today, so one room might hold objects from different civilizations made around the same period. In the European rooms, the walls were covered with paintings in heavy gold frames.

[图]

[图]

In this one, a group of men play cards around a table while another lounges on the sofa, as if just watching. I stood in front of it for quite a while.

[图]

A few rooms on, it suddenly jumps to the modern era: great splashes of red, and human figures printed on paper by bodies dipped in blue paint.

[图]

At the end there was an almost completely dark room with a single black circle in the middle, every line around it converging on it. Standing inside made me a little dizzy. I can't say I understood it, but it stayed with me.

[图]

Step out of the galleries and the sea is right at the edge of the dome, with Abu Dhabi's towers across the water.

[图]

[图]

By the time we finished it was afternoon, and next was the presidential palace. And here's the problem: Abu Dhabi's sights are spread across different islands and districts, several to a dozen-plus kilometres apart, linked by wide highways and flyovers. Walking is out of the question. Public transport barely exists, and when it does, who knows how often it runs. The only real option is a taxi, and taxis here are not cheap at all. Over the day, taxi fares were the most painful expense of the whole trip. My wallet bled.

Only later did I learn that in 2025 Time Out ranked cities by how satisfied locals are with their public transport, and Abu Dhabi came fourth in the world. Watching the taxi meter climb, I couldn't work out how. My best guess: the locals who voted all drove there in their own cars.

The palace is called Qasr Al Watan, "Palace of the Nation". It's where the UAE's president and government receive foreign heads of state and hold meetings, and in recent years it has opened to visitors. One step inside and you understand what lavish means: white stone walls, golden domes, a Great Hall ceiling dozens of metres high and covered in patterns, with a huge chandelier hanging from the centre.

[图]

[图]

The courtyards outside are just as white, with rows of lanterns hanging under the arcades, and beyond the doorways, neatly trimmed palms and lawns.

[图]

We rested for a while outside the palace, with the Abu Dhabi skyline right across the water.

[图]

As we were leaving the sun was already low, and riders in white robes passed the gate on horseback, the whole scene glowing gold.

The last stop was the Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque. Another taxi. When we first saw it from a distance it was still light, its white domes and minarets rising behind a stream of traffic, even bigger than I'd imagined.

[图]

The mosque was completed in 2007 and named after Sheikh Zayed, the UAE's founding president, who is buried here. It has more than eighty domes and over a thousand columns; the walls and floors are white marble, and the columns are inlaid with vines of coloured stone. Entry is free, but there is a dress code: women wear a long robe and cover their hair.

[图]

Our timing was perfect, and we caught the sunset. After the sun went down the sky slowly turned blue and violet, the lights at the foot of the columns came on, and their reflections appeared in the pools alongside.

[图]

[图]

Inside the prayer hall is another level of lavish. The floor is covered by what is said to be one of the largest hand-knotted carpets in the world, and overhead hang several huge crystal chandeliers, gold, green and red, tier upon tier, almost too bright to look at.

[图]

[图]

Once it was fully dark, the mosque's walls were lit in blue, and the building and its reflection in the water joined into one, even more beautiful than by day. I'd heard the lighting changes with the phases of the moon.

Coming out, we faced the same old problem: how to get anywhere. The roadside at night was empty, just streetlights and cars roaring past. We walked a long way along the big road before finding a spot to photograph the mosque's reflection.

[图]

In the end I just sat down by the water, loaded the photos from my camera onto my laptop and started editing them, with the mosque right in front of me. That's how Abu Dhabi felt to me: every place is so lavish it leaves you speechless, but getting from one to the next is all down to your wallet.

stories.title: 恶土里的银手
stories.text:
从迪拜市中心往东开，不到一个小时，楼就没了。路两边先是零零星星的厂房和围栏，再往外就只剩下沙子，橙里透红，被风吹出一道一道的波纹，像一块揉皱了又摊平的绸子。

这片沙漠是阿拉伯沙漠的一角。沙丘看着不动，其实一直在被风推着走：迎风的一面坡缓，背风的一面坡陡，沙脊细得像刀刻出来的。夏天白天能晒到四五十度，太阳一落温度又掉得很快。没有树、没有水，看久了会有种错觉，好像世界上只剩下沙子和天。

在石油被发现之前，在这片沙子里讨生活的是贝都因人。他们是游牧的阿拉伯部落，赶着骆驼和羊，跟着水井和草场迁徙，住在羊毛织的黑帐篷里。骆驼是他们的命，能驮东西、能产奶，几天不喝水也走得动；猎鹰是他们的帮手，驯好了能在沙漠里抓野兔和鸟。沙漠里的规矩也是从那时候来的：来者是客，哪怕是陌生人，进了帐篷也要先端上咖啡和椰枣。

后来有了石油，有了今天的迪拜，大部分阿联酋人早就住进了城里、开上了越野车，但沙漠没从他们的生活里离开：冬天开车去沙漠露营，养骆驼、赛骆驼，猎鹰到现在还是阿联酋的国家象征，有专门的猎鹰医院，据说坐飞机还能有自己的座位。

我们去沙漠那天，上午还在朱美拉海滩泡水，下午包了一辆车，司机带着我们往城外开。第一站是沙漠边上的一个集合点，一排排越野车停在那里等着进沙漠，旁边有卖小吃的棚子，还有人架着猎鹰让游客合影，同伴也上去架了一回。

[图]

就是在这个集合点，我看见了他。披肩的黑长发，飞行员墨镜，山羊胡，一身白衣服，手里好像还夹着根烟，站在小吃摊的草棚底下，冷冷地往我这边看了一眼。那一瞬间我脑子里只剩一个名字：强尼·银手。《赛博朋克 2077》里那个摇滚歌手兼恐怖分子，住在主角脑子里的幽灵，基努·里维斯演的那位。我赶紧举起相机拍了几张，一瞬间甚至以为大脑被 Relic 入侵了。

[图]

进了沙漠，车先停在一座高沙丘上看日落。太阳被沙尘滤成一个橙红色的圆点，一点一点沉进沙丘后面，远处的越野车和人都变成了小黑点。

[图]

在沙丘上又碰到了几个巴基斯坦小哥，穿着白袍，热情得不得了，拉着我们一起拍合照。在迪拜，连在沙漠里遇见的都是巴基斯坦人。拍完合照，我们的司机走到沙脊上，背着手看太阳往下落，指间还夹着根烟。

[图]

日落之后才是重头戏：冲沙。越野车冲上沙丘的脊，在顶上顿半秒，整个车头往下一扎，再侧着身子在沙坡上滑下去，车身斜得让人怀疑下一秒就要翻。司机倒是很淡定，一手搭着方向盘，像是在开去超市的路上。我在后座举着手机想录下来，结果录到的大多是车顶和司机的后脑勺，窗外的沙丘只在角落里一闪一闪。

[图]

冲完沙，车在沙漠边上的一家小店门口停了一会儿，维护、加油。太阳刚落山，正是昏礼的时间，广播里响起了诵经声，两个穿白袍的人在屋檐底下铺开一块垫子做礼拜，旁边停着几辆车，远处飘着阿联酋国旗。穆斯林一天礼拜五次，昏礼就在日落之后，到了时间，在哪儿都可以就地铺开垫子。

[图]

天黑以后到了营地。门口有人牵着马等着游客，穿白袍、裹着黑头巾的大哥搂着马头站在灯底下，像一张老照片。

[图]

晚饭就在营地里吃，大家围着中间的舞台坐，一边吃一边看表演。第一个上场的是坦努拉旋转舞，这种舞起源于埃及，和苏菲派的旋转仪式有关。舞者穿着好几层彩色大裙摆，原地一圈一圈地转，好像永远不会晕，转着转着还把裙子一层层举过头顶。后来灯一关，裙子上的灯亮起来，他就变成了一个发光的陀螺。

[图]

接着是火舞。表演者在舞台外的沙地上甩着火球，火星子溅得到处都是，围观的人都往后退了一步。最后是肚皮舞，舞者披着纱巾上场，全场的手机都举了起来。

[图]

我的充电宝就在这一天永远留在了沙漠里。后来怎么找都找不到，只能确定它落在了沙漠的某个地方：也许是在冲沙的时候被甩出了口袋，也许留在了营地的哪张椅子上。不知道它现在是被谁捡走了，还是正埋在哪座沙丘底下，慢慢跟着沙丘往前走。

回城的路上，迪拜的楼一栋一栋亮起来，高架上有送外卖的小哥骑着摩托从楼群前面开过去。从荒漠里开回来，再看这片灯，忽然想起下午那位“银手”，觉得迪拜还真有点像夜之城：一片荒原中间凭空长出来的城市，摩天楼、霓虹灯、满街的豪车，有钱人住在高处，撑起这一切的人住在城边。游戏里夜之城外面也是一片沙漠，叫恶土；银手的尸体，最终也被随意遗弃在了恶土油田。

[图]

[图]

只是这里没有义体，也没有荒坂塔。不过哈利法塔顶上要是真住着个荒坂三郎，我大概也不会太惊讶。

[图]
stories.textEn:
Drive east out of central Dubai and in less than an hour the towers are gone. First there are scattered warehouses and fences along the road, then nothing but sand, orange shading into red, combed by the wind into ripples like a sheet of silk that's been crumpled and smoothed out again.

This is one corner of the Arabian Desert. The dunes look still, but the wind keeps pushing them along: the windward side slopes gently, the leeward side drops steeply, and the crests are as sharp as if they'd been carved with a knife. In summer the days can hit forty-five degrees, and once the sun goes down the temperature falls fast. No trees, no water. Stare at it long enough and you start to feel the world is only sand and sky.

Before oil was discovered, the people who made a living out here were the Bedouin, nomadic Arab tribes who herded camels and goats, moved between wells and grazing land, and lived in black tents woven from animal hair. Camels were their lifeline: they carried loads, gave milk, and could walk for days without water. Falcons were their helpers, trained to catch hares and birds in the desert. The desert's rules come from those days too: a guest is a guest, even a stranger, and anyone who enters the tent is first offered coffee and dates.

Then came oil, and the Dubai of today. Most Emiratis have long since moved to the city and swapped camels for SUVs, but the desert never really left their lives: they still camp in the dunes in winter, raise and race camels, and the falcon is still a national symbol, with dedicated falcon hospitals and, so I've heard, its own seat on a plane.

We went to the desert on 21 November. In the morning we were still splashing around at Jumeirah Beach; in the afternoon we hired a car and a driver took us out of the city. The first stop was a meeting point on the edge of the desert, rows of 4x4s lined up waiting to head into the sand, snack stalls on the side, and men holding falcons for tourists to pose with. My travel buddy had a go too.

[图]

It was at this meeting point that I saw him. Shoulder-length black hair, aviator sunglasses, a goatee, all in white, what looked like a cigarette between his fingers, standing under the straw roof of a snack stall and giving me a cool, sideways look. In that moment only one name was in my head: Johnny Silverhand. The rocker-slash-terrorist from Cyberpunk 2077, the ghost living in the main character's head, the one Keanu Reeves plays. I grabbed my camera and fired off a few shots. Mine on the left, the one from the game on the right. You be the judge.

[图]

Once we were in the desert, the car first stopped on top of a high dune for the sunset. The dust filtered the sun into an orange-red dot that sank bit by bit behind the dunes, and the cars and people in the distance turned into little black specks.

[图]

Up on the dune we ran into a few Pakistani guys in white robes, ridiculously friendly, who pulled us in for group photos. In Dubai, even the people you meet in the desert are Pakistani. After the photos, one of them walked off to the crest of the dune and stood there with his hands behind his back, a cigarette between his fingers, watching the sun go down.

[图]

After sunset came the main event: dune bashing. The 4x4 charges up to the crest of a dune, hangs there for half a second, then the whole nose tips over and the car slides sideways down the slope, tilted so far you're sure it's about to roll. The driver couldn't have been calmer, one hand resting on the wheel, like he was driving to the supermarket. I sat in the back trying to film it, and what I got was mostly the roof and the back of the driver's head, with the dunes flashing past in one corner of the frame.

[图]

After the dune bashing the car stopped for a while outside a little shop on the edge of the desert. The sun had just set, which meant it was time for Maghrib, the sunset prayer. Two men in white robes spread a mat under the awning and prayed, a few cars parked beside them and a UAE flag flying in the distance. Muslims pray five times a day, and Maghrib comes right after sunset; when the time comes, you can roll out a mat wherever you are.

[图]

After dark we got to the camp. At the entrance there were men waiting with horses for the tourists, and one man in a white robe and a black head wrap, his arm around his horse's head under the lights, looked like an old photograph.

[图]

Dinner was at the camp, everyone seated around a stage in the middle, eating and watching the shows. First up was tanoura, a whirling dance that comes from Egypt and is related to the Sufi whirling ritual. The dancer wears several layers of huge, colourful skirts and spins on the spot, round and round, never seeming to get dizzy, lifting the skirts over his head one layer at a time. Then the lights went out, the skirts lit up, and he turned into a glowing spinning top.

[图]

Next was the fire show: a performer on the sand beyond the stage swinging balls of fire, sparks flying everywhere, the crowd taking a step back. Last was a belly dancer who came on wrapped in veils, and every phone in the place went up.

[图]

This was also the day I left my power bank in the desert. I looked for it everywhere afterwards and never found it; all I know is that it stayed somewhere out there. Maybe it got flung out of my pocket during the dune bashing, maybe it was left on a chair at the camp. I wonder whether someone picked it up, or whether it's buried under some dune, slowly travelling along with it.

On the drive back, Dubai's towers lit up one after another, and a delivery rider on a motorbike sped along the overpass in front of them. Coming in from the empty desert and looking at all those lights, I thought of the afternoon's Silverhand and realised Dubai really is a bit like Night City: a city that sprang out of nowhere in the middle of a wasteland, skyscrapers, neon and supercars everywhere, the rich living up high and the people holding it all up living on the edges. In the game, Night City is surrounded by desert too. They call it the Badlands.

[图]

In fact, the night before, I'd already stumbled onto a street that looked a lot like Night City: a glass roof overhead, neon signs hanging all along both sides, most of them in Chinese. At first glance it could have been Kabuki straight out of the game.

[图]

No cyberware here, of course, and no Arasaka Tower. But if Saburo Arasaka turned out to live at the top of the Burj Khalifa, I don't think I'd be all that surprised.

[图]

stories.title: 名人墓
stories.text:
十一月中旬，莫斯科下了那年的第一场雪。我早上先在麻雀山转了一圈，快十一点的时候走到了新圣女公墓。它就在新圣女修道院的南墙外面，俄罗斯的作家、艺术家、政治家很多都葬在这里。门口有地图，标着名人墓的位置，我就照着一个一个找过去。

[图]

进门没多远，就看到了叶利钦。他的墓不是一块碑，而是一面摊在地上、像被风吹皱了的俄罗斯国旗：白色的大理石，蓝色的马赛克，红色的石头。叶利钦是苏联解体以后俄罗斯的第一任总统，2007 年去世。那天上面落了一层薄雪，蓝色那一条被雪点得斑斑点点。

[图]

接着是果戈理，写《死魂灵》《钦差大臣》的那位。他原来葬在丹尼洛夫修道院，1931 年才迁到这里。墓上是一个金色十字架立在一块粗糙的黑石头上，石板最下面刻着《耶利米书》里的一句：“我将以我辛酸的话语发笑。”据说他原来墓上的那块黑石头，后来被挪去给了布尔加科夫当墓碑，因为布尔加科夫一辈子把果戈理当老师。

旁边不远是阿列克谢·尼古拉耶维奇·托尔斯泰。第一次看到“托尔斯泰”几个字母我还愣了一下，后来才反应过来不是列夫·托尔斯泰，列夫·托尔斯泰葬在他自己的庄园里。这位是苏联作家，写过《彼得大帝》和《苦难的历程》。墓碑是一整面浮雕，中间是他的侧脸，两边站着他书里的人物，最左边那个高个子就是彼得大帝。

[图]

然后是契诃夫。他的墓是白色的，顶上像个小尖屋顶，字体也是那个年代的老写法，“Антонъ Павловичъ Чеховъ”，名字最后还带着硬音符。左边那块棕色的是他父亲帕维尔的墓。契诃夫 1904 年死在德国，遗体是装在运牡蛎的冷藏车厢里运回莫斯科的，这件事听起来很像他自己会写的小说。

[图]

再往里走，到了赫鲁晓夫。这是我这一路最想看的一个。墓碑一半白色大理石、一半黑色花岗岩，互相咬在一起，中间夹着他的铜头像。设计者是雕塑家涅伊兹韦斯特内，1962 年赫鲁晓夫在展览上当众把他的作品骂得一文不值，结果赫鲁晓夫去世后，家里人请的正是他。黑和白，一般被解释成赫鲁晓夫这个人身上的功与过。

[图]

这一片有一排一排的将军，石碑上都顶着半身像，看着有点像在列队。我认得出名字的是米哈伊尔·格里戈里耶维奇·格里戈里耶夫，碑上写着上将、列宁奖获得者，再多的我就不知道了。

旁边是日里诺夫斯基，自由民主党那位，以在电视上吵架出名，2022 年去世。他是一座全身铜像，穿着长大衣，戴着帽子，两手背在后面站着，像在等人。墓前的花很新鲜，红的、白的，还有一束蓝色的。

[图]

最后找到的是戈尔巴乔夫。墓前立着的那个女人雕像是他的妻子赖莎，她 1999 年先走了，戈尔巴乔夫 2022 年去世，葬在了她旁边。石板上刻着“ГОРБАЧЕВЫ”，戈尔巴乔夫一家。花上面也积着雪。

一个上午走下来，感觉像翻了一遍俄罗斯的近代史，从果戈理、契诃夫一直到叶利钦和戈尔巴乔夫，前后隔了一百多年，现在都在同一片墙里面，隔着几条小路。

[图]

第二年七月在圣彼得堡，我又进了一座公墓。当时也不知道它叫什么，下着小雨，就跟着人走进去了。后来照着照片查，才知道那是亚历山大·涅夫斯基修道院里的拉扎列夫公墓，是圣彼得堡最古老的墓地，十八世纪的很多贵族和学者都葬在这里。入口那条路的对面是季赫温公墓，柴可夫斯基和陀思妥耶夫斯基葬在那边。

拉扎列夫公墓里我认出来的第一个，是数学家欧拉。红色花岗岩的石棺，正面用拉丁文刻着他的名字。他是瑞士人，大半辈子在彼得堡科学院工作，1783 年在这里去世，原来葬在别的公墓，二十世纪五十年代才迁过来。上数学课的时候天天见到这个名字，没想到会在这里碰上他本人。

旁边还有一个四根柱子撑着顶的石棺，上面趴着一个铜的哀悼者，名牌是空的，我没认出是谁。再往里走，看到一块绿色的十字碑，上面居然刻着汉字。查了才知道这是比丘林，俄罗斯早期的汉学家，在北京当过东正教传教团的团长，回国后写了很多关于中国的书。在彼得堡的墓地里看到中文，是那天最意外的事。
stories.textEn:
In mid-November, Moscow got its first snow of the year. I spent the early morning wandering around Sparrow Hills, and a little before eleven I walked over to Novodevichy Cemetery. It sits just outside the south wall of Novodevichy Convent, and a great many Russian writers, artists and politicians are buried there. There is a map at the entrance marking the famous graves, so I just went from one to the next. What follows is pretty much a log.

[图]

Not far from the gate was Yeltsin. His grave isn't a headstone at all but a Russian flag spread on the ground, rippling as if in the wind: white marble, blue mosaic, red stone. Yeltsin was Russia's first president after the Soviet Union fell apart, and he died in 2007. That day a thin layer of snow had settled on it, speckling the blue stripe.

[图]

Next came Gogol, the author of Dead Souls and The Government Inspector. He was first buried at the Danilov Monastery and moved here in 1931. His grave is a golden cross standing on a rough black rock, and at the bottom of the slab is a line from the Book of Jeremiah: "I shall laugh my bitter word." The story goes that the original black stone from his grave later ended up on Bulgakov's grave, since Bulgakov had always thought of Gogol as his teacher.

A little further on was Alexei Nikolayevich Tolstoy. Seeing the letters "Tolstoy" made me stop for a second before I realized it wasn't Leo Tolstoy, who is buried on his own estate. This one was a Soviet writer, author of Peter the First and The Road to Calvary. His monument is one big relief: his profile in the middle, characters from his books on either side, and the tall man on the far left is Peter the Great.

[图]

Then Chekhov. His grave is white, with a small pointed roof on top, and the lettering is the old pre-revolutionary spelling, "Антонъ Павловичъ Чеховъ", hard sign and all. The brown stone to the left belongs to his father, Pavel. Chekhov died in Germany in 1904, and his body was brought back to Moscow in a refrigerated railway car meant for oysters, which sounds like something he would have written himself.

[图]

Further in was Khrushchev, the one I most wanted to see. The monument is half white marble and half black granite, the two halves locked together with his bronze head between them. It was made by the sculptor Ernst Neizvestny, whose work Khrushchev had publicly torn apart at an exhibition in 1962. When Khrushchev died, his family asked Neizvestny to make the monument anyway. The black and white are usually read as the good and the bad in the man.

[图]

This part of the cemetery has row after row of generals, each headstone topped with a bust, so they look a bit like they're standing in formation. The only name I could make out was Mikhail Grigoryevich Grigoryev; the stone says colonel general and Lenin Prize laureate, and that's all I know.

Next to them is Zhirinovsky, the Liberal Democratic Party leader famous for shouting matches on TV, who died in 2022. He's a full-length bronze statue in a long coat and cap, hands clasped behind his back, as if waiting for someone. The flowers on the grave were fresh: red, white, and one bunch of blue.

[图]

The last one I found was Gorbachev. The statue of a woman standing over the grave is his wife Raisa. She died first, in 1999; Gorbachev died in 2022 and was buried next to her. The slab reads "ГОРБАЧЕВЫ", the Gorbachevs. There was snow on the flowers here too.

One morning there felt like flipping through modern Russian history, from Gogol and Chekhov all the way to Yeltsin and Gorbachev: more than a hundred years apart, and now all inside the same wall, a few paths from each other.

[图]

The next July, in Saint Petersburg, I wandered into another cemetery. I had no idea what it was called; it was drizzling and I just followed the people going in. Only later, going through the photos, did I work out that it was the Lazarevskoe Cemetery inside the Alexander Nevsky Lavra, the oldest cemetery in the city, where many eighteenth-century nobles and scholars are buried. Across the path from the entrance is the Tikhvin Cemetery, where Tchaikovsky and Dostoevsky lie.

The first person I recognized in Lazarevskoe was the mathematician Euler. A red granite sarcophagus, his name carved on the front in Latin. He was Swiss, spent most of his life working at the Saint Petersburg Academy of Sciences, and died here in 1783. He was originally buried in another cemetery and moved here in the 1950s. I'd seen his name in every other math class, and never expected to run into the man himself.

Nearby was a sarcophagus under a roof held up by four columns, with a bronze mourner lying on top. The name plate was blank and I couldn't tell whose it was. Further in I found a green cross-shaped headstone with Chinese characters on it. It turned out to be Bichurin, one of Russia's first sinologists, who headed the Orthodox mission in Beijing and wrote many books about China after he came home. Finding Chinese in a Petersburg cemetery was the biggest surprise of the day.
