stories.title: 被抬上救护车的那个早晨
stories.titleEn: The morning I left on a stretcher
stories.text:
那是一个再普通不过的早晨。醒来没多久，下腹部就传来一阵隐约的不适，说不上疼，只是闷闷的、沉沉的，像有什么东西在里面慢慢挪了一下位置。

这种感觉我太熟悉了。结合以往的经验，我几乎一下子就反应过来：肾结石又要犯了。最绝望的地方在于，明明知道接下来会发生什么，我却什么也做不了，只能等着它来。

它果然来了。不适变成了疼，疼又变成了剧痛，最后发展成严重的肾绞痛。这种疼常被拿来和分娩相比，而这已经是我第二次领教。坐不住，躺不下，怎么换姿势都没用，整个人只能蜷成一团，冷汗一层一层往外冒。

同学见状，赶紧叫了一辆网约车带我去医院。那段路不算远，却漫长得像没有尽头。我缩在后座上，疼得意识一阵阵发虚，窗外的街道长什么样，一点印象都没有了。

好不容易熬到下车，却发现那家医院因为太早了根本没开门。

没有别的办法，只能等。我在门口站也不是、坐也不是，一分一秒地熬。就在这时，我下意识去摸口袋：手机不见了。大概是刚才疼得太厉害，丢在了网约车上。

那一刻，整个人都要炸了。身体疼成这样，人在异国他乡，医院不开门，现在连手机也没了。好在同伴还算冷静，一边照顾我，一边想办法联系司机。语言不通，只能靠翻译软件加连比带划，来来回回不知道说了多少遍，费了九牛二虎之力，手机总算是拿了回来。

后来终于来了一位医生。我以为这下得救了，他却告诉我们：这里是一所大学的校医院，处理不了我这种情况。

又是一记重击。

最后是门卫给我们出了主意：叫救护车。他帮我们打了电话，没过多久救护车就到了，几个人把我抬上担架，送进车里。一针止痛剂打下去，疼痛像退潮一样慢慢散开，我躺在车里，才终于觉得自己又活了过来。

医生给我开了药，让我们自己去药店买。我们准备付钱，对方却摆摆手：一分钱也不用。后来才知道，在这里，急救本来就是免费的医疗服务。

就这样，第一次在俄罗斯看病，是被抬上救护车完成的。折腾了一整个早上，算是换来一条经验：下次有急事先叫救护车。
stories.textEn:
It was the most ordinary of mornings. Not long after I woke up, a faint discomfort started in my lower abdomen. Not pain exactly, just a dull, heavy feeling, as if something inside had quietly shifted.

I knew that feeling far too well. From past experience I understood almost at once: the kidney stone was back. The worst part was knowing exactly what was coming and being able to do nothing about it except wait.

And it came. The discomfort turned into pain, the pain into agony, and finally into full renal colic, the kind of pain often compared to childbirth. This was my second time. I couldn't sit, couldn't lie down, no position helped; all I could do was curl up while the cold sweat kept coming.

My classmate called a ride-hailing car and took me to the hospital. The drive wasn't long, but it felt endless. I was folded up in the back seat, drifting in and out, and I remember nothing of the streets outside.

When we finally got out, the hospital wasn't open.

There was nothing to do but wait. I couldn't stand and couldn't sit, just endured it second by second. That was when I reached into my pocket: my phone was gone. I must have dropped it in the car while I was doubled over.

In that moment I was ready to explode. In this much pain, in a foreign country, the hospital closed, and now no phone either. Luckily my friend kept a cool head, looking after me while trying to reach the driver. With no common language it took a translation app, a lot of gesturing and who knows how many rounds of back and forth, but against all odds we got the phone back.

Eventually a doctor turned up. I thought I was saved, but he told us this was a university's campus clinic and it couldn't handle a case like mine.

Another blow.

In the end it was the security guard who told us what to do: call an ambulance. He made the call for us, and before long it arrived. They lifted me onto a stretcher and into the back, gave me a shot of painkiller, and as the pain slowly ebbed away, lying there in the ambulance, I finally felt alive again.

The doctor wrote me a prescription to buy at a pharmacy. When we went to pay, he just waved us off: nothing to pay. Only later did we learn that emergency care here is simply free.

So my first time seeing a doctor in Russia happened on a stretcher in the back of an ambulance. A whole morning of chaos and a lot of cold sweat bought me one lesson: next time there's an emergency, don't run around. Call the ambulance first.

stories.title: 差点上了莫斯科电视
stories.text:
那天下午去了扎里亚季耶公园，走上那座悬在莫斯科河上空的观景廊桥。天阴着，桥下的河岸大街堵成一条长长的红色尾灯，对面就是克里姆林宫的红墙和金顶。我端着相机正准备拍，一个拿话筒的小哥走了过来，说他们是莫斯科的一个电视台，想采访我几句。

[图]

我愣了一下，就答应了。站好位置，背后是克里姆林宫，面前是一支话筒和一部架在稳定器上的手机，阵仗还挺像那么回事。

主持人的英语不太灵光，一个问题要拆成好几截说：来俄罗斯多久了？对俄罗斯印象怎么样？最喜欢这里的什么？我的英语也好不到哪去，于是就成了两个都不说母语的人，各自用蹩脚的英语，对着镜头艰难地交流。

最难说的是名词，脑子里明明有答案，一到嘴边就卡住：想夸地铁站修得像宫殿，「吊灯」「马赛克」全想不起来了；想说喜欢这里的老建筑和教堂的洋葱顶，「洋葱顶」英语到底怎么说？只好连比带划，拿形容词去凑名词，一个词绕三个弯。中文、俄语、英语在脑子里搅成一团，好几次说到一半，自己都想笑。对面的主持人倒是很配合，频频点头，像是全听懂了。也可能他也没全听懂，我们都很体贴地没有拆穿对方。

正当我渐入佳境，开始组织下一句的时候，一个警察走了过来。他跟主持人说这里不能采访。主持人解释了两句，还掏了工作证，都没用。话筒放下了，手机从稳定器上卸了下来，刚才还热热闹闹的采访现场，几秒钟就散了。好不容易憋出来的那几个英语单词，就这么被一位警察叔叔打断在了克里姆林宫跟前。

后来也就没有后来了。那半段采访最后有没有播出来、是哪个台哪个节目，我到现在也不知道。我还认真幻想过：某天晚上，莫斯科的某户人家打开电视，看到一个中国人对着镜头，用磕磕巴巴的英语夸他们的城市。
stories.textEn:
That afternoon I went to Zaryadye Park and walked out onto the viewing bridge that hangs over the Moskva River. The sky was grey, the embankment road below was one long ribbon of red tail lights, and right across from us stood the red walls and golden domes of the Kremlin. I had my camera up, about to take a shot, when a guy with a microphone walked over. He said they were from a Moscow TV channel and wanted to ask me a few questions.

[图]

I hesitated for a second, then said yes. I took my spot: the Kremlin behind me, a microphone in front of me, and a phone mounted on a gimbal. It looked surprisingly legit.

The host's English wasn't great, and each question came out in several pieces: How long have you been in Russia? What do you think of it? What do you like most here? My English wasn't much better. So there we were, two people neither of whom was speaking their own language, struggling through broken English in front of a camera.

The hardest part was the nouns. I knew exactly what I wanted to say, and then it would jam right before it left my mouth. I wanted to say the metro stations look like palaces. "Palace" was fine, but "chandelier" and "mosaic" were nowhere to be found. I wanted to say I loved the old buildings and the onion domes on the churches, but what on earth is "onion dome" in English? So I waved my hands around and stacked adjectives where the nouns should have been, taking three detours for every word. Chinese, Russian and English were all tangled up in my head, and more than once I nearly laughed at myself mid-sentence. The host was very supportive, nodding along as if he understood everything. Maybe he didn't either, and we were both kind enough not to call each other out.

Just as I was getting into it and putting together my next sentence, a police officer walked up. He said a few words to the host in Russian, roughly: you can't film interviews here. The host tried to explain. It didn't help. The microphone came down, the phone came off the gimbal, and within seconds the whole "interview set" had dissolved.

I stood there and completely lost it. All those English words I had squeezed out with such effort, cut off by a policeman right in front of the Kremlin.

And that was the end of it. Nobody left any contact details. Whether that half of an interview ever aired, which channel it was, which show, I still have no idea. I did seriously imagine it, though: some evening, a family somewhere in Moscow turns on the TV and sees a Chinese guy stumbling through English, praising their city.

I never made it onto Moscow TV. What I got instead was this one photo: me, a microphone, the Kremlin, and a police officer about to make his entrance.

stories.title: 第一笔稿费：250 卢布
stories.text:
[图]

玩摄影一年多，我给不知道多少人拍过照：有朋友、有同学，也有路上刚认识的陌生人。有人拍完急着要返图，有人摆摆手说不用了；也有人拍完提出要给我钱，我一次都没收过。

直到那天在阿尔巴特街。崔墙那边有个很经典的机位：一条窄窄的老街，尽头正对着外交部大楼的尖顶。我路过时，看见两个人举着相机在那儿拍，就凑过去问，能不能也帮我拍一张。

他们很爽快地答应了。可拍完一看，我不是很满意。想了想干脆问：要不我先给你们拍几张，做个示范？

[图]

结果他俩一看照片，立马高兴得不行，一个劲儿夸我拍得好，非要我返图，还坚持要给我钱。我推了好几次，实在拗不过，只好收下。就这样，我靠摄影赚到了第一笔钱：250 卢布。

返图之后，又被一顿夸，问我用的什么相机，问还有没有更多照片。说实话，真挺受用的，嘿嘿。

250 卢布不多，但这是第一次有人因为我拍的照片，心甘情愿地掏钱。
stories.textEn:
[图]

I had been shooting for a little over a year, and I had taken photos of more people than I could count: friends, classmates, strangers I had just met on the street. Some wanted the photos right away, some waved them off, and a few offered to pay me. I never took the money.

Then came a day on the Arbat. Near the Tsoi Wall there is a classic spot: a narrow old street that ends right at the spire of the Foreign Ministry building. Walking past, I saw two people with cameras shooting there, so I went over and asked if they would take one of me too.

They happily agreed. But when I looked at the result, I wasn't really happy with it. So I said: how about I take a few of you first, just to show what I mean?

[图]

The moment they saw the photos they lit up, kept saying how good they were, asked me to send them over, and insisted on paying me. I said no several times, but they wouldn't take no for an answer, so in the end I gave in. And that is how I earned my first money from photography: 250 rubles.

After I sent the photos, the praise kept coming: which camera did I use, did I have any more shots? Honestly, it felt pretty great, hehe.

250 rubles isn't much. But it was the first time someone gladly paid for a photo I had taken.

stories.title: 莫斯科遇见的两个人
stories.titleEn: Two people I met in Moscow
stories.text:
在莫斯科交换留学的那一年，我认识了两个给我留下很深印象的人。

他们的年龄、性格和人生经历都完全不同，一个是和我年纪相仿的女生，一个是四十多岁的大叔。但回头去看，这两段相遇却奇妙地缠绕在一起：他们让我感受到人与人之间关系的复杂，让我看到一个人的外在与内心之间可能有多大的距离，也让我第一次在别人身上，看清了自己。

## 一、在公园认识的女生

第一个人是一个和我年龄相仿的俄罗斯女生。当时我读大四，她读大三。

我们是在莫斯科华明公园里认识的，那是一个中国风格的小公园。那天我们都是一个人出来。她注意到我手里拿着相机，便主动走过来，问我能不能帮她拍几张照片。我给她拍完之后，她对照片非常满意，我们就互相加了 Instagram，之后慢慢聊了起来。

一开始只是普通的寒暄，但因为彼此之间有不少共同话题，交流很快变得深入，后来甚至聊到一些很私人、很内心的事情。

### 一个与我截然不同的人生

随着了解的加深，我发现她的人生经历非常丰富，和我相比，简直不在一个量级。

她从小就跟着父母到世界各地旅行，见过很多不同的国家和文化。对她来说，出国似乎是一件再平常不过的事情。

而我恰恰相反。如果不是后来有了出国留学的机会，我甚至觉得自己可能一辈子都不会走出国门。我的成长基本上是在学校、课堂、考试和各种学习任务中度过的：上学、刷题、考试、升学，一步一步，沿着一条早就画好的线走到了大学。

所以认识她之后，我能非常明显地感受到我们之间的差异。

她见识很广，接触过各种各样的人和文化，兴趣爱好也多得惊人。她学 K-pop，学过日本的忍术，家里摆着一堆忍具和武士刀；她对中国佛教很感兴趣，也很喜欢音乐。她还参加过一些政治运动，甚至因此被逮捕过。

她也是一个非常敢于表达自己的人。在公园里看到一个拿着相机的陌生人，她可以非常自然地走过来请对方帮自己拍照。她喜欢打扮自己，也很享受被别人欣赏的感觉，从不吝于展现自己的魅力。她身上有一种很强烈的自我表达的意识：愿意尝试不同的东西，也愿意主动去探索这个世界。

这些对当时的我来说，都很新鲜。

我感觉她的人生好像有无数种可能性，而我的人生在此前很长一段时间里，几乎只有一条既定的轨道。

### 以色列：她的第二故乡

她经常跟我说，她非常不喜欢俄罗斯，甚至可以说是讨厌这个国家，想要离开俄罗斯、逃离俄罗斯。这里面可能有政治上的原因，也有家庭的原因。

十七岁那年，她独自一人去了以色列留学，在那里度过了一段非常快乐、对她来说意义非凡的时光。她和另外几个女生住在一起，一起生活、学习，她一边在一家餐厅打工，一边上学。她们来自乌克兰、俄罗斯，背景各不相同，却组成了一个属于她们自己的小团体。

在她的讲述里，以色列早已不只是一个曾经留学过的国家，更像是她的第二故乡。那是她真正感到快乐、自由，能够按照自己的意愿生活的一段日子。即使后来离开了，她对那个地方依然有着很深的感情。

这段经历让我产生了很强的共鸣。

因为莫斯科对我来说，也是这样一个地方。

在莫斯科留学的这一年，可以说是我人生中最快乐的一段时光。我在这里认识了很多朋友，接触到了不同的文化和生活方式，也看到了很多此前从未想象过的人生可能。它在很大程度上改变了我看世界的方式，也让我开始重新思考，自己究竟想要怎样生活。

我们的成长背景截然不同，但都曾在离开熟悉的环境之后，在另一个国家短暂地拥有过一种不一样的人生。以色列之于她，大概就像莫斯科之于我。我想，这也是我们能够聊得那么深的原因之一。

### 丰富的外在，脆弱的内心

不过，随着交流越来越深入，我逐渐发现，她的精神状态并不像外表看起来那么好。

她给我的第一印象是一个非常正常、乐观、外向的人。但她自己说，她其实是一个非常敏感、很容易多想的人。后来她甚至告诉我，自己长期在接受心理咨询，也一直在服用相关的药物。

她的家庭关系也比较复杂。她说她的母亲控制欲很强，对她有着很强的掌控欲，这似乎也是她长期精神压力的来源之一。

有一次，她跟我讲了一件学校里的事。

她曾经被一个女生霸凌过。后来，两个人都到了另一所学校。到了新学校，她结识了新的朋友，慢慢有了自己的社交圈子；而那个曾经霸凌过她的女生却没什么朋友，处在被孤立的状态，于是也想加入她现在的朋友圈。

但她非常抗拒这一点，她不想让现有关系遭到破坏。问题在于，她的朋友圈里有一个比较神经大条的人。她说她曾经明确告诉过这个朋友，自己和那个女生过去有过一些不愉快，希望对方相处时注意一点，不要主动提起那些往事。对方当时答应了，但后来还是发生了摩擦。

我不确定那个朋友究竟是有意为之，还是单纯性格大大咧咧，没有意识到事情的严重性。但这件事让她非常焦虑。她害怕那个女生会因此和她起冲突，也担心自己的社交关系受到影响。她为这件事担心了很长时间，一次又一次地向我倾诉。

从这些事情里，我能明显感觉到，她的内心其实非常脆弱。

这和她给我的外在印象形成了巨大的反差。她可以主动和陌生人搭话，可以参加政治运动，可以到处旅行、接触各种各样的文化，看起来似乎什么都敢做；可与此同时，她又会因为朋友圈里的一点摩擦，反反复复地担忧很久。

她自己也跟我解释过：虽然在别人面前看起来非常外向，但那其实只是她戴上的一层面具，真正的她是比较内向的。

我不知道她对自己的判断是否完全准确，但至少在我看来，她确实是一个内心非常敏感的人。

而这一点，恰好让我产生了一种微妙的共鸣。因为我自己也是一个敏感、容易多想的人，只不过我的内向更加直接、更加明显；而她能在外部社交中表现得非常活跃，活跃到让人很难察觉她内心的脆弱。

我们在人生经历上几乎是两个极端，却在某些精神层面上，有着相似的地方。

### 一段没有继续下去的关系

我们曾经约出来见过一次面，相处得还不错。

后来有一天，她约我出去，我也答应了。

但奇怪的是，从答应之后，她就再也没有回应过我。我尝试主动联系她，她也像人间蒸发了一样，再没有任何实质性的回复。

这段关系，就这样莫名其妙地停了下来。

### 她让我看到的另一种可能

认识她之前，我在网上看到过一些关于东欧女性心理健康的讨论，有人把她们的精神困境归因于家庭环境、父权结构、家庭暴力，以及成长中积累下来的创伤。那时我对此嗤之以鼻，觉得不过是以偏概全的刻板印象。

认识她之后，我的感受确实变了。一个人的经历当然说明不了整个地区，但她让我第一次如此具体地看到：一个人可以拥有丰富多彩的外部世界，十几岁独自出国，在异国有过一段意义非凡的生活，参加过政治运动，兴趣广泛、见多识广；可这些并不一定能变成内心的安全感和幸福感。

我曾以为自己的人生已经有了一条相对明确的轨迹，认识她之后才知道，原来有人从十几岁起就在过一种完全不同的人生。而这样一个人，内心却可能和我一样敏感、脆弱、容易多想。

## 二、在网上认识的大叔

第二个人是一个四十多岁的俄罗斯男人。

我们是在网上认识的。刚开始聊天也就两三个小时，他便主动约我出来见面。我当时其实有些顾虑，但脑子一热，还是答应了。于是当天，我们就在一家咖啡厅见了面。

原本还有些担心，但真正见面之后，我发现他是一个非常好相处的人。

他来自克里米亚，妥妥的莫斯科社会里的精英阶层，事业和经济条件都相当不错，看起来已经实现了财富自由。他去过很多国家旅行，尤其熟悉中国，光是中国就去过十多次。

他给我的印象非常深刻：成熟、稳重、有主见，思想也很有深度。和他聊天，能明显感受到他的人生阅历，以及他看待事物时的那种从容和豁达。

他对我也非常包容。我们见面的那段时间，他经常请我去咖啡厅，也送过我不少礼物。

[图]

他还给我看过自己二十多岁时的照片。照片里的他意气风发，充满活力。而现在的他虽然已经四十多岁，看起来却依然非常年轻，我一度以为他只有三十多岁。

不过，他的人生似乎也有一些不为人知的故事。

聊天时，他曾隐约提到过，自己的家庭经历并不幸福，似乎发生过一些比较悲剧性的事情。但他没有展开，只说以后有机会、时间合适的时候，再慢慢告诉我。

新年的时候，我问他是不是和家人一起过节。他说会和姐姐一起过，姐姐住在莫斯科郊外。

我没有继续追问。但从他的描述里，我隐约感觉到，他可能已经没有父母，也没有自己的家庭。我不知道他究竟经历过什么，只能感觉到，他的人生背后，藏着一些不太愉快的往事。

然而，这些经历似乎并没有让他失去对生活的热情。

### 一个我非常向往的人生样本

后来回想起来，这个大叔最吸引我的，可能不只是他的性格和阅历，而是他整个人的生活状态。某种程度上，他就是我非常想要成为的那种人。

他没有结婚，也没有子女，不需要按照传统的家庭轨迹去安排人生。他有自己的事业，经济上相当自由，可以自己决定做什么、去哪里、怎样生活。虽然一个人住，他却一点也不与世隔绝：经常主动去找朋友，也会在网上认识各种有趣的人，再约出来聊聊。像我这样一个刚认识不久的外国年轻人，他也愿意花时间来往。

他的英语完全是自学的，口语已经非常接近母语者，这一点让我相当佩服。

当然，他的身体并不算好。工作很忙，又有胃病，平时看起来多少有些疲惫。但即便如此，他整个人给我的感觉依然非常积极向上：清楚自己想要什么，也有能力按自己的意愿安排生活。一个人生活，但并不孤独；经济自由，但没有停止探索；经历过不愉快的事，却依然在用心经营自己的日子。

他身上还有一种难得的成熟和稳定。有时候仅仅是和他坐在咖啡厅里聊天，我就会不自觉地被吸引进去：他说话的方式，思考问题的角度，对生活的态度，都很有魅力。

以前，我对未来的想象只是一些模糊的概念：经济自由、环游世界、过自己的生活、不受太多约束。是他让我发现，这些东西真的可以组合成一种真实存在的活法：不以结婚、生子、买房、按部就班地工作为必经的节点，而是以自己的意愿为中心，决定如何分配时间、金钱和精力，如何与这个世界建立联系。

我想要的，不是拥有他的财富或旅行经历，而是成为像他这样的人：既不依赖别人来定义自己的人生，也不因为一个人生活而感到匮乏。

## 三、一次没有好好结束的告别

后来，我和这个大叔的联系逐渐中断了。

那时正好临近毕业，我被毕业论文压得喘不过气；与此同时，过年期间的各种社交和旅行，也消耗了我大量的精力。

那段时间，我开始不太想回消息。起初只是拖几天，后来拖得越来越久。等到我意识到自己已经很久没有回复他的时候，反而产生了一种心理负担：不知道该怎么重新开口，也觉得自己已经没有脸面再去面对他。

于是，我没有做任何解释，也没有好好告别，就这样主动中断了联系。

现在回想起来，我非常后悔，也很内疚。因为我突然意识到，我对他做的事，正是当初那个女生对我做过的事。她在邀约我之后突然消失，让我困惑了很久；而后来，我却在另一个人身上重复了几乎一样的行为。

也许我们真的有些相似：都不是有意要伤害谁，只是在某些时候，被自己的状态、情绪或生活里的压力压着，选择了逃避沟通，最终让一段关系在没有任何解释的情况下结束了。

但两段关系留给我的感受并不一样。对那个女生，更多的是困惑和遗憾；对这个大叔，更多的是内疚。他一直对我很好，给了我很多善意，我却连一个简单的交代都没有给他。我失去的也不只是一个对我很好的朋友，还是一个我视为未来榜样的人。他说过以后再慢慢告诉我的那些往事，我大概再也没有机会听到了。

## 四、这两段经历留给我的

人与人的相遇有时真的很偶然。一台相机，几个小时的聊天，就可能开始一段意想不到的交流。

而我们往往并不了解一个人的全部。一个开朗外向的人，可能长期独自承受着心理上的痛苦；一个成熟从容的人，背后也可能有不愿提起的往事。我们能看到的，只是对方愿意展现的那一部分。

那个大叔还让我明白，向往的生活并不需要永远精力充沛、一帆风顺。他也有自己的疲惫和伤痛，却依然把日子过得很好。这一点对我的触动尤其大。

另一方面，我也看清了自己：我会因为疲惫而逃避，会因为拖延而错过重新联系的时机，又因为不知道如何面对自己的过失，最终选择彻底消失。但这不代表我不珍惜那些对我好的人。恰恰是因为还记得他们，才会对没有好好结束的关系感到遗憾。

有些人只在生命里出现很短的一段时间，但他们确实真实地参与过我的生活。我怀念的，不只是一个曾经认识的朋友，也是那个曾经的我。

而有时候，真正让人遗憾的，并不是一段关系没有继续下去，而是它本来可以有一个更好的结束方式。
stories.textEn:
During my exchange year in Moscow, I met two people who left a deep mark on me.

They could hardly have been more different in age, personality and life story: one was a Russian girl about my age, the other a Muscovite in his forties. Looking back, though, the two encounters are strangely intertwined. They showed me how complicated relationships between people can be, how far apart someone's outside and inside can lie, and, for the first time, they let me see myself clearly in someone else.

## I. The Russian girl I met in a park

The first was a Russian girl close to my age. I was in my fourth year of university; she was in her third.

We met in a small Chinese-style park in Moscow. I can no longer quite remember its name; something like Minghua Park, or Huaming Park. We had both come out alone that day. She noticed the camera in my hands, walked over and asked if I could take a few pictures of her. She was delighted with them, we followed each other on Instagram, and gradually we started talking.

It began as small talk, but we had a lot in common, and our conversations quickly deepened until we were talking about very personal, inner things.

### A life utterly unlike mine

The more I learned about her, the more I realized how rich her life had been. Next to mine, it was on another scale entirely.

Since childhood she had travelled the world with her parents and seen many countries and cultures. Going abroad seemed the most ordinary thing in the world to her.

I was the exact opposite. If I hadn't later had the chance to study abroad, I sometimes think I might never have left my country at all. I grew up in schools, classrooms, exams and endless assignments: go to school, drill practice problems, sit exams, move up, step by step along a line drawn long in advance, all the way to university.

So once I got to know her, the difference between us was impossible to miss.

She had seen a great deal, met all kinds of people and cultures, and had an astonishing range of interests. She was learning K-pop, had studied Japanese ninjutsu, and kept a pile of ninja gear and katanas at home. She was fascinated by Chinese Buddhism and loved music. She had also taken part in political protests, and had even been arrested for it.

She was someone who dared to express herself. Seeing a stranger with a camera in a park, she could walk right up and ask him to photograph her. She loved dressing up, enjoyed being admired, and never hesitated to show her charm. She had a strong urge for self-expression: willing to try different things, willing to go out and explore the world.

All of this was new to me at the time.

Her life seemed to hold countless possibilities, while mine, for a very long time, had had only one set track.

### Israel, her second home

She once told me that she really disliked Russia, even hated it. She often talked about wanting to leave, to escape. Some of that was probably political, and some of it about her family.

At seventeen she went to Israel to study on her own, and spent a very happy and meaningful time there. She shared a home with a few other girls, living and studying together, while she worked in a restaurant alongside her classes. They came from Ukraine and Russia, from different backgrounds, yet formed a little group of their own.

In the way she told it, Israel was no longer just a country where she had once studied; it was more like her second home. It was the time in her life when she had truly felt happy and free, able to live as she wished. Even after she left, she kept a deep attachment to the place.

That struck a strong chord with me.

Because Moscow is that kind of place for me.

This year in Moscow has been one of the happiest times of my life. I made many friends here, encountered different cultures and ways of living, and saw possibilities in life I had never imagined. It changed the way I see the world, and made me start to rethink how I actually want to live.

Our backgrounds could not have been more different, but we had both, after leaving everything familiar, briefly lived a different life in another country. Israel was to her roughly what Moscow is to me. I think that was one of the reasons we could talk so deeply.

### A rich outside, a fragile inside

But as our conversations went deeper, I gradually saw that her state of mind was not as good as it looked.

My first impression was of a perfectly normal, optimistic, outgoing person. She herself said, though, that she was actually very sensitive and prone to overthinking. Later she told me she had been in therapy for a long time and was on medication.

Her family situation was complicated, too. She said her mother was extremely controlling, and that seemed to be one of the sources of her long-running stress.

Once she told me about something at school.

A girl had bullied her. Later, both of them transferred to another school. At the new school she made new friends and slowly built a circle of her own, while the girl who had bullied her had hardly any friends, was left isolated, and wanted to join her circle.

The trouble was that one person in her circle was rather oblivious. She said she had told this friend plainly that she and that girl had a painful history, and asked the friend to be careful and not bring up the past. The friend agreed, but friction broke out anyway.

I can't say whether the friend did it on purpose or was simply careless and didn't grasp how serious it was. But it made her extremely anxious. She was afraid the girl would turn on her, and worried about what it would do to her friendships. She fretted over it for a long time, and came back to me about it again and again.

From things like this, I could clearly feel how fragile she really was inside.

It was a striking contrast with the impression she gave. She could strike up a conversation with strangers, join political protests, travel everywhere and immerse herself in all kinds of cultures, as if there were nothing she wouldn't dare to do; and yet a little friction in her circle of friends could keep her worrying for ages.

She explained it to me herself: although she looked very outgoing in front of others, that was just a mask she wore; the real her was rather introverted.

I don't know whether she judged herself entirely accurately, but to me, at least, she was clearly someone with a very sensitive heart.

And that struck a subtle chord in me. I am sensitive and prone to overthinking too; it's just that my introversion is more direct and obvious, whereas she could be so lively socially that it was hard to notice how fragile she was underneath.

In life experience we were almost opposite extremes, and yet on some level of the mind we were alike.

### A relationship that didn't go on

We met up in person once, and it went well.

Then one day she asked me out, and I said yes.

But strangely, from then on she never replied to me again. When I tried to reach her, she seemed to have vanished into thin air, with no real answer ever coming back.

And so the relationship simply stopped, inexplicably.

### Another possibility she showed me

Before I met her, I had come across online discussions about the mental health of Eastern European women, with some people blaming their struggles on family environment, patriarchal structures, domestic violence and trauma built up while growing up. At the time I scoffed at it as a sweeping stereotype.

After meeting her, I did feel differently. One person's story says nothing about a whole region, of course, but she showed me more concretely than ever that someone can have a vivid outer world, going abroad alone as a teenager, a life overseas that meant everything to her, political protests, wide interests and broad horizons, and none of it necessarily turns into inner security or happiness.

I used to think my life already had a fairly clear trajectory. Meeting her, I learned that some people have been living a completely different life since their teens. And someone like that could be just as sensitive, fragile and prone to overthinking inside as I am.

## II. The Moscow man I met online

The second was a Russian man in his forties.

We met online. We had been chatting for only two or three hours when he suggested meeting up. I had my doubts, but on an impulse I said yes, and that same day we met in a café.

I had been a little worried, but once we actually met, I found him very easy to be around.

He was from Crimea and could fairly be called part of Moscow's elite. His career and finances were excellent; he seemed to have reached financial freedom. He had travelled to many countries and knew China especially well, having been there more than ten times.

He made a strong impression on me: mature, steady, independent-minded, a deep thinker. Talking with him, you could clearly feel his experience of life, and the calm, open-hearted way he looked at things.

He was also very generous with me. During the time we saw each other, he often took me to cafés and gave me quite a few presents. These were his New Year gifts to me.

[图]

He once showed me photos of himself in his twenties, full of drive and energy. Even now, in his forties, he still looked remarkably young; for a while I thought he was only in his thirties.

Still, his life seemed to hold stories no one else knew.

When we talked, he once hinted that his family history had not been a happy one, that something rather tragic had happened. But he didn't go into it, saying only that when there was a chance, when the time was right, he would tell me slowly.

At New Year I asked whether he would celebrate with his family. He said he would spend it with his sister, who lives outside Moscow.

I didn't press further. But from what he said, I had a vague sense that he no longer had parents, and had no family of his own. I don't know what he went through; I could only feel that behind his life lay some unhappy past.

And yet none of it seemed to have taken away his passion for life.

### A sample of the life I long for

Thinking back, what drew me to him most may not have been his personality or experience, but his whole way of living. In a way, he was exactly the kind of person I want to become.

He had never married and had no children, and didn't need to arrange his life along a traditional family track. He had his own career and real financial freedom, and could decide for himself what to do, where to go and how to live. Though he lived alone, he was anything but cut off: he often sought out friends and met interesting people online for a chat. Even a young foreigner like me, whom he had only just met, was someone he was willing to spend time on.

He had taught himself English entirely on his own, and his spoken English was close to a native speaker's, which impressed me a great deal.

Of course, his health wasn't great. His work was demanding, he had a stomach condition, and he often looked a little tired. Even so, he came across as thoroughly positive: he knew what he wanted and had the means to arrange his life his own way. Living alone, but not lonely; financially free, but still exploring; having been through unhappy things, yet still carefully building his days.

He also had a rare maturity and steadiness. Sometimes just sitting in a café talking with him, I would be drawn in without noticing: the way he spoke, the angles from which he thought, his attitude to life, all of it was compelling.

Before, my picture of the future was a set of vague ideas: financial freedom, travelling the world, a life of my own, few constraints. He showed me that these things can come together into a real way of living, one that doesn't treat marriage, children, buying a home and a step-by-step career as required milestones, but is centred on one's own wishes: deciding how to spend time, money and energy, and how to connect with the world.

What I want isn't his wealth or his travels, but to become a person like him: not relying on others to define my life, and not feeling lacking for living alone.

## III. A goodbye that never happened

Later, my contact with him gradually broke off.

It was right before graduation, and my thesis was crushing me. At the same time, all the socialising and travel around New Year drained a great deal of my energy.

During that time I stopped wanting to reply to messages. At first I just put it off for a few days; then longer and longer. By the time I realised how long it had been since I had answered him, it had turned into a weight on me: I didn't know how to start again, and felt I no longer had the face to meet him.

So without any explanation, without a proper goodbye, I cut off contact myself.

Looking back now, I deeply regret it and feel guilty. Because it suddenly dawned on me that what I did to him was exactly what that girl had done to me. She vanished after asking me out and left me confused for a long time; later I repeated almost the same thing with someone else.

Perhaps we really were alike: neither of us meant to hurt anyone, but at certain moments, weighed down by our state of mind, our emotions or the pressures of life, we chose to avoid talking, and in the end let a relationship end without any explanation.

But the two leave me with different feelings. With her, it is mostly confusion and regret; with him, mostly guilt. He was always good to me and showed me so much kindness, and I didn't give him even a simple explanation. What I lost wasn't only a friend who treated me well, but someone I saw as a model for my future. The past he said he would tell me about some other time, I will probably never get to hear.

## IV. What these two encounters left me

There is so much chance in how people meet. A camera, a few hours of chatting, and an unexpected connection can begin.

And we rarely know the whole of anyone. A cheerful, outgoing person may be carrying long-term pain alone; a calm, mature one may have a past they would rather not talk about. What we see is only the part they choose to show.

He also taught me that the life I long for doesn't require being always energetic and lucky. He had his own tiredness and old wounds, and still lived well. That moved me more than anything.

At the same time, I saw myself more clearly: I run away when I'm tired, miss the moment to reconnect because I procrastinate, and, not knowing how to face my own mistakes, end up disappearing completely. But that doesn't mean I don't treasure the people who were good to me. It's precisely because I still remember them that I regret the relationships that didn't end well.

Some people are in your life only briefly, but they really were part of it. What I miss is not only a friend I once knew, but also who I was back then.

And sometimes the real regret is not that a relationship didn't go on, but that it could have ended in a better way.
